> ### THE ROUND 0.5 ACCEPTANCE THEOREM WAS FALSE IN THE TREE THAT PUBLISHED IT.
>
> ```
> NO R2, NO POSTGRESQL:
>   local HTTP server + the REAL global fetch  ->  AuthoritativeR2Sweep  true
>   registerLedgerConnection({}) + any query   ->  AuthoritativeLedger   true
>                                              ->  absenceEstablished    true
>                                              ->  a delete refusal emitted
> ```
>
> Round 0.5 published *"no R2 and no PostgreSQL means absence can never be
> established"* and verified it by re-running ONE attack — the injected transport
> — from the shipped tar. The reviewer ran a different one. Nothing about that
> check was wrong; what was wrong was concluding a universal from an instance, in
> a round whose entire subject was the difference between having evidence and
> having a shape that looks like evidence.
>
> **A THEOREM VERIFIED AGAINST ONE ATTACK IS AN EXAMPLE.** The acceptance battery
> is now five separate tests, one per clause, each carrying the reproduction that
> falsified its predecessor.

> ### THE PROGRESSION, AND WHERE THIS ROUND SITS ON IT.
>
> ```
>   shape of evidence
>         -> protocol that earns evidence            8.3 / 8.4
>         -> authenticated operation                 8.5
>         -> IDENTITY OF THE AUTHORITY THAT ANSWERED     <- 8.6
>         -> identity of the SUBJECT it answered about   <- 8.6
>         -> stable snapshot / version it belongs to     <- 8.6
> ```
>
> A signature authenticates the request to WHOEVER OWNS THE ENDPOINT — and
> `endpoint` was a caller argument, so an ordinary local HTTP server reached by
> the real `fetch` earned the brand. On the database side the brand proved one
> object had been registered while the rows came through a different object
> entirely. And `txid_current()` was being called a snapshot: PostgreSQL's
> DEFAULT isolation is READ COMMITTED, under which *"two successive SELECT
> commands can see different data ... within a single transaction"*, while the
> transaction id is stable across exactly that.
>
> **A REAL NETWORK IS NOT A PROVIDER. AN AUTHORITY TOKEN AND AN OBSERVATION ARE
> NOT CONNECTED MERELY BECAUSE THE SAME FUNCTION RECEIVED BOTH ARGUMENTS. AN
> ISOLATION LEVEL YOU EXPECT IS NOT ONE YOU HAVE.**

> ### SIX OF THIS ROUND'S OWN VECTORS SCORED MISSED BEFORE THEY SCORED CAUGHT.
>
> Every one for the same reason: the property was real and nothing could observe
> it. `native-fetch-to-non-r2-endpoint` because no test asserted
> `endpointVerified`; `r2-lister-A-mints-sweep-B` because the capability no
> longer exposes a lister to rebind; `registered-connection-plus-unrelated-query`
> because the parameter it re-introduces had been deleted outright.
>
> **A GUARD WHOSE VIOLATION CANNOT BE CONSTRUCTED IS NOT VERIFIED — IT IS
> UNTESTED.** Making a defect unrepresentable is the right fix, and it silently
> retires the test that proved the defect existed.
>
> Three were closed by sharpening tests and three by making the code MORE
> expressible: the ledger adapter takes an options object specifically so that
> *"it ignores a caller-supplied query"* is a line a vector can break. Third
> consecutive round in which the battery caught the round's own fixes blinding
> its own evidence.

## 0a. What this round says about instruments

**A lesson written next to a hand-maintained list does not maintain the list.**
Finding 104's copy list sat directly under a comment block explaining that an
evidence package must reproduce its own evidence — written after the same defect
one round earlier. The generator now *executes* the artifact it produced. It
went red immediately, on a second staging list nobody had thought about.

**A law closed for one resource is not closed.** Finding 91 ruled that an
attestation's subject must be the runtime's subject, and fixed the queue. Three
more subjects then arrived from the caller's environment, one of them under the
exact variable name finding 91 deleted, in a file citing finding 91. The fix
that generalises is a shape, not a rule: there is one derivation and the gates
cannot express the other option.

**"Complete" is not a boolean a response carries.** Finding 107 is the round's
most transferable result.  is a true statement about a page
that says nothing about a bucket, and reading it as completeness produced a gate
that alleged deletion of objects it had itself just enumerated. Completeness is
an epistemic fact earned by a protocol — start at the beginning, verify every
cursor, terminate normally — and it now has a type that only that protocol can
mint.

**The mutation battery keeps holding, and this round it caught the fixes.** Its
current tally is **139 vectors, 139 caught** — DERIVED from the run
captured in §2, not typed here. FINDING 126: this paragraph used to type
`84 vectors, 84 caught`, which was true one round earlier and was still being
published beside an artifact identity that said 93. That is finding 119 again in
the same document — a derived number sitting next to the variable that derives
it — so the numbers are now interpolated and the generator refuses to publish a
current-section count that disagrees with the battery.

## 0b. What we could not settle, and what is checkable now

**`message_id` absorbs redelivery only if the id is STABLE across attempts.**
Cloudflare documents `Message.id` as "a unique, system-generated ID for the
message" and `attempts` as consumer processing attempts — but does not say the
id survives a retry, and documents no cross-queue uniqueness scope either.
Because **R2 is the producer**, the documented remedy for at-least-once —
"generate a unique ID when writing the message and use it as an idempotency
key" — is unavailable to us. **An unstable id duplicates PROVENANCE; it does not
double-charge the ledger** (finding 75, GPT's correction to us: the charge is
`v_after - v_prior` under the row lock, so 100→100 is zero, pinned by check
K43). Falsifier case **E** measures stability; the cross-queue half is case **J**.

**The provisioning half of R77 is PROPOSED, not measured.** Nothing has
enumerated a real queue's producers, because no account exists. That is live
case **P**. `scripts/check-queue-authority.mjs` exits **2** — not 0 — when it has
no credentials, so a CI job that forgot them cannot report the property as held.

**The run order is DERIVED, not typed here** (finding 111). It is
`status.json`'s `falsifier_order`, read from the falsifier's exported
`SEQUENCE`, which the falsifier itself cross-checks against its own case list:

```
S -> Q -> P -> P2 -> H -> A -> D -> D2 -> F -> G -> I -> B -> C -> E -> J -> N
```

**The subjects those cases attest come from the DEPLOYED WORKER, not the caller
and not the manifest** — `resolveLiveSubjects()` reads
`GET /accounts/{a}/workers/scripts/{name}/settings`, requires exact agreement
with `worker/wrangler.toml`, and returns the deployed values; `worker/topology.json`
says what those resources must be. Both files are in this bundle.

> **FINDING 131.** The two paragraphs that stood here said
> `deploymentSubjects()` still reads the file, cited the wrong endpoint
> (`/bindings`, where the implementation uses `/settings`), and said *"Case Q's
> VPC-service endpoint is not confirmed"* — all three closed by findings 114,
> 121 and 127, two of them in the very round that shipped this section. Finding
> 126's fix interpolates COUNTS, and a count is the easy case:
>
> **A DERIVED NUMBER CAN BE CHECKED MECHANICALLY. A STALE PROPOSITION HAS TO BE
> DERIVED OR DELETED.**
>
> These were deleted. `check-status-prose.mjs` was green throughout, because a
> lexical gate cannot know that a sentence stopped being true.

Separately, the docs get most of the way to one-message-per-event by forbidding
the **configuration**: overlapping or conflicting notification rules are not
allowed. That makes single-notification an obligation on OUR rule set, checked at
provisioning — not a provider guarantee we may assume. **That sentence has been
in this bundle for two rounds and was not a check** (finding 99). It is one now:
case **P2**, which requires exactly one rule to our queue and refuses a set that
merely covers jointly, because proving an arbitrary rule set equivalent to the
intended one is a harder claim than provisioning the one rule that plainly is it.

**Whether ambiguity is reachable at all decides whether it needs a migration.**
Finding 97 established that a listing repair cannot settle a tied tip: applied at
the same provider instant, the tip still holds two distinct `(etag, size)`
pairs. The honest representation — direct provider state ranked above an
unordered notification set — is a schema change, and `0027` is frozen. **Case J
decides whether it is ever needed.** If tied provider instants are unreachable in
practice, nothing gets built; if they occur, this is the one thing so far that
would justify a post-freeze migration. Manufacturing `T + 1ms` is refused — that
is inventing provider chronology, which is exactly what R75 declined to do.

**R17 has never been attested and could not have been.** Hyperdrive's SQL
response cache is configured on the CONFIGURATION, not the binding, so it appears
in no file in this repository. Live case **Q** is the first instrument that can
read it. Note the default: `caching.disabled` is **not required** and defaults
to **false**, so an absent field means the cache is ON (finding 101).

**Two things case Q still will not buy.** `origin.password` is write-only and
the API never returns it, so Q proves which user each configuration NAMES and
never that the two secrets differ — only the privilege witness through each
connection (`current_user`; request credential cannot `EXECUTE`
`app.observe_storage_object()`; jobs credential can) proves the grant, and that
needs the driver. And in the VPC-service topology TLS cannot be configured on the
Hyperdrive at all; `sslmode` would have to be pinned on the VPC Service
(finding 102).

**And a first-party contradiction worth a live experiment.** Cloudflare's S3
compatibility table lists `Content-MD5` for `PutObject` and **no SHA-256
checksum header**; the R2 release notes, dated **2023-06-16**, say S3
`putObject` gained sha256 and sha1 checksum support. One page is stale and no
amount of re-reading settles which. Case **B** is three signings —
`Content-MD5`, `x-amz-checksum-sha256`, `Content-Length` — because if the
second works we bind **the same SHA-256 the chunk is already named by** and MD5
never enters the design.

## H-0 (round 4.1). Ambiguity accounting and channel admission

**M2.0 round 4.1 — ambiguity accounting and channel admission.** `0027`, plus the
Worker's first `queue()` handler. Every defect below was **reproduced against the
shipped tree before it was fixed**; two of them were reproduced by the reviewer
first and confirmed here.

> ### THE ROUND'S SHAPE, WHICH IS THE MOST USEFUL THING IN IT.
>
> ```
> 86   ambiguity  ->  crossing into  ->  the quota partition
> 87   ambiguity  ->  crossing into  ->  the Worker adapter
> 89   channel provenance  ->  crossing into  ->  admission
> ```
>
> Three of four are the same shape: **a new invariant meeting a boundary that
> predates it.** Not a foundation wobbling — R75 and R77 are both intact and
> both were applied incompletely. **A NEW INVARIANT IS NOT FINISHED WHEN THE
> MIGRATION THAT STATES IT APPLIES.** Where to look next is therefore a
> searchable question rather than a hope: wherever the newest rule meets older
> code.

### H-0a (round 4.1). Two laws that round was about

**A GATE THAT CAN ONLY BE EXERCISED IN PRODUCTION IS A GATE NOBODY EXERCISES.**
Finding 88 is the sharpest thing here. `check-queue-authority.mjs` carried a
correct doctrine in its header — *it refuses rather than passes when it cannot
see* — and violated it three lines from the assertion, because nothing could
run it: the whole file only executed when someone had a Cloudflare account, and
nobody does. The fix that matters is not the stricter predicate. It is that the
judgement was **extracted from the I/O and became a pure function**, at which
point fifteen falsifiers fit around it and the reviewer's two reproducers became
the first two tests.

**ABSENCE IS NOT PERMISSION.** Finding 89's subtler half: a consumer with no
attested channel refuses everything, including the right queue. Almost every
system that has had this bug read *no rule configured* as permissive.

And one instrument note. `queue-authority.test.mjs` imports
`../../scripts/check-queue-authority.mjs`, while `sabotage.sh` copied `src/` and
`test/` into a FLAT temp dir — so the import resolved outside the copy and the
baseline failed. **It refused to run rather than scoring 54 CAUGHT against an
already-broken suite**, which is the baseline guard added two rounds ago doing
precisely its job. The stage now mirrors the repository layout.


## H-0 (round 4). Provider order and the authority channel

**M2.0 round 4 — provider order and the authority channel.** `0026`. Every
defect below was **reproduced against the shipped tree before it was fixed**, and
one hypothesis of my own was **refuted** by the same method and is recorded as
such.

> ### THE SAME TWO PROVIDER FACTS PRODUCED TWO DIFFERENT TRUTHS.
>
> ```
> two genuine writes to one key, IDENTICAL eventTime
>
>     key    delivered   projected etag   projected size
>     tie1   A -> B      "B"              20
>     tie2   B -> A      "A"              10
>
>     committed_bytes charged for the pair:  30
> ```
>
> 30 is neither order-independent answer. The staleness guard is
> `p_event_time >= so.last_event_at`, which is sound below and silent at
> equality — where `>=` is true and the last delivered wins. Cloudflare
> documents `eventTime` as when the action occurred, at millisecond resolution,
> and nowhere as a sequence number.
>
> **A PROJECTION OF A SET OF OBSERVATIONS IS A FUNCTION OF THE SET, NOT OF THE
> ORDER WE SAW THEM IN.** R68 exists to say occupancy is the provider's number;
> at equality it was still ours.

| | Finding | Where |
|---|---|---|
| 82 | 🔴 **Equal `eventTime` made occupancy delivery-order dependent.** O5 could not see it — O5 varies which event is *older*, and this is the case where neither is | `0026` / **R75**; the projection is DERIVED from the observation set (`app.project_object_state()`). A tied tip with disagreeing state is `ambiguous_event_at`, `etag` and `current_observation_id` **NULL**, quota at `max(size)`. Checks **O23/O23b/O28**, live case **J** |
| 83 | 🟠 **R74's claim was stronger than the schema's proof of it.** The FK said *some* observation; nothing said it was **this intent's** or that the copied clocks were **its** clocks. The write-once trigger only refuses a *second* assignment | `0026` / **R76**; a four-column composite FK with the intent's own primary key as column 2. Checks **O24/O25** |
| 84 | 🟠 **"R2 is authoritative" meant "anything in this Queue is trusted as R2."** Cloudflare: *"Any Worker can write to a queue."* The body carries no signature and no event id. And `Message.id` is documented unique with **no stated cross-queue scope** | `0026` / **R77**; identity is `(queue_name, message_id)`. `CLOUD_V1.md` §6.8 rules the dedicated channel; `scripts/check-queue-authority.mjs` **checks** it — live case **P**, before D. Checks **O26/O27** + 3 Node tests |
| 85 | 🟡 **This bundle contradicted itself in three places** | This section, rewritten from the tree; superseded narrative moved under `<details>` |

### H-0a (round 4). Three things that round found about its own instruments

**A refuted hypothesis is worth the same shelf space as a confirmed one.**
Designing the 82 fix I predicted a pre-existing defect: `storage_divergence`
joined objects through `current_observation_id`, so an *unattributed* overwrite
would move that pointer off the attributed row and drop the object — and
`overwrite_count`, the alarm for exactly that event — out of the reservation's
totals. **Measured, and it did not reproduce.** Attribution is by `object_key`
and is stable, so a later write to the same key attributes to the same intent.
The join was still changed, because R75 makes `current_observation_id` NULL on
an ambiguous tip and the un-fixed join *would* then have hidden the ambiguity in
the one report whose job is surfacing divergence.

**`DROP FUNCTION` discards the ACL; `CREATE OR REPLACE` keeps it.** `0026` drops
the seven-argument observer so no un-channelled overload can silently resolve,
and the `GRANT ... TO computedriven_jobs` that made it reachable was five
migrations back in `0017`. MEASURED: the migration applied cleanly and the
battery went to **33 failures**, every one `permission denied for function
observe_storage_object`. This is `0023`'s CREATE-OR-REPLACE trap from the other
side — there, replacing kept too much; here, dropping kept too little. Both are
apply-time assertions now, in the file that does the thing.

**Two checks that would have passed while measuring nothing.** A zero-row
`UPDATE` satisfies `expect_err` — O24's first draft targeted an intent group O
creates *later in the file*, matched nothing, and "succeeded"; rewritten as an
INSERT, which cannot match nothing. And the mutation vector
`event-id-not-passed` anchored on the call `0026` changed, so the verdict line
printed `1 stale` beside `0 missed`. **`stale` is a defect in the evidence, not
a rounding error**, which is why the tally prints it.


## H-0a1. What round 2 (capability closure, `0024`) fixed

Round 1's own fix had shipped a **cross-tenant read**, a **caller-chosen safety
constant**, and **two clocks under one name**.

> ### THE ROUND THAT HARDENED THE LEDGER ADDED THREE READ PATHS THAT NAME A TENANT.
>
> ```
> org A's API connection:
>   app.storage_ledger(B)         ->  outstanding=777
>   app.storage_divergence(B)     ->  B's row
>   app.storage_divergence(NULL)  ->  EVERY TENANT'S ROWS
>
> the same data, read directly:
>   SELECT ... FROM cd.storage_usage WHERE organization_id = B   ->  0 rows

>
> RLS worked. The `SECURITY DEFINER` functions `0023` added are owned by
> `computedriven_ledger`, which holds `USING (true)` policies **by design**
> because a queue consumer is cross-tenant — so the definer was the only door,
> and the migration built it. The most convenient call an API caller could
> write, `storage_divergence(NULL)`, was the one that returned the cluster.
>
> **THE REQUEST SUPPLIES INTENT, NOT AUTHORITY.** `reserve_storage()` has taken
> no organization argument since `0014` for exactly this reason.

## H-0a (round 2). Two things about the gates themselves

**O0b cannot see a capability nobody realised they created.** It enumerates
*known* cross-tenant capabilities from a hand-maintained list; it passed
throughout `0023`. **O0c** asks the catalog instead — and the same assertion,
running at apply time, **refused the first draft of `0024`**, naming
`storage_outstanding`: `REVOKE … FROM PUBLIC` does nothing to a grant held by a
named role, and that function was not dropped and recreated like its neighbours.

**A fixture's constants encode the relationships the code happened to care about
when they were written.** The O group used three fixed `2026-08-22` timestamps,
correctly ordered relative to each other and unrelated to when their intent was
created. R72 compares exactly that — so on the first day after, every O-group
event correctly became unattributed and O6 returned no rows.

> ### 7.2 RULED R54 — PROVIDER-OBSERVED TRUTH IS MONOTONIC — AND APPLIED IT TO
> ### THE INTENT STATE. IT DID NOT APPLY IT TO THE BYTE LEDGER.
>
> ```
> storage_usage.committed_bytes    documented "bytes actually in R2"
> written by                       app.finalize_storage()   <- the CLIENT
> ```
>
> Everything in this round follows from closing that one gap. **MEASURED, no
> race and nothing in flight:** reserve 100 → offer → the R2 event arrives and
> COMMITS → the client crashes before finalize → the TTL passes → the ledger
> reads `committed 0, reserved 0` while R2 holds 100, and the next 100-byte
> reservation is admitted.
>
> The reproduction found the worse half. `finalize_storage()` refuses a
> terminal reservation, and finalize was the only writer of
> `committed_bytes` — so **after expiry there is no path left to ever charge
> them.** The drift is permanent, not a lag that reconciliation catches up with.
>
> **A NUMBER THAT DESCRIBES THE PROVIDER MAY ONLY BE MOVED BY THE PROVIDER.
> OUR CLOCK ENDS OUR OWN WILLINGNESS TO MINT AUTHORITY AND NOTHING ELSE.**

## H-0a2. What round 1 (settlement, `0023`) closed

R68–R71: the ledger's provider column was CLIENT-written, so a confirmed write
plus an expiry made 100 bytes free and nothing could ever charge them again;
`reserved_bytes` was dropped for a derived hold; `abort_storage()` was the same
defect with no clock at all (**finding 71**, which neither review raised); and
`upload_intents.state` became a GENERATED projection and therefore unwritable.

## H-0b (round 2). One thing we could not settle

**`message_id` absorbs redelivery only if the id is STABLE across attempts.**
Cloudflare documents `Message.id` as "a unique, system-generated ID for the
message" and `attempts` as consumer processing attempts — but does not say the
id survives a retry. The counter living *on the message* is strong evidence it
does; it is not a documented guarantee. And because **R2 is the producer**, the
documented remedy for at-least-once — "generate a unique ID when writing the
message and use it as an idempotency key" — is unavailable to us. ~~Since this round that is a charge to
`committed_bytes`, not just a duplicate log line.~~ **STRUCK — this was WRONG,
not merely superseded, and the reviewer corrected us: finding 75.** The charge is
`v_after - v_prior` under the row lock, so a duplicate that re-projects the same
occupancy moves the ledger by zero. An unstable id duplicates PROVENANCE. Check
**K43** pins it. Falsifier case **E** measures the stability itself.

Separately, the docs get most of the way to one-message-per-event by forbidding
the **configuration**: overlapping or conflicting notification rules are not
allowed. That makes single-notification an obligation on OUR rule set, checked
at provisioning — not a provider guarantee we may assume.

**And a first-party contradiction worth a live experiment, raised by the review
and confirmed here.** Cloudflare's S3 compatibility table lists `Content-MD5`
for `PutObject` and **no SHA-256 checksum header**; the R2 release notes, dated
**2023-06-16**, say S3 `putObject` gained sha256 and sha1 checksum support. One
page is stale and no amount of re-reading settles which. Case **B** is now three
signings — `Content-MD5`, `x-amz-checksum-sha256`, `Content-Length` — because
if the second works we bind **the same SHA-256 the chunk is already named by**
and MD5 never enters the design.

>
> **PROVIDER-OBSERVED TRUTH IS MONOTONIC. `observed` IS A FACT ABOUT THE WORLD,
> NOT A STAGE IN OUR WORKFLOW.**

**Three lessons about the batteries themselves, all learned by running them:**

- **A reproduction that depends on the bug's mechanism stops being a test the
  moment the bug is fixed.** R2's first draft held the reservation row from a
  third session, which worked only because the observer needed no reservation
  lock. Under `0022` the observer queues there too — so the check **deadlocked
  the battery** on a foreground psql with no timeout.
- **A control that breaks two things measures neither of them.** The first
  narrowing of `CD_SABOTAGE=offer` also removed the intent lock, so it broke
  group R and the verdict printed `MISDIRECTED`. Correctly.
- **O0 was widened from one role to a shape**, and O0b added: every cross-tenant
  `SECURITY DEFINER` capability now needs a **positive accept witness**, recorded
  by the check that exercises it and only on a pass. Finding 59 existed because
  every check that touched the observer exercised a refusal.

**M2.0 is append-only, as a stated restriction (R56):** no user delete, no
storage GC, no R2 lifecycle deletion. `DeleteObject`/`LifecycleDeletion`
projection is **M2.1**, required before any surface lets a user delete a world —
and it does **not** block the first restore.

**Two rulings are PROPOSED and deliberately built against rather than assumed:**
**R31** (write authority may not exceed its reservation — *byte-exactness is not
claimed*, it is falsifier case B) and **R32** (committed bytes are
provider-observed — built with fixture events so it can be ruled with a number).

**R23 stays ruled** as of round 6, with the non-retroactive-revocation caveat.

**Is:** nineteen ruled architecture decisions (R7–R30), a PostgreSQL schema with
fail-closed tenant isolation, function-level privilege separation, column
authority and a storage-admission ledger (**27** migrations, **196**-check
battery with a working negative control **and** a regression proof), a
**concurrency battery that hand-steps two real sessions**, a Worker slice with
**486** tests and **139** mutation vectors, and a five-page static site
whose numbers are now *derived* from the batteries rather than typed.

*(Those counts are interpolated from the run that built this file — the same
source as the identity block above. They were hand-typed once and were stale
within a round.)*

**Is not:** any deployed infrastructure, any live integration, or a Hyperdrive
driver adapter. `connect()` and the real R2 provider both refuse by name rather
than stubbing. No account exists, nothing was provisioned, nothing was purchased.
The status manifest says which capabilities are `local` and which are `spec`.

> `cloud.computedriven.com/tools/render-status.mjs` with `--verify`; my search
> missed it because the tool builds its sentinel as `STATUS:${name}:BEGIN`, so
> grepping for the literal marker finds the pages and not the thing that writes
> them. A duplicate renderer written on that false premise was deleted before it
> could become the second source of truth it was accusing the tree of lacking.

### The rulings this implements (R7–R24)

| # | Ruling |
|---|---|
| R7 | Cloud v1's control plane stays Cloudflare-native. No server-hosted BEAM. Workers reach Pigsty via Hyperdrive → Workers VPC → Cloudflare Tunnel |
| R8 | The R2 credential minter is preserved and widened into the API surface. Bulk bytes flow client ↔ R2 directly |
| R9 | PlanetScale stays Keycloak-only — rationale changed from price to IAM/data-plane failure isolation |
| R10 | `principals`/`organizations` are provider-independent roots; IdP bindings live in separate tables with status and history |
| R11 | Three world sizes, three names: WORLD (10 GB–10 TB) · WORLD VERSION (manifest root) · WRL GRAPH (247 KB–213 MB) |
| R12 | Delivery reordered: world sync + restore is M2; Hetzner hosted compute drops to M5 |
| R13 | Hosted compute is a separate metered SKU, not included in storage tiers |
| R14 | RLS fails closed by RAISING. Missing tenant context is an error, never an empty result set |
| R15 | studbook stays at `spec`; holds no confidential Cloud state this round |
| R16 | `CLOUD_COMPUTEDRIVEN_FABLE_BUILD_BRIEF.md` is external research, not a repo source — it does not exist in the tree |
| R17 | Control-plane database traffic uses a **cache-disabled** Hyperdrive binding — the cache cannot see the RLS predicate PostgreSQL adds |
| R18 | `principal.status` and `organization.status` are enforced at authorization, not decorative |
| R19 | R14 narrowed: **no row may pass without a valid tenant context** — not "every statement raises" |
| R20 | Organizations resolve by **stable provider id, never by alias** |
| R21 | **The client may request an operation; the client never chooses its authority** |
| R22 | JWT: `iat` required, `crit` refused, forced JWKS refresh rate-capped |
| R23 | **RULED 2026-08-22.** The M2 key question: a random **World Data Key** for world content only, stored wrapped under a client-held **User Recovery Key**. Restore takes two independent admissions — Cloud authorizes the ciphertext, the user unwraps the key — and transfers **data state only**. Plus the caveat: revocation governs *future* Cloud access; **no retroactive cryptographic erasure is claimed** |
| R24 | **Storage admission moves ahead of M2**; only commerce stays at M6. Entitlement and quota are authorization, not billing. **Built this round** |
| R30 | `resolve_principal()` must be idempotent under **concurrency**, not only in sequence. **The MECHANISM was superseded in round 7** — the advisory lock it originally named is unsupported by Hyperdrive; `0015` serializes on the unique partial index instead. The ruling stands, the implementation changed |
| R31 | **PROPOSED / OPEN** — storage authority may never authorize more bytes than the reservation that produced it. **Not claimed**: R2 documents no byte ceiling on a temporary credential, and Content-Length is not documented as a signed/enforced presigned header. Falsifier case B |
| R32 | **PROPOSED / OPEN** — committed storage is provider-observed, never client-asserted. R2 object-create events carry `object.size`; Queues is at-least-once, so exactly-once comes from a unique constraint |
| R33 | Pigsty targets **PostgreSQL 17.x** for v1, because Hyperdrive documents known support for 9.0–17.x. PG18 is not refused, it is unproven through the transport — falsifier case H |

### Three contradictions found in the tree and retracted in place

1. `CLAUDE.md` described R4 as *"recommended over Fly and not yet ruled"* — six
   days after it was ruled, in the file injected into every session.
2. `agents/C-infrastructure.md` ruled Keycloak onto Fly, then budgeted
   *"Keycloak wants 2 GB"* into the Hetzner box sizing.
3. The same file justified PlanetScale by beating *Fly Managed Postgres at $38*
   — an alternative that stopped being the live one once Pigsty entered the plan.


</details>

## 1. Still open

<details>
<summary><strong>What round 1's review settled — history</strong></summary>


**Settled, with the fix inlined below:**

| Finding | Outcome |
|---|---|
| `SECURITY DEFINER` functions kept default `PUBLIC EXECUTE` — `readonly` could mint principals | Fixed, `0009`. Reproduced first: check D16 shows the escalation succeeding pre-fix |
| `principal.status` was decorative — a suspended principal resolved and authorized | Fixed, `0008`. Group G, six checks |
| R14 overclaimed "a missing context always raises" | Narrowed, and the measured boundary was **narrower than either party predicted** — an empty table *does* raise; only a constant-false qualifier elides the scan. A7 asserts the limit on purpose |
| Pricing relapsed into the WORLD/WRL conflation | Fixed. Machine bytes metered; WRL graph history unlimited |
| "One scheduler" claimed while placement is `spec` | Fixed — "one placement model", with M4 named |
| Assets referenced but unproven | `tools/check-assets.mjs` is now an M0 gate |
| Bootstrap role shape | **Upheld** by the reviewer, hardened rather than replaced |


</details>

**REWRITTEN FROM THE TREE EVERY ROUND.** Round 4 struck two items that had
survived as quasi-history: `expire_storage_reservations()` subtracting bytes at
`expires_at` (**R69/`0023` removed the mechanism**) and "can *is this capability
cross-tenant?* be derived" (**O0c derives it**).

**The dominating fact is that the bundle still says 0 live.** The list is
ordered by that.

1. **Nothing has touched Cloudflare.** Capabilities: **24 local / 16 spec / 0 live**. Every remaining
   item here is downstream of that. The order the live cases should run is

   ```
   S -> Q -> P -> P2 -> H -> A -> D -> D2 -> F -> G -> I -> B -> C -> E -> J -> N
   ```

   with **Q** first because it is the only case that can refuse the path every
   other case runs over. FINDING 119: both the order and the counts in this
   paragraph were hand-typed, and the order was five cases and two rounds stale —
   *in the section listing what is still open*, beside a `$FALSIFIER_ORDER`
   the same document already renders correctly two sections earlier. Finding
   111 built the deriver and did not convert this instance. **A deriver that
   exists is not a deriver that is used.**

2. **The Hyperdrive driver adapter does not exist**, so `connect()` and
   `connectJobs()` both throw `CD-CRED-NOTDEPLOYED` and the live falsifier's
   `--run` branch has no execution path. Round 4.1 added the `queue()` handler
   and its channel admission, which is the piece that had to exist before a real
   consumer could be wired — the admission decision is made and tested, and the
   next statement in that handler is the one that cannot run yet. **This is the
   next thing to build, and it is not a finding.**

3. **The provisioning half of R77 is unverified**, and it is the only rule in
   `CLOUD_V1.md` that can be false while every line of code is correct. A
   producer binding granted to any Worker on the notification queue is the
   authority to mint occupancy for any tenant. Case **P** — whose predicate is
   now unit-tested, so what remains unverified is the account, not the gate.

4. **Two constants are still guesses.**
   `app.provider_clock_skew_allowance()` is 5 minutes and nothing has compared
   R2's `eventTime` clock to Pigsty's (case **D2**);
   `app.settlement_quiet_period()` is 1 hour and nothing has measured how late a
   PUT R2 admitted before expiry can land (case **I**). R72 is a **lower** bound
   only until case I gives the upper one, after which it should become the
   interval `created_at − skew ≤ provider_event_at ≤ expires_at + inflight`.

5. **Whether `ambiguous_event_at` is a live alarm or dead code.** `0026` makes
   an equal-`eventTime` tie representable and order-independent. Whether R2 can
   produce one at millisecond resolution is case **J**. If case **C** proves
   `If-None-Match: *` makes content-addressed chunks write-once through the
   presigned path, the state should be unreachable for normal chunks — and then
   it is a should-never-fire, which is the most useful kind.

6. **An ambiguous object has no resolution path yet.** The database now says "we
   do not know which write is current" and charges conservatively. Nothing HEADs
   the real object to settle it. That is deliberate for M2.0 — the honest state
   first, the reconciler second — but it is an open loop and it should not stay
   open past the first live round.

7. **The asynchronous seam is closed at ONE boundary and the boundary count is
   six.**

   ```
   HTTP request  ·  Postgres transaction  ·  presigned R2 authority
   R2 object commit  ·  Queue delivery  ·  local client state
   ```

   The lock protocol covers the first two against the fifth. **Nothing covers
   the third and fourth**, because they are not ours to lock — the whole of R55
   and case **I**. Is there a way to enumerate seams of this kind rather than
   discover them one review at a time?

8. **`client_abandoned` releases nothing, so what is it FOR?** It records that a
   client disowned an authority, which an M2.1 GC will need, and today it changes
   no number. Honest, and close to decorative — a shape this tree has removed
   twice. Keep it for M2.1, or delete it until the GC exists?

9. **The reservation row is a serialization point and nothing has measured its
   contention.** Benchmark **concurrent offerers** (8/16/32/64), not total chunk
   count: row-lock contention depends on simultaneous transactions, not World
   size. Not done.

10. **Whether any of this survives Hyperdrive**, unchanged and still the largest.
   `FOR UPDATE` is ordinary MVCC that any pooler forwards — exactly the kind of
   "should be fine" that produced round 7's unshippable advisory lock. Case **H**
   and group **L** are the instruments; neither has run against real Hyperdrive.

**Struck since the last bundle, and named so the deletion is visible:** the
`expire_storage_reservations()` oversubscription seam (R69 removed the
mechanism); O0b's hand-written capability list (O0c derives it from the
catalog); whether `DeleteObject` consumption blocks M2 (no — R56 scopes M2.0
append-only); whether the finding-59 gate should parse `pg_proc.prosrc` (no —
structural reachability plus accept witnesses instead).

### 2.3 Regression proof — the new checks against the UNFIXED schema

The fixes under test withheld — the withheld set is DERIVED from
`status.json`'s `regression_removed`, not typed here, and it is every fix plus
everything that cannot APPLY without one. A check added after a fix is worthless
until it is shown to fail before it. **`0026` was added to the tree and not to
that list in this round's first attempt**, so the reduced set tried to
`ALTER cd.storage_objects` with no `0021` to create it; the counts script
reported `REGRESSION RUN PRODUCED NO TALLY` rather than republishing the
previous number, which is what that guard is for.

in-process and the JWKS is served from a function, so these exercise the code
that would actually run on workerd.

### 2.5 Worker mutation battery — `./worker/test/sabotage.sh`

Each vector breaks exactly one security decision in a copy of the source and
re-runs the UNMODIFIED suite. Note the baseline line: an earlier version of this
script invoked `node --test test/` (a directory, not a glob), which fails with
MODULE_NOT_FOUND on node 25 — so it reported **10/10 caught while every vector
was detecting a broken invocation rather than a broken decision**. The baseline
control now refuses to run if the unmutated suite does not pass.

### 2.6 Concurrency battery — `./worker/test/concurrency.sh`

The battery `tenant-isolation.sh` structurally cannot be. It runs one session on
one connection, so every property it can express is **sequential** — which is how
a duplicate-key failure on simultaneous first login survived five rounds behind a
check named "resolve_principal is idempotent".

Group **N** hand-steps two sessions to a deliberate interleaving (S1 resolves and
does not commit · S2 enters the same call · S1 commits · what does S2 do?) rather
than racing and hoping. Group **P** is the same discipline pointed at quota.

#### 2.6.2 Control — `CD_SABOTAGE=quota` (the atomic admission replaced by read-then-write)

The naive form is correct in every sequential test. Here it reserves **2000

lock must break N *and leave P alone*; if the other group also fails, the run
prints `MISDIRECTED` rather than crediting itself. A control that fires for the
wrong reason is not a control.

### 2.9 The live falsifier — PLAN ONLY, nothing contacted

Eight questions the local batteries structurally cannot answer, each written down
with **what it would falsify and what we would do about it** before it is run —
so a negative result stays informative instead of becoming something to explain
away. It provisions nothing and refuses to run without real bindings.

```

  LIVE FALSIFIER — plan only. Nothing has been contacted.

  Run order: S -> Q -> P -> P2 -> H -> A -> D -> D2 -> F -> G -> I -> B -> C -> E -> J -> N

  S. Does the DEPLOYED Worker trust exactly the subjects worker/wrangler.toml declares? (finding 121)
     method     GET /accounts/{account}/workers/scripts/{name}/settings and read `bindings[]` in Cloudflare's own vocabulary — plain_text.text, hyperdrive.id, r2_bucket.bucket_name, queue.queue_name. scripts/check-deployed-subjects.mjs is this check; its predicate is pure and unit-tested in worker/test/deployment-subjects.test.mjs. Per subject: the binding exists, is of the expected KIND, carries a value, and that value equals the manifest's. Across the pair: HYPERDRIVE_CONTROL and HYPERDRIVE_JOBS are DIFFERENT configurations, which is R80 asserted at the deployed layer instead of the file layer.
     falsifies  That subject continuity is closed. Finding 105 closed the caller-chosen half — no gate may take a subject from its environment — and left the manifest-versus-runtime half, which was unreachable while nothing was deployed and is reachable the moment one is.
     if it fails STOP. Every case after this one is attesting the wrong system, and the failure mode is silent and total: objects land in a bucket outside the accounting path with no anomaly counter, no DLQ and no retry to notice, exactly as in finding 105's reproduction. Redeploy from the manifest, or rule the deployment correct and change the manifest.
     if it passes The subject chain runs tree -> deployed -> P/P2/Q, and `origin` may finally read "deployed" rather than "wrangler.toml".

  Q. Do the two Hyperdrive bindings carry two PostgreSQL credentials, with the SQL response cache off? (R17, R80)
     method     GET both Hyperdrive configurations. scripts/check-hyperdrive-authority.mjs is this check; its predicate is pure and unit-tested in worker/test/hyperdrive-authority.test.mjs. Per config: origin.user is the expected login, origin.database is Pigsty's, the origin matches one of Cloudflare's three documented shapes, and caching.disabled === true. Across the pair: distinct ids, distinct users, SAME origin — two authorities over one database.
         THEN, once the driver exists, the privilege witness through each connection: current_user; the request credential CANNOT execute app.observe_storage_object(); the jobs credential can; the jobs credential holds no unrelated request capability.
     falsifies  R80's separation, at the layer where it is actually implemented. R80 was proved at the level of BINDING NAMES — two [[hyperdrive]] entries, two function names, a gate reading both. Reproduced (finding 95): point the jobs binding at the request binding's id and check-channel-identity.mjs exited 0 saying 'two Hyperdrive authorities'. That half is closed in the file now. The half a file CANNOT close is that two distinct ids may still authenticate as one PostgreSQL user, and that caching is configured with `wrangler hyperdrive create --caching-disabled` — on the CONFIGURATION, not the binding — so NO wrangler.toml can ever assert R17. It is provider state and only a provider read attests it.
     if it fails Do not go live. A collapsed authority means the request path holds EXECUTE on the observer, which is the boundary R68 and R80 exist to draw; a live cache on a tenant-sensitive path means Hyperdrive is keyed on a query string that is byte-identical across tenants for every RLS-filtered SELECT, and the first cross-tenant read is a correctness failure nothing downstream can detect. Recreate the configuration — caching is settable on an existing one with `wrangler hyperdrive update <id> --caching-disabled`.
     if it passes R17 stops being an unattested ruling. NOTE WHAT IT STILL DOES NOT BUY: origin.password is write-only and the API never returns it, so this proves WHICH USER each configuration names and never that the two secrets differ. Only the privilege witness above proves the grant. Re-run it on every provisioning change — a cache re-enabled later is exactly as bad as one enabled now, and nothing in the data plane would notice.

  P. Is the provider-observation queue a dedicated R2-only authority channel? (R77)
     method     GET the queue through the Cloudflare API and enumerate BOTH sides. PRODUCER side: producers_total_count agrees with the returned list; exactly one entry; its type is exactly `r2_bucket`; its bucket_name is exactly ours. CONSUMER side (finding 89): no consumer other than the observer Worker, and at least one. scripts/check-queue-authority.mjs is this check; its predicate is a pure function unit-tested in worker/test/queue-authority.test.mjs, and ANY producer type it does not positively recognise is a REFUSAL rather than a note — which is finding 88, where the first version of this gate exited 0 on a queue carrying an unclassified producer.
     falsifies  The premise under every occupancy number this system publishes. observeBatch() trusts R2 for size and etag and derives tenancy from the key -- correctly -- but what it actually knows is 'a Queue delivered something shaped like an R2 notification'. Cloudflare documents that ANY Worker can write to a queue, and the notification body carries no cryptographic R2 provenance, so a Worker holding a producer binding on this queue can mint occupancy. Checking `account` does not help: a producer that can forge the rest of the JSON can forge that string too.
     if it fails Do not go live on the shared queue. Provision a dedicated queue whose only producer is the bucket notification rule, and make THAT a standing provisioning gate rather than a sentence in an architecture document. If Cloudflare cannot express producer restriction at all, the honest fallback is that the consumer HEADs the named object before charging it -- slower, and it makes R2 rather than the envelope the authority.
     if it passes The channel is the credential, and (queue_name, message_id) records which credential spoke. Re-run it on every provisioning change: a producer binding added later is exactly as bad as one added now, and nothing in the data plane would notice. The runtime half is already closed regardless of this case — the Worker's queue() handler refuses any batch whose MessageBatch.queue is not env.PROVIDER_QUEUE, BEFORE it connects, and refuses everything when no channel is attested at all. Case P is what stops the provisioning drifting under a correct handler.

  P2. Does the R2 notification rule route EVERY admitted write to that channel? (R77, R79)
     method     GET /accounts/{account}/event_notifications/r2/{bucket}/configuration. scripts/check-notification-coverage.mjs is this check; its predicate is pure and unit-tested in worker/test/notification-coverage.test.mjs. Asserts: bucketName is ours; exactly one queue entry for the attested PROVIDER_QUEUE carrying exactly one rule; the rule's actions cover PutObject, CopyObject and CompleteMultipartUpload; NO delete action (M2.0 is append-only, R56); nothing outside Cloudflare's five-action enum; no suffix filter; and a prefix that is absent or a prefix of `org/`. The required action list is IMPORTED from reconcile.mjs rather than retyped, so a fourth admitted action becomes a coverage requirement without an edit.
     falsifies  The completeness of the channel case P proved AUTHENTIC. Case P reads the queue's producer and consumer sides; it never opens the bucket's notification configuration, and those are two different objects in the account. So this passes case P:
         producer = OUR bucket, consumer = OUR observer, DLQ configured
       while the rule behind it is:
         actions = [PutObject], prefix = "wrong-prefix/"
       and every CopyObject, every CompleteMultipartUpload — which is how a large world chunk lands — and every key outside that prefix is never produced at all. There is no retry budget to exhaust, because no message was ever created. It is finding 65 arriving from below the database with no trace anywhere.
     if it fails Re-provision the rule to the exact intended shape rather than adding a second rule to patch the gap: Cloudflare allows 100 rules per bucket and prohibits overlaps that fire twice for one event, and proving an arbitrary set equivalent to the intended one is a harder claim than provisioning the one rule that plainly is it. If a delete action is present, that ALSO contradicts the premise inventory.mjs's `extra` refusal rests on, and R56 has to be revisited before the rule is.
     if it passes Case P's 'the channel is the credential' becomes 'the channel is the credential AND it carries every admitted write'. Neither case implies the other and both are standing provisioning gates: P asks whether the thing speaking is really R2, P2 asks whether R2 is speaking about everything.

  H. Which PostgreSQL major does Hyperdrive actually accept?
     method     Connect through Hyperdrive to the target cluster and read server_version_num.
     falsifies  The local battery's relevance. Cloudflare documents known support for 9.0–17.x. This said 'this box runs 18.4', which stopped being true when R33 made /opt/pgsql-17 the default and the battery banner started printing 17.10 — the same stale-in-prose drift as finding 63, in the file that lists what we have not measured.
     if it fails Pin Pigsty to 17.x for v1 and run the battery with CD_PGBIN pointed at a 17 build. That is the recommended default REGARDLESS until this case has a result.

  A. Does a presigned PUT of EXACTLY the offered byte count succeed?
     method     Offer expectedBytes=N for one object key; sign a PutObject; upload N bytes.
     falsifies  Nothing — this is the control. If A fails the harness is wrong, not R2.
     if it fails Stop. Every result below is meaningless until the happy path works.

  D. Does an object-create event arrive, and does object.size match?
     method     Configure a notification rule to a queue; PUT N bytes; pull the message.
     falsifies  R32's feasibility.
     if it fails Client-asserted finalize stays the only number available, and the honest response is to SAY SO on the security page rather than quietly keep trusting it.

  D2. How far can R2's eventTime precede our own clock for a write we caused? (R72)
     method     Many real cycles: offer (recording intent.created_at from Pigsty), PUT immediately, consume the notification, record `intent.created_at - eventTime`. Report the distribution and the WORST legitimate negative delta, not the median — the constant has to cover the tail or it strips attribution from real writes.
     falsifies  app.provider_clock_skew_allowance() = 5 minutes, and with it the earned half of R72. The ruling has two halves: *a lower bound exists* is measured; *this is the right lower bound* is PROPOSED until this runs. Too small and legitimate chunks are recorded unattributed, which looks exactly like the defect R72 prevents; too large and a stale delayed event can still be credited to an intent that did not cause it.
     if it fails If the observed skew is unbounded or drifts, a timestamp comparison is the wrong instrument and attribution needs something the provider echoes back rather than something two clocks agree about — which points at case B's bound digest, not at a bigger constant.
     if it passes The allowance gets a measured value. NOTE WHAT IT STILL DOES NOT BUY: R72 is a lower bound only. A write arriving long after expires_at could not plausibly have been caused by the intent either, and case I measures that in-flight bound — after which R72 should become an interval, `created_at - skew <= provider_event_at <= expires_at + inflight`.

  F. Does the tenant-context transaction survive Hyperdrive's pooling?
     method     Through HYPERDRIVE_URL: BEGIN; set_organization_context(A); SELECT; COMMIT — then on the next transaction, SELECT with no context and require CD-TENANT-MISSING.
     falsifies  The core §6.1 assumption. set_config(...,true) is transaction-scoped and Hyperdrive is transaction-pooled, so this SHOULD hold — and 'should' is what §6.1 already had to retract once.
     if it fails Tenant isolation does not work over the production transport. Stop everything.

  G. Does the request path work with NO advisory locks, over Hyperdrive?
     method     Through HYPERDRIVE_URL: two concurrent connections, same fresh OIDC subject, resolve_principal on both. Require two successes and one principal.
     falsifies  R30-as-amended. 0015 replaced the advisory lock with unique-index serialization specifically because Hyperdrive lists advisory locks as unsupported.
     if it fails Identity resolution has to move somewhere Hyperdrive is not in the path.

  I. How long after our expiry instant can a write we authorized still show up?
     method     Sign a PutObject whose URL expires at T. Begin a large slow body at T-1s so the request is in flight across the boundary. Record the interval from T to (a) the object becoming readable and (b) the notification arriving on the queue. Repeat with the body started AFTER T, which should be refused. Repeat at several body sizes, because (a) is bounded by upload duration and (b) is not. The answer is the MAXIMUM of (b) observed, plus margin -- not the median.
     falsifies  app.settlement_quiet_period() = 1 hour. Settling earlier than the real bound releases bytes for a write still on its way, which is finding 65 with a smaller window; settling much later leaks quota on every crashed client for no reason.
     if it fails ONE HEAD AFTER EXPIRY IS NOT A PROOF and must not be built as one: HEAD 404, in-flight PUT completes, object appears. If the bound turns out to be unbounded or unmeasurable, settlement has no safe automatic trigger and the honest options are (a) settle only on an explicit operator action, (b) a small controlled data-plane boundary for writes so the authority is ours to revoke, (c) softer quota semantics stated plainly on the security page. Pick one CONSCIOUSLY; do not let the local clock keep standing in for a provider guarantee.
     if it passes settlement_quiet_period() gets a measured value and stops being a guess. Note what PASSING does NOT buy: it bounds how late a write we authorized can land, not how late an out-of-band write can, and O10 is the check that keeps those separate.

  B. Can a presigned PUT be made BYTE-EXACT? (R31)
     method     Three signings against the same N-byte body, each then given a DIFFERENT body — (i) N+1 bytes, (ii) N bytes with different content — and required to fail.
         B1  Content-MD5 in SignedHeaders          documented in the compatibility table
         B2  x-amz-checksum-sha256 in SignedHeaders  documented only in the release notes
         B3  Content-Length in SignedHeaders       undocumented; diagnostic only
     falsifies  R31 as a provider-enforced law. Content-MD5 is documented as supported for PutObject; the presigned-URL page documents Content-Type as signed AND enforced (403 SignatureDoesNotMatch on mismatch) and does not mention Content-MD5, Content-Length or conditionals at all. So there are TWO enforcement questions hiding in one: does the signature bind the header, and does R2 verify the DIGEST against the body rather than just matching the header string? Only the second one gives R31.
     if it fails THIS IS THE ARCHITECTURAL RESULT, not a bug: hard pre-write quota and fully direct client->R2 uploads cannot both be claimed with the current grant primitive. Then choose CONSCIOUSLY between (a) a small controlled data-plane boundary for writes and (b) softer asynchronous quota via R32 with an over-write alarm. Do not ship a page that says 'quota enforced' either way until this is answered.
     if it passes R31 becomes provider-enforced by CONTENT rather than by a byte ceiling, which is strictly stronger: a bound digest refuses a longer body, a shorter body and a same-length different body alike. WHICH ONE passes decides the design. If B2 works, the bound digest IS content_digest — one hash, computed once, naming the chunk and enforcing the write. If only B1 works, the client computes an MD5 alongside the sha256 the chunk is already named by, and that MD5 does integrity-against-accident, never integrity-against-an-adversary. Do not standardize on MD5 before B2 has been tried.

  C. Does If-None-Match: * bind THROUGH a presigned URL?
     method     Sign a PutObject carrying If-None-Match: * in SignedHeaders; upload twice; require the second to fail with 412. Then upload twice WITHOUT the header present at request time, to find out whether the condition is enforced by the signature or merely permitted by it.
     falsifies  Not 'does R2 support conditional PutObject' — it does, and the S3-compatibility page says so. The open question is narrower: whether the condition survives the presigned path, whose own page documents only Content-Type as signed-and-enforced.
     if it fails Overwrites stay possible, so the split in 0021 is load-bearing rather than tidy: cd.storage_observations keeps keying on etag and cd.storage_objects stays the only thing occupancy may be read from. Cost is accounting complexity, not correctness.
     if it passes A content-addressed chunk key can be made write-once at the provider, and storage_objects.overwrite_count becomes an alarm that should always read zero rather than a number to reconcile.

  E. Does a redelivered queue message keep the SAME id, and does one object event ever produce two different message ids?
     method     Consume a real R2 notification; record id and attempts. Force a retry (throw, or message.retry()). Require the redelivery to carry the SAME id with attempts > 1, and require exactly one observation row. Separately: PUT once and watch the queue for the full visibility window, requiring exactly one message id for that one write.
     falsifies  R57's mechanism. `message_id` is UNIQUE in 0022, so it absorbs redelivery ONLY IF the id is stable across attempts -- and Cloudflare documents the retry counter without documenting that the id survives it. A retry under a NEW id gets past the constraint and writes a second observation row.
         CORRECTED 2026-08-23, by outside review, against a claim this file made: that second row does NOT double-charge the ledger. 0023 charges `v_after - v_prior` read under the inventory row lock, and for the same write 100 -> 100 is a delta of ZERO. MEASURED, and pinned by check K43. What unstable ids cost is a duplicated PROVENANCE log and an inflated event_count -- which is why this case now ranks BELOW I, B, F and G for M2.0, and rises again in M2.1 when delete/create histories make the log load-bearing.
     if it fails Note what is NOT available as a fallback: the documented remedy for at-least-once is 'generate a unique ID when writing the message and use it as an idempotency key', and R2 is the producer here, so we cannot inject one. The remaining options are the (bucket, key, etag, event_time) fallback index -- which cannot tell a redelivery from a genuine identical re-PUT at the same instant, which is finding 62 coming back -- or moving object-create detection off notifications entirely.
     if it passes R57 is sound as EXACTLY-ONCE QUEUE-MESSAGE PROCESSING. It still does not establish that R2 cannot emit two messages for one object event; the docs get us most of the way there by forbidding the CONFIGURATION -- 'overlapping or conflicting rules that could trigger multiple notifications for the same event are not allowed' -- which makes single-notification an obligation on OUR rule set, checked at provisioning, rather than a provider guarantee we may assume.

  J. Can two genuine writes to one key carry the same eventTime? (R75)
     method     PUT two different bodies to one key as fast as the API allows, many times, and record the eventTime pairs. Cloudflare documents eventTime as the time the triggering action occurred and its example has millisecond resolution; it does not document it as a sequence number. Separately: does Message.id ever repeat across two queues fed by the same bucket? That is the other half of R77 and needs two notification rules.
     falsifies  Whether cd.storage_objects.ambiguous_event_at is a live alarm or dead code. If ties are unreachable it is the second; if they are reachable at any rate at all, every occupancy number depends on 0026 having been written.
     if it fails Ties DO occur. Then the reconcile path needs the HEAD-and-settle step 0026 leaves as a TODO, and `ambiguous` in storage_divergence() needs an operational response rather than a column. Quota stays conservative (max) in the meantime, which is the safe direction.
     if it passes Ties are unobservable at R2's resolution. 0026 stays -- an unreachable state that is correctly represented costs one column -- but the alarm becomes a should-never-fire, which is exactly what case C would make it for content-addressed chunks anyway.

  N. When a notification exhausts max_retries, is it recoverable? (R79)
     method     Point the consumer at an unreachable Pigsty, PUT a known object, let all five attempts fail. Then: (a) is the message in the dead letter queue, and how long does it stay; (b) with the DLQ removed, is it gone as documented; (c) run the R2-listing reconciliation and confirm it recovers the same object, with the same bytes, at R2's own upload time. Measure the listing's own limits too — page size, and whether a bucket with 10^6 keys can be walked inside a Worker's CPU budget or needs a durable cursor.
     falsifies  R79's second half. The first half is documented -- Cloudflare says an exhausted retry with no DLQ deletes the message permanently -- and the second half, that an R2 listing recovers what the queue dropped, is asserted by worker/src/inventory.mjs and has never met a bucket.
     if it fails If reconciliation cannot walk the bucket at realistic scale, the repair path needs a cursor and a schedule rather than a pass, and until it has one the honest statement on the security page is that committed_bytes converges only while the queue holds. That is a much weaker claim than the one this system is built to make.
     if it passes The ledger's correctness stops resting on a transport with a finite retry budget. Note what it still does NOT buy: the pass repairs `missing`, `divergent` and `ambiguous` and REFUSES `extra`, so an out-of-band delete remains an operator decision -- correctly, under R56.

  Not runnable. Missing bindings:

     CF_ACCOUNT_ID          Cloudflare account id

### 2.11 The ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES measurement — `./worker/test/default-acl-probe.sh`

**This is finding 57, settled by running it.** 0009 assumed the mechanism worked;
0018 measured that it did not and generalized to "the REVOKE-from-PUBLIC form
stores nothing"; the round-7 review said the `IN SCHEMA` clause is the defect.
The review is right, and this is the run that says so — kept as a file rather
than a paragraph, because the previous round's version of this claim *was* a
paragraph and the paragraph was wrong.

Case **J** is the one that decides what 0020 does: a role with **no** rule
**leaks**, so per-role defaults do not cover a role added by a future migration.
The event trigger is therefore kept rather than replaced, and a canary created
only as the migration role could never have seen the difference.

  PASS  A2  and a new function IS PUBLIC-executable — the schema-scoped form protects nothing

== B/C. the GLOBAL form — what 0009 MEANT ==

### 2.12 The SECOND drift boundary — `node scripts/check-status-prose.mjs`

`cloud-status-counts.mjs` re-derives the numbers; `render-status.mjs` keeps the
HTML in step with them. Neither looked at the PROSE, and a capability note was
still saying *"18 migrations apply clean … to PostgreSQL 18.4 … L7 WARNs on every
run"* while the derived block said 22 / 17 / 0 — with the renderer faithfully
synchronizing the stale sentence onto the public page.

> **Single-source rendering does not help if the single source itself contains
> duplicated facts.**

It is a DENYLIST, not a rewriter, and historical strings are exempted by exact
match: *"this file said 10 migrations against a tree of twelve"* is a true account
of a past defect, and a sweep that updated it to 22 would turn it into a false one.

```
  ok    no derived fact is duplicated in prose  (1 named historical exemption(s))
```

## 3. Two things the test run found that the design did not predict

1. **FORCE RLS vs SECURITY DEFINER** — described above. Found by running it, not
   by reading it.
2. **A policy admits; a GRANT is still required.** Three checks failed with
   *"permission denied for table organizations"* while holding a correct policy.
   Two independent gates, and both are needed.

There was also a defect in my own test: check F4 was built on a data-modifying
CTE, whose siblings run against the same snapshot — so it measured nothing and
returned an empty string instead of a verdict. Fixed and commented in place. A
test that reports a result while measuring nothing is the exact failure mode the
rest of the battery exists to catch.

**Opened 2026-08-21.** Read this before touching `worker/` or `cloud.computedriven.com/`.

## 1. The sentence the product has to earn

> **Keep the world, not just the files.**

State moves. **Authority does not.** A restored world on a second machine is not the first machine
wearing its clothes — it is a new machine that has been *granted* the world, and the grant is a
separate, refusable act.

That distinction is the whole product. It is also why M2 comes before M5: a sync-and-restore round
proves the sentence, and a VM-provisioning round does not.

---

## 2. Vocabulary — frozen, because we already got this wrong once

`WORLD_SIZE.md` §11 records the scope error being made and corrected: the world layer was measured
at **247 KB realistic, 212.70 MB at the shell's caps**, and then reported as a conclusion about
*the product* — which is 100 GB to 10 TB of the user's machine. **0.21% was mistaken for the whole.**

Four terms. They are not interchangeable and no field may mean two of them.

| Term | What it is | Size | Lives in |
|---|---|---|---|
| **WORLD** | the persistent machine-sized ComputeDriven environment | **10 GB – 10 TB** | conceptually the user's machine; its backup is R2 |
| **WORLD VERSION** | a content-addressed description of that machine state at one instant | KB (it is a *root*) | Pigsty holds `manifest_root`; R2 holds the manifest |
| **WRL GRAPH** | the semantic/topological/control layer *inside* a world | **247 KB – 212 MB** | its own head, referenced separately |
| **TRVM** | verification semantics over transitions and artifacts | n/a | only where the runtime actually checks |

**The rule that prevents the relapse:** there is no `current_head` field anywhere. A head is always
qualified — `manifest_root` (the machine) or `wrl_head` (the graph). If you find yourself writing a
column that could hold either, you are about to reintroduce §11.

**Why this is a good property, not an accounting chore:** the WRL graph — the provenance, the
tracks, the part nobody else sells — is **~0.2% of a backup at its ceiling**. It rides along free
inside a tier priced for the bulk. **You charge for the world-sized machine state; the WRL
graph rides along almost free.**

> **CORRECTED 2026-08-22.** This read *"you charge for the machine; the world costs nothing
> to carry"* — which was true before R11 and self-contradictory after it, because R11 makes
> the world **be** the machine. The pricing page was fixed on 2026-08-21 and this line was
> not. Same sentence, same error, two files; only one got swept.

## 3. Where things run

```text
                    IDENTITY
              Keycloak  ·  Fly iad
                       │
              PlanetScale PS-5 HA
              KEYCLOAK DATABASE ONLY
                       │
                       ▼
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
                  CLOUDFLARE
    marketing · portal BFF · API · authorization
      R2 credential minting · presence (later)
                       │
                   Hyperdrive
                       │
                  Workers VPC
                       │
                Cloudflare Tunnel
                       │
                       ▼
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
                    HETZNER
                   PIGSTY PG
           queryable ComputeDriven truth
                       │
                       │ refs only — never bytes
                       ▼
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
                       R2
              machine-sized worlds
            chunks · manifests · data
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
                       ▲
                       │  direct transfer, scoped credential
                       │
              SUPER / USER MACHINES
           compute + local authority (BEAM/OTP)
```

**Three things this diagram is asserting, each of which was nearly lost:**

1. **No BEAM in the cloud** (R7). A proposed brief put Phoenix at the centre and silently reversed
   `STACK_HUB.md` §0.6, which had ruled Workers *and named the cost*: "if any product ever needs to
   be server-hosted again, Workers is the wrong host and that decision has to be revisited rather
   than patched." R7 declines to revisit it. Super being Elixir is not a reason for the cloud to be.
2. **Bytes never transit the Worker** (R8). The Worker authorizes and mints; the client talks to R2.
3. **Pigsty has no public Postgres port.** The Tunnel is why it can stay private.

## 4. Delivery order

Reordered 2026-08-21 (R12). The previous order shipped two rounds of infrastructure before any
world data moved — deferring the only thing with a modelled margin
(`STACK_HUB.md` §314: **75% / 61% / 55%** on Driver / Fleet / Factory) for the thing with no
priced model at all.

| | Milestone | The proof it owes |
|---|---|---|
| **M0** | Site + status surface | public pages whose every claim reads from `status.json` |
| **M1** | Identity, tenancy, credential minter | a Keycloak subject becomes a principal; org A cannot see org B; a scoped R2 credential is minted and is narrow |
| **M1.5** | **Storage admission** (R24) — entitlement, quota, reservation | no write credential is issued without an active entitlement and reserved bytes |
| **M2** | **World sync + restore** | **the product sentence, below** |
| **M3** | Node identity, Fleet, presence | a node key is durable across disconnect; revoke refuses the next connection |
| **M4** | LOCAL/FLEET placement | a run lands somewhere on purpose and the receipt says where |
| **M5** | Hetzner hosted capacity | provisioning saga, one-time bootstrap, machine-generated key |
| **M6** | **Commerce** — checkout, payment, subscription lifecycle | a metered SKU that is not a storage tier |

### M2 is the round that matters

```text
Super machine
     │  chunk + hash
     ▼
ComputeDriven auth  ──►  scoped R2 credential
     │
     ▼
R2  ·  machine world
     │  manifest root indexed
     ▼
Pigsty
─────────────────────────────────────
     THEN, on a SECOND machine
─────────────────────────────────────
authenticate
     ▼
retrieve manifest
     ▼
retrieve + hash-check chunks
     ▼
restore world
```

> **STATE MOVES. AUTHORITY DOES NOT.**

It exercises Keycloak, the Worker, Pigsty, R2, Super, world identity and restore semantics in one
vertical slice — and it is the thing customers pay for.

## 5. Pricing — what the tiers actually buy

| Tier | Price | Bytes | COGS | Margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Driver | $6/mo | 100 GB | $1.50 | **75%** |
| Fleet | $19/mo | 500 GB | $7.50 | **61%** |
| Factory | $69/mo | 2 TB | $30.72 | **55%** |

Measured first-party, `STACK_HUB.md` §0.6/§314. **These buy persistence, sync, restore and fleet
control. They do not include a VM** (R13).

Hosted compute needs its own metered SKU — compute-hour, GB-hour, GPU-hour, egress — before it is
purchasable. The arithmetic that forces this: one permanent 16-core hosted runner costs multiples of
Factory's entire price. A storage tier cannot absorb it, and

```text
Factory $69  +  $143.82 hosted compute usage
```

is a legitimate invoice, where "Factory includes a runner" is a bankrupt one.

**No purchase CTA ships until billing and provisioning are actually connected.**
