## 6. Two contracts that are easy to get subtly wrong

### 6.1 Tenant context raises; it does not return nothing

PostgreSQL's `current_setting(name, true)` returns **NULL** when the setting is absent, and an RLS
`USING` clause that evaluates to NULL merely *hides the row*. So a forgotten tenant context looks
exactly like "this organization has no worlds" — a silent wrong answer, in the direction that looks
normal.

Every policy goes through one function whose contract is:

```text
valid setting      →  UUID
setting missing    →  RAISE
setting malformed  →  RAISE
```

and context is established **transaction-locally** (`set_config(..., true)`), from a
**server-derived** organization id. Never from anything the browser sent.

Hyperdrive is transaction-pooled and resets transaction state when returning a connection, so
transaction-scoped settings are the correct primitive — and the battery must prove that rather than
assume it.

**NARROWED 2026-08-21 (R19), on outside review.** The first version of this section claimed a
missing context *always* raises. It does not, and the overclaim is retracted here rather than left
to be discovered later. A policy expression is evaluated **per row**, so a statement the planner can
prove scans nothing never reaches the function. Measured — and the line falls in a narrower place
than the reviewer or I predicted:

```
SELECT ... FROM cd.worlds WHERE false     no raise, returns 0    <- the whole gap
SELECT ... FROM cd.audit_events (empty)   RAISES
SELECT ... FROM cd.worlds LIMIT 0         RAISES
SELECT ... FROM cd.worlds                 RAISES
```

An **empty table still raises**; only a constant-false qualifier elides the scan. So the honest
guarantee is:

> **No row may pass without a valid tenant context.**

and *not* "every statement touching a tenant table raises". This does not weaken isolation — a
statement returning no rows leaks nothing — but it does demote the raise from primary control to
loud backstop. **The Worker therefore establishes tenant context on entering the transaction**, and
does not rely on a policy noticing later. Battery checks A7–A9 pin the boundary, with A7 asserting
the limitation on purpose.

### 6.2c Storage admission — what M1.5 actually enforces (R24)

Built 2026-08-22. `0014_storage_admission.sql` + `worker/src/admission.mjs`.

The sentence:

> **No write credential is issued without an active entitlement and reserved bytes.**

R8 sends bulk bytes client → R2 **directly**, so the Worker never sees an upload. By the time an
over-quota world is visible it is an R2 invoice. The reservation is the only place it can be
refused, and it has to be refused *before the credential exists*.

```text
VerifiedClaims
      ▼
tenant + membership + world
      ▼
StorageAdmission      entitlement · quota reservation · expiry
      ▼
AuthorizedScope       ← cannot be constructed without the admission above
      ▼
ProviderNativeGrant   ← r2native.mjs, R2's own action names
      ▼
signed credential
```

Read downward that says: **credential authority is the OUTPUT of admission, not an INPUT to
minting.** A provider can never mint because somebody handed it an organization uuid and a prefix.

**The hard property, and it is the only one worth building for:**

```text
limit 100 GB · used 90 GB · A wants 8 GB · B wants 8 GB · arrive together
NEVER   both accepted  →  106 GB
```

A read-then-write cannot give this — two Workers both read 90, both compute 98 ≤ 100, both write.
So the admission **serializes on the ledger row before it reads anything**:

```sql
INSERT INTO cd.storage_usage (organization_id) VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT (organization_id) DO UPDATE SET updated_at = now()   -- creates-or-LOCKS
RETURNING committed_bytes;                                        -- the loser waits here
-- new statement, new snapshot: this sum SEES the winner's reservation
SELECT app.storage_outstanding(...);
```

Under READ COMMITTED every statement takes a fresh snapshot, so the loser's arithmetic runs after
the winner committed. `DO UPDATE` rather than `DO NOTHING` because only the former takes the row
lock when the row already exists. Measured: 20 simultaneous requests for 100 against a limit of
1000 → **exactly 10 admitted, 10 refused**; with the locking statement removed, **oversubscribed**
(`CD_SABOTAGE=quota`).

> **CHANGED 2026-08-22 (R68/R69).** This was one `UPDATE ... WHERE committed + reserved + n <=
> limit`, which is atomic for a STORED counter and cannot work for a derived one — a subquery in
> that `WHERE` is evaluated against the pre-wait snapshot, which is the read-then-write window
> wearing a lock.

**Three properties of the design, each an existing rule pointed at money:**

- **`reserve_storage()` takes no organization argument.** It reads `app.current_organization_id()`,
  which raises without context. Reserving against another tenant is not rejected — it is
  *unspeakable*, the same shape as §6.1's prefix being built rather than validated.
- **The API role holds `SELECT` on the ledger and nothing else.** No `UPDATE` grant exists to revoke
  a column of. Round 5's law, read forward.
- **One stored number, one writer.** `committed_bytes` is what R2 is *observed* to hold, and
  **only `observe_storage_object()` may move it (R68)** — asserted at apply time and again by check
  K35 against the installed catalog. The hold is **derived**:

  ```text
  occupancy(org)   = current provider-held bytes                    cd.storage_objects
  outstanding(org) = Σ over unsettled reservations of
                       GREATEST(0, bytes − observed-and-attributed)
  used             = occupancy + outstanding
  ```

  > **CHANGED 2026-08-22 (R68/R69).** This said *"two numbers … `reserved_bytes` is held and
  > unwritten … a client that crashed mid-upload costs quota until its reservation expires and
  > nothing after."* That last clause was **finding 65**: the provider had already confirmed the
  > bytes, expiry zeroed the hold, and `finalize_storage()` then refused to record them, so the
  > quota was permanently wrong in the direction that gives storage away. `reserved_bytes` was a
  > counter four functions incremented and decremented; every finding in round 7.3 was one of the
  > four getting it wrong. Deriving it makes a fully-observed reservation contribute zero **without
  > anything having released it**, which is why there is no longer a release to double-fire.

The state machine has one more state, and only one of them releases anything:

```text
reserved ──► finalized   the client says it is done   ┐
         ├─► aborted     the client gave up           ├─► settled   reconciled past the
         └─► expired     our clock passed             ┘             quiet period; RELEASES
```

**The first three release nothing (R69).** Expiry, abort and finalize are all statements about *us*;
none is evidence about what R2 holds. `app.settle_storage_reservations()` is the single release
path and requires `expires_at + app.settlement_quiet_period()` to have elapsed — **currently 1 hour
and openly a guess**, because it must cover a PUT R2 admitted just before our expiry instant plus
R2 → Queue → consumer latency, and Cloudflare documents neither. Live falsifier **case I** measures
it.

A finalize arriving after the window has closed is still a **refusal** — but for a reason that is
now true. It refuses a late *assertion*, not bytes that were given away; the hold survived either
way.

### 6.2b The M2 key question — three keys, not one

**RULED (R23) 2026-08-22**, with the non-retroactive-revocation caveat. Raised by outside review
2026-08-22, ruled after the round-6 review.

M2 says machine A encrypts and uploads, machine B authenticates and restores. For a
private-single-user world the confidentiality answer is already ruled to be **client-side keys**.
So: *how does machine B get the decryption key?*

The wrong answer is to sync A's device secret, because that is the product's central claim failing
in one step — bytes would carry authority with them.

The distinction that makes it tractable is that **three different things are currently called "the
key"**:

```
WORLD DATA KEY      decrypts world state
NODE KEY            identifies and authorises a machine
EXECUTION GRANTS    permit a machine to cause effects
```

Machine B can legitimately acquire **data-read authority** through a separately authorised
unwrapping step while holding **zero node or execution authority**. Which reframes what M2 earns:

> **Machine authority is not restored. Data access is separately reacquired.**

M3 then earns the other half — authority re-established in the Cloud identity model, by B
generating its own node key and enrolling.

**What was ruled** (R23, full text in `REVISION_REGISTER.md`): the WDK is random, world-content-only,
and stored **only** wrapped under a client-held **User Recovery Key**. Restoring onto machine B needs
**two independent admissions** — ComputeDriven authorizes the *ciphertext*, the user locally unwraps
the WDK. Success transfers **data state only**: not A's node key, credentials, sessions or execution
grants. Losing all recovery material means the plaintext is genuinely unrecoverable, and we say so
rather than quietly keeping a server-side copy. Convergent encryption stays refused by name;
shared-private distribution stays deferred.

And the caveat the ruling added, because "revoke" means two things and only one is achievable:

> Once an authorized machine has recovered a WDK or plaintext, later Cloud revocation cannot make
> that machine forget what it already obtained. **Revocation governs future Cloud access; key
> rotation governs future encrypted state.** No retroactive cryptographic erasure is claimed.

The five authorities this leaves, which stay different forever:

```text
Cloud identity + storage admission   →  may obtain CIPHERTEXT
User Recovery Key                    →  may unwrap the WDK
World Data Key                       →  may decrypt world state
Node key                             →  may identify a machine
Execution grant                      →  may cause an effect
```

### 6.4 The request path must survive HYPERDRIVE, not just PostgreSQL

**Added 2026-08-22 (round 7), after this cost a ruling's implementation.**

R30 closed a concurrent-first-login race with `pg_advisory_xact_lock`. Correct PostgreSQL, proven
green by a battery that hand-steps two sessions. And Cloudflare's Hyperdrive compatibility page lists,
verbatim:

> *"Advisory locks, `LISTEN` and `NOTIFY`, `PREPARE` and `DEALLOCATE`, any modification to
> per-session state not explicitly documented as supported elsewhere."*

R7 puts every control-plane query through Hyperdrive. So the battery went green on a mechanism the
transport refuses.

> **A local battery proves the database's behaviour, not the transport's.**

This is a different class of blind spot from rounds 1–6. Every earlier finding was something the
battery *could* have tested and did not. This one it **structurally cannot**: it speaks to PostgreSQL
over TCP, and there is no Hyperdrive to test against until an account exists.

**What replaces it**, and what the substitutes actually buy:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Battery group L** | asks the DATABASE which functions `computedriven_api` may execute and reads their bodies from `pg_proc`. Derived, so a function added next year is covered the day it is granted. Catches advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY, PREPARE/DEALLOCATE/DISCARD |
| **L4/L5** | the one per-session mutation the design relies on. `set_config(..., true)` is *transaction*-scoped, and L5 proves empirically that a context does not survive its transaction — Hyperdrive is transaction-pooled, so a session-scoped `SET` would be a cross-tenant leak, not a style preference |
| **L7** | Checks the running major against Hyperdrive's documented 9.0–17.x. It **WARNed** while the box ran 18.4; since R33 made `/opt/pgsql-17` the battery default it **passes** on 17.10. Both the verdict and the version come from the run — this row named `18.4` and `WARN` for six days after neither was true, which is finding 63 in the anchor document |
| **`live-falsifier.mjs`** | the questions no local test can answer, written down *before* they are run, each with what it would falsify and what we would do about it |

**The serialization primitive is now the unique partial index** (`0015`), via a subtransaction that
rolls the losing candidate back for free. The review suggested `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`; that was
written first and needed `DELETE` on `cd.principals` for the loser's cleanup — widening the narrowest
role in the schema so a rare path could tidy up. Letting the index raise costs nothing and the
database does the cleanup.

> **The cheapest cleanup is the one the database already does.**

### 6.5 M1.5 is admission-safe. It is NOT hard-quota-safe. (R31, OPEN)

The distinction M2 must not blur:

```text
reserve 1 MB  →  receive PutObject authority  →  upload 500 MB
     →  R2 HAS ALREADY ACCEPTED 500 MB  →  finalize(500 MB) refused
```

The refusal is correct and it is **too late**. Verified first-party: R2 temporary credentials
constrain bucket, operations, prefixes/objects and TTL and document **no byte ceiling**; presigned
URLs document `Content-Type` as signed *and enforced* and say nothing about `Content-Length`.

**The experiment has been re-aimed (2026-08-22), and the change matters.** Case B used to lead with
`Content-Length` and list `x-amz-checksum-sha256` beside it. Re-reading the S3-compatibility page
first-party: neither is documented for `PutObject`. What *is* documented is **`Content-MD5`**, along
with `If-Match` / `If-None-Match` / `If-Modified-Since` / `If-Unmodified-Since`. So the old
experiment's likeliest outcome was "an undocumented header did nothing", which would have been a
result about our header choice rather than about R2.

The re-aimed question is **content-exactness, not a byte ceiling** — and it is strictly stronger,
because a bound digest refuses a longer body, a shorter body and a same-length different body alike:

```text
does the SIGNATURE bind Content-MD5?           the presigned page documents this only for Content-Type
does R2 VERIFY the digest against the body?    the S3 page documents Content-MD5 as supported
                                               ─────────────────────────────────────────────
                                               only BOTH gives R31
```

**So no page, no status entry and no comment may say quota is enforced at the provider.** Whether a
presigned PUT can be made byte-exact is `live-falsifier.mjs` case B. If it cannot, the result is
architectural rather than a bug:

> Hard pre-write quota and fully direct client→R2 uploads cannot **both** be claimed with the current
> grant primitive.

and the choice between a small controlled data-plane boundary and softer asynchronous quota (R32)
becomes a decision instead of an accident.

### 6.6 The M2 write shape — one chunk, one key, one short grant

```text
WORLD  (10 GB – 10 TB)
   │ content-defined chunks — the size is TO BE MEASURED, not frozen here
   ▼
bounded content-addressed objects
   │ one reservation · one EXACT object key · one short-lived write artifact
   ▼
R2
```

**A 2 TB world is not a 2 TB object.** R2 recommends ordinary `PutObject` below ~100 MB and supports
single PUT to 5 GiB, so tens of thousands of ordinary puts carry a multi-terabyte world — and this is
what dissolves the reservation-lifetime question round 6 could not answer. It was unanswerable
because it asked one object to be both the session and the grant:

> **The session can live for days; a chunk grant does not.**

**The reservation row is the serialization boundary for its own intents.** Round 7 built this layer
with the same read-check-write shape round 6 had just removed from the layer below, and group Q
measured it: two 80-byte offers for *different* keys against one 100-byte hold, both admitted, **160
against 100**. The unique constraint on `object_key` cannot help, because the keys differ — which is
the point of a chunked upload. `finalize_storage()` and `abort_storage()` have taken `SELECT … FOR
UPDATE` on that row since 0014; `offer_upload()` was the only member of the family reading it
unlocked. Different reservations stay fully parallel.

**R40 — an intent's bytes are released by an explicit abandon or by its reservation dying, never by
the clock.** The obvious reading is that a dead grant should stop speaking for its bytes. It must
not, and the reason is R8: the bytes are on a wire we do not see.

> The window governs whether we **mint a URL**. It does not govern whether the bytes are **spoken
> for**.

A grant that expired a second ago may have a PUT in flight against a presigned URL R2 will still
honour, because R2's clock is not ours. There is no grace period anywhere in the implementation,
because a grace period is a guess about clock skew.

**R43 — an object key names a promise, not a row:** `{reservation, key, bytes, digest}`, immutable.
This keeps two things apart that were quietly becoming one:

```text
REQUEST IDEMPOTENCE     same (reservation, key, bytes, digest)  →  same intent
CONTENT DEDUPLICATION   the object already exists in R2         →  do not upload
```

0017 checked bytes and digest, then returned whatever `reservation_id` the stored row happened to
carry — so a dead hold's write authority was handed to a live reservation asking about the same
chunk. Deduplication is a real thing to build, it needs proof the object is *present* (R32's
business), and it is **not** a replay. An already-written object now returns `already_observed` and
**no write authority**.

**Multipart stays unauthorized.** `r2native.mjs` used to say "M2 chunking will need it" — an
assumption wearing the clothes of a plan, now retracted. Granting `CreateMultipartUpload`,
`UploadPart`, `ListParts`, `CompleteMultipartUpload` and `AbortMultipartUpload` is five capabilities
nothing has measured a need for. If a single chunk ever exceeds 5 GiB they arrive as their own
ComputeDriven capability, with a row in the translation table, visible in a diff.

### 6.7 Committed bytes are provider-observed, not client-asserted (R32, OPEN)

`finalize(actualBytes)` trusts the uploader, bounded above by its reservation. R2 event notifications
carry `object.size` and `object.eTag` on `PutObject` / `CopyObject` / `CompleteMultipartUpload`, over
Queues.

**Queues is at-least-once**, so a duplicate notification is normal operation, and every exactly-once
property comes from the unique constraint on `(bucket, object_key, etag)` — never from delivery.

**An event log is not an inventory (0021).** That unique key is exactly right for the log and it is
the wrong key for occupancy, because R2 fires an object-create event on **overwrite** too:

```text
chunk/x   PUT        10 bytes, etag A       sum of the log      22      ← what round 7 reported
chunk/x   overwrite  12 bytes, etag B       actual occupancy    12      ← what is true
```

So the two are separate tables and neither answers the other's question:

```text
cd.storage_observations   append-only provider evidence   (bucket, key, etag)   audit · provenance
cd.storage_objects        current provider state          (bucket, key)         billing · occupancy
```

Two things the split forced into the open. **Queues does not guarantee order**, so every "current"
field in the projection is guarded by `event_time` — a redelivered older write is history arriving
late, not a rollback of the present. And `overwrite_count` is carried beside the bytes rather than
absorbed into them: on a content-addressed key a second body under one name is a *defect* — a
collision, a client ignoring its own digest, or multipart — and reporting it as a byte delta would
hide the only interesting thing about it.

**No delete event is consumed anywhere**, so `cd.storage_objects` is current state *for objects that
were created* and occupancy is a high-water mark against deletion. There is deliberately no
`present boolean` standing in for the part that is not built.

**M2.0 IS APPEND-ONLY, AND THAT IS A RESTRICTION RATHER THAN AN OMISSION (R56).** Cloudflare
supports notification actions for both `DeleteObject` and `LifecycleDeletion`, so nothing at the
provider blocks doing deletion properly. It is *scoped out* so the first machine-A → machine-B
restore is not held behind it:

```text
M2.0    immutable / append-only world objects · NO user delete · NO storage GC
        · NO R2 lifecycle deletion policy
        -> under that restriction, storage_objects is a valid inventory

M2.1    delete/GC authority + DeleteObject/LifecycleDeletion projection
        + present/deleted state + quota reclamation
        -> required BEFORE any surface lets a user delete a world, and BEFORE
           billing may say deleted storage was reclaimed
```

So: consuming `DeleteObject` does **not** block the first restore. It absolutely blocks calling this
table *current occupancy* in a product that supports deletion.

**Delivery identity is not object identity is not object state (R57).** `(bucket, key, etag)` answers
"does the provider now hold different bytes under this name?" and it was also being used to answer
"is this the same delivery?" — so a genuine second `PUT` of identical bytes was dismissed as a queue
redelivery. Cloudflare gives every queue message a system-generated `id`, and it comes from the
**envelope**, never from a field a producer could set.

```text
delivery identity   queue message.id    is this the same DELIVERY?
object identity     bucket + key        is this the same OBJECT?
object state        etag, event_time    is this the same CONTENTS?
provider event id   NOT EXPOSED         — R2's notification body has none
```

> **CORRECTED 2026-08-23 (finding 67, second pass).** R57 was narrowed to *queue-message*
> identity in the round that raised it, and this section went on calling `message.id` "the event
> identity" for another day — including in the table, which is the copy a reader trusts. What we
> possess is exactly-once processing of a **queue message**. The R2 event notification body carries
> `account`, `action`, `bucket`, `object{key,size,eTag}` and `eventTime`, and **no event id at all**,
> so provider-event identity is a thing we do not have rather than a thing we hold under another
> name. This is also the limit of `check-status-prose.mjs`: it catches a number that drifted, and
> cannot catch a term that quietly went on meaning the old thing.

Fourth time this distinction has had to be drawn — after user identity vs binding, WORLD vs VERSION
vs GRAPH, and request idempotence vs content dedup.

The trust boundary, which is the only reason consuming these events is safe:

```text
R2 is authoritative for WHAT WAS WRITTEN         size, etag
the key prefix is authoritative for WHOSE IT IS  org/<uuid>/world/<uuid>/
and WE MINTED THAT PREFIX                        scopeForWorld()
```

The organization is **derived from the key**, never read from a field in the message. That parse
exists in two languages — `reconcile.mjs` and `app.parse_object_key()` — so both read one shared
fixture and battery group M asserts them against the same cases. Two parsers for one format is how a
tenancy bug gets written.

**R32 is not ruled, and is built anyway.** `app.storage_divergence()` reports where the client and the
provider disagree, so the ruling can be made with a number instead of an argument.

### 6.8 The notification queue is a dedicated R2-only authority channel (R77)

**Ruled 2026-08-23, from finding 84.** Not a database rule — a *provisioning* rule, and the only
one in this document that can be false without any code being wrong.

`observeBatch()` trusts R2 for `size` and `etag`, derives tenancy from the key, and refuses a
body-supplied organization id. All three are right. Underneath them sits a premise nothing checks:

```
what it knows        a Queue delivered something shaped like an R2 notification
what it assumes      R2 sent it
```

Cloudflare's Queues configuration page says **"Any Worker can write to a queue."** The R2
notification body carries `account`, `action`, `bucket`, `object{key,size,eTag}`, `eventTime`,
`copySource` — **no signature, no nonce, no event id.** So a Worker holding a producer binding on
this queue can mint occupancy for any tenant whose key format it can guess. Checking `account` buys
nothing: a producer that can forge the rest of the JSON can forge that string too.

So:

- **No application Worker ever receives producer authority to the provider-observation queue.**
  Its only producer is the bucket's notification rule.
- **That is verified, not documented.** `scripts/check-queue-authority.mjs` enumerates the queue's
  producers through the Cloudflare API and refuses when it cannot. It is **live falsifier case P**
  and it runs **before case D** — every other live case assumes the property it tests.
- **Delivery identity is `(queue_name, message_id)`,** not `message_id`. Cloudflare documents
  `Message.id` as "a unique, system-generated ID" and documents no cross-queue uniqueness scope,
  while `MessageBatch.queue` names the channel on every batch. The tuple records *which authority
  spoke*, which is worth having even once provisioning guarantees there is only one.

The general shape, which is the part worth carrying to the rest of the stack:

> **Authority should carry its provenance, not merely arrive bearing plausible data.**

### 6.9 The queue converges; R2 inventory recovers (R79)

**Ruled 2026-08-23, from finding 92.** `max_retries = 5`, and until this round no dead letter queue.
Cloudflare documents the consequence in one sentence: *without a DLQ configured, messages that reach
the retry limit are deleted permanently.* So a long enough Pigsty outage reaches:

```
R2                object exists, 100 MB
Queue             notification retried five times, then deleted
storage_objects   no row
committed_bytes   unmoved
```

which is **finding 65 — occupancy the ledger does not know about — arriving from *below* the
database instead of above it.**

> **QUEUE NOTIFICATIONS MINIMIZE CONVERGENCE LATENCY. R2 INVENTORY ESTABLISHES RECOVERABILITY.**
> A transport with a finite retry budget is a buffer, not a durability theorem, and the ledger's
> correctness must not rest on one.

- **A DLQ is configured** (`computedriven-r2-notifications-dlq`), and case **P** refuses a consumer
  without one. It *bounds* the loss; it does not close it — an unconsumed DLQ retains four days.
- **The closure is a reconciliation pass over the R2 listing.** R2 object listing is strongly
  consistent — a list operation lists all objects at that point in time — so for an append-only
  M2.0 (R56) the listing is an authoritative repair source rather than a second opinion.
- **Absence is a property of a COMPLETE ENUMERATION, not of a listing's last page
  (R79.1, finding 107, 2026-08-24).** Finding 103 taught the planner to refuse absence from a
  truncated response. That was still wrong, and it shipped: `IsTruncated = false` means *there is no
  next page*, not *this page is the whole bucket*. MEASURED against the shipped tree — bucket holds
  A and B, ledger holds A and B, listing paginates:

  ```
  page 1   [A]  IsTruncated=true    ->  0 refusals            correct
  page 2   [B]  IsTruncated=false   ->  "the ledger holds A and the complete listing does not"
  ```

  **The first-page bug was not fixed. It was moved to the last page**, where it alleges an
  out-of-band delete of an object page 1 had just reported present. So the abstraction changed
  rather than the predicate: a page carries no completeness flag at all, and `beginSweep()` earns
  completeness by protocol — the first request carried no cursor, every later one carried exactly
  the token the previous page returned, and the last page said it was not truncated. Only a
  `CompletedSweep` reaches `reconciliationPlan()`.
  **Positive evidence is safe page by page; negative evidence is not.**
- **And that proof object was a claim anybody could mint (finding 113, R81).** The admission check
  was `scan?.__completeScan !== true`, so a hand-typed literal carrying the field was accepted as a
  completed enumeration and the planner read absence out of it. Worse, `Object.freeze()` froze the
  POINTER: `presentKeys` was a live `Set`, and deleting a key from a supposedly frozen scan flipped
  the plan from **0 refusals to 1**, alleging a deletion of an object R2 had just named. Membership
  in a module-private `WeakSet` is the proof now — the pattern `jwt.mjs`, `admission.mjs` and
  `r2creds.mjs` already used — and `presentKeys` is a frozen facade over a private Set.
  **Evidence used for a negative conclusion must be both unforgeable and immutable.**
- **The cursor chain was attested by the party being checked (finding 115).** `requestedWith` came
  from the caller, so a provider echoing `ContinuationToken: "WRONG"` against a caller claiming
  `"tok1"` still yielded `chainVerified: true`. `sweepBucket()` now owns the pagination loop, and
  S3's echoed token is checked when present. **Provenance supplied by the claimant is not
  provenance.**
- **A finished sweep is not a snapshot (finding 116, R79.2).** Cloudflare documents point-in-time
  consistency for **one** list operation; a multi-page sweep is many, and nothing first-party joins
  them. The type asserts *every page traversed through a verified cursor chain* and explicitly not
  *a point-in-time image of the bucket*. Recoverability is **eventual, through repeated sweeps**.
- **Presence and usable state are independent facts (finding 108).** A key R2 named whose metadata
  we cannot use was being reported as an out-of-band delete — about an object the provider had just
  told us exists. A scan accumulates `presentKeys` beside `entries`; absence checks the first and
  state repair uses the second, and the difference is surfaced as `unreadable`.
- **The listing does not say which API call produced the state (finding 109).** `observeArgsFor()`
  refused to synthesize a queue message id — with a paragraph explaining why — and then passed
  `"PutObject"`. A lost notification could have been any of the three create actions. It now
  REQUIRES provenance with a closed basis (`upload_intent`) naming the intent. **CORRECTED
  2026-08-24, finding 118** — this line read *"the only case where we minted the credential that
  performed the write"*, which assumes the conclusion. An intent proves we **authorized** a
  capability for that key; it does not prove the bytes now in R2 came from it, and an out-of-band
  write is exactly what this pass exists to find. The basis records `proves: "authority"` /
  `doesNotProve: "causation"`, and repairs stay candidates.
  **Authority to cause an event is not evidence that the event was caused by that authority.**
  A third fabricated argument went with it: `providerStateTime` is a listing's `LastModified` and
  the observer's `p_event_time` is when the triggering action occurred (finding 117). Nothing
  first-party equates them, so `EVENT_TIME_BASES` is **empty** and application refuses until a live
  case measures it.
  **UPDATED 2026-08-24 (finding 124): the causation blocker is now ENFORCED, not printed.**
  `observeArgsFor()` checked the clock list and nothing else, so with one line changed to model a
  successful case N an `upload_intent` provenance returned a valid observer argument vector —
  silently satisfying a blocker nothing had resolved. `applicationBlockers()` is one computation
  behind both the candidate's `blocked` field and the refusal, and `CAUSATION_BASES` is a
  **separate** empty list, because satisfying one blocker must never satisfy another.
  **A blocked reason that is only printed is not a gate.** The multipart etag suffix is recorded as
  an observation and **not** promoted to a derived action, because a copy can carry one too.
  **This does not open `0028`**: the natural schema — `observation_source = queue_event |
  inventory_state`, with `provider_action` meaningful only for the first — is earned by case N
  showing general direct-state reconciliation is needed, not by this argument.
- **A set difference needs completeness on BOTH operands (finding 122, R82).** Two rounds earned
  `CompletedSweep` and handed it to `reconciliationPlan(sweep, known)` where `known` was an ordinary
  array. MEASURED both ways: a short ledger fabricates a repair for a row it never read, and — the
  bad direction — **erases the out-of-band delete** the pass exists to catch. The likeliest cause is
  RLS, because the jobs role carries no tenant context by design and a policied read returns a subset
  that is indistinguishable from a clean bucket. `beginLedgerInventory()` earns a
  `CompleteLedgerInventory` by the same keyset-chain protocol, carrying bucket, authority and
  snapshot; a `tenant` authority cannot support absence at all.
- **An adapter that does not perform the authenticated act cannot attest it (findings 128/129, R85).**
  R83 confined authority to a "credentialed adapter" that took a `transport` callback, checked four
  strings were non-empty, and branded the closure — **no signing anywhere in it.** MEASURED with a
  fake key and no network: `isAuthoritativeSweep()` true. The ledger side had the identical hole,
  taking `authority: "jobs"` and a snapshot string as ARGUMENTS. Both now derive what they attest:
  `worker/src/s3sig.mjs` signs a real `ListObjectsV2` with SigV4 (verified byte-equal against AWS's
  published worked example), and `ledgerInventoryAdapter()` reads `current_user` and
  `txid_current()` from the database and measures finality from a short page. The test seam sits
  BELOW each, so **no authoritative operand is reachable offline** — which is the correct state at
  0 live, and makes the acceptance gate true by construction: *no R2 and no PostgreSQL means
  absence can never be established.*
- **Provider provenance is required for provider facts, presence included (finding 130, R86).**
  R83 modelled authority as something only absence needed. *R2 named this key* is true the moment it
  is read — but only if R2 named it; MEASURED, a synthetic page produced a 10 TB repair candidate
  for a key R2 never mentioned. Authority has two dimensions: **presence requires it, absence
  requires it AND completeness.**
- **Protocol-complete is not provider-authoritative (finding 123, R83).** `sweepBucket()` runs a
  caller-supplied lister, so the R81 brand proved the state machine ran and not that R2 answered —
  MEASURED with a synthetic closure and no R2 anywhere. `AuthoritativeR2Sweep` is minted only for
  pages that came through `r2ListingAdapter()`. Repairs still compute either way, because *R2 named
  this key* is positive evidence true the moment it is read; **absence** without authority is
  reported as `absenceUnknown` with its reasons, and there is no flag to override that.
- **`worker/src/inventory.mjs` is a pure planner**, for finding 88's reason applied in advance: the
  judgement is separated from the I/O so it is exercisable with no account, no bucket and no
  database. It classifies `missing` / `divergent` / `ambiguous` as repairable and **refuses `extra`**
  — an object the ledger holds and R2 does not cannot happen legitimately under R56, so it is
  surfaced and a human rules. Auto-crediting bytes back on an out-of-band delete or a truncated
  listing is worse than the divergence.
- **The pass REPORTS an ambiguity; it does not settle one. CORRECTED 2026-08-23, finding 97** — this
  line said *"the pass is also the ambiguity resolver §6.8's R75 left open… a tied tip the database
  could not settle is settled by the listing"*, and that is false. `app.project_object_state()` calls
  a tip ambiguous when `count(DISTINCT (etag, size_bytes)) > 1` over the maximum `event_time`, and a
  repair enters as an ordinary observation at the provider's own instant — which, in a tie, IS that
  instant. Applying it leaves the tip holding two distinct pairs, so **the ambiguity survives** and
  `size_bytes = max()` does not move either. Only `event_count` changes. The test that claimed
  otherwise asserted the planner *emits* the repair; it never applied it and required
  `ambiguous_event_at` to clear.
  The planner now returns `ambiguityCandidates` with `applied: false`, and `observeArgsFor()`
  **refuses** one. **`T + 1ms` is refused too** — manufacturing provider chronology is precisely what
  R75 declined to do. What is actually true is epistemic and the schema cannot yet say it: a direct
  read of R2's state is stronger evidence than an unordered notification set, and today both enter as
  the same row type with the same rank. Representing that is a migration; **case J decides whether one
  is ever needed.** If tied provider instants are unreachable, nothing gets built.
- **A repair is an observation WITHOUT a delivery identity.** It did not arrive on the authority
  channel, so under R77 it has none to claim; it takes the fallback uniqueness key `0022` built for
  exactly this caller. A synthesized message id would make a repair indistinguishable from a
  notification in the provenance log.

### 6.10 Two authorities, two credentials (R80)

**Ruled 2026-08-23, from finding 94.** `computedriven_api` and `computedriven_jobs` are separate
PostgreSQL roles, and the separation is load-bearing: the request role deliberately holds **no
EXECUTE** on `app.observe_storage_object()`, because telling the ledger that bytes landed is the
client-asserted path R68 replaced.

A Hyperdrive configuration carries **its own origin user and password**. One binding is therefore one
database credential, and `connect()` / `connectJobs()` reading the same binding would have made the
two roles one authority wearing two function names — silently, at the moment the driver was
implemented, with both names still reading correctly.

```
HYPERDRIVE_CONTROL   origin user computedriven_api_login   INHERITS computedriven_api
HYPERDRIVE_JOBS      origin user computedriven_jobs_login  INHERITS computedriven_jobs
```

Both cache-disabled (R17). The login principals are provisioner work (Pigsty), not migrations — the
existing roles stay `NOLOGIN`.

**The alternative is refused.** One login granted both roles, with `SET ROLE` at runtime, leaves a
credential holding the union of both authorities and a boundary enforced by application convention.
`scripts/check-channel-identity.mjs` fails the build if either helper reads the other's binding.

#### R80.1 — and a config file can only attest what it contains (finding 95)

**2026-08-23.** R80 above was proved at the level of **binding names**: two `[[hyperdrive]]` entries,
two function names, a gate reading both. Reproduced against the shipped tree — point the jobs binding
at the request binding's id and the gate exited **0** saying *"two Hyperdrive authorities"*:

```
HYPERDRIVE_CONTROL   id = X
HYPERDRIVE_JOBS      id = X          ->  ok, exit 0
```

Two names over one configuration is **one credential** — finding 94 surviving the fix for finding 94.

> **A BINDING NAME IS OURS. THE CREDENTIAL BEHIND IT IS THE PROVIDER'S. A FILE CAN ONLY ATTEST THE
> FIRST.**

- **The half that is in the file is closed there.** `check-channel-identity.mjs` now refuses two
  bindings sharing an id, and its success line was narrowed to *two distinct Hyperdrive configuration
  ids* — it had been claiming a property it could not see.
- **The half that is not in any file is live case Q**, `scripts/check-hyperdrive-authority.mjs`. Two
  distinct config ids may still authenticate as one PostgreSQL user, and **caching is configured with
  `wrangler hyperdrive create --caching-disabled`, on the configuration rather than the binding** —
  so **no `wrangler.toml` can ever assert R17**, and R17 has been unattestable since it was ruled.
  Q asserts, per configuration: `origin.user`, `origin.database`, a recognised origin variant, and
  `caching.disabled === true`; across the pair: distinct ids, distinct users, and the **same** origin
  — two authorities over one database.
- **`caching.disabled` is not a required field and defaults to `false`** (finding 101). `caching: {}`
  is legal and means the cache is **ON**. A gate written `!== false` passes on absence and attests the
  opposite of the truth, on the path R17 exists for.
- **What Q still will not buy.** `origin.password` is write-only and never returned, so Q proves which
  user each configuration *names* and never that the two secrets differ. The privilege witness —
  `current_user`; the request credential cannot `EXECUTE app.observe_storage_object()`; the jobs
  credential can — is Q's second half and needs the driver.
- **In this topology TLS is not Hyperdrive's to configure** (finding 102). CLOUD_V1 reaches Pigsty
  over Workers VPC → Cloudflare Tunnel, and Cloudflare states that mTLS and `sslmode` cannot be set on
  a Hyperdrive with a VPC-service origin — TLS is managed on the VPC Service. That origin variant also
  carries **no host or port**, only `service_id`, so a check demanding `origin.host` would refuse the
  correct topology.

### 6.11 An authentic channel is not a complete one (P2, findings 99 and 112)

**2026-08-23.** §6.8's case **P** answers *is the thing speaking on this channel really R2?* — one
producer, of type `r2_bucket`, being our bucket, with no unexpected consumer. It never opens the
**bucket's** notification configuration, and those are two different objects in the account. So this
passes case P:

```
producer = OUR R2 bucket        consumer = OUR observer        DLQ = configured
```

while the rule behind it is `actions = [PutObject]`, `prefix = "wrong-prefix/"` — and every
`CopyObject`, every `CompleteMultipartUpload` (which is how a large world chunk lands), and every key
outside that prefix is **never produced at all**. There is no retry budget to exhaust because no
message was ever created: finding 65 arriving with no trace anywhere.

> **CASE P ASKS WHETHER THE THING SPEAKING IS REALLY R2. CASE P2 ASKS WHETHER R2 IS SPEAKING ABOUT
> EVERYTHING. NEITHER IMPLIES THE OTHER.**

`scripts/check-notification-coverage.mjs` reads
`GET /accounts/{a}/event_notifications/r2/{bucket}/configuration` and requires **exactly one rule** to
the attested `PROVIDER_QUEUE` covering all three provider object-create actions, with **no delete action** (M2.0 is
append-only, R56 — and a delete rule would also contradict the premise `inventory.mjs`'s `extra`
refusal rests on), no suffix filter, and a prefix that is absent or a prefix of `org/`. The required
action list is **imported from `reconcile.mjs`**, not retyped, so a fourth admitted action becomes a
coverage requirement without an edit. The bundle had said for two rounds that single-notification is
*"our provisioning obligation, checked at provisioning"* — this is that check; it was a sentence.

### 6.13 The subject of an attestation is not the caller's to choose (findings 104, 105, 106)

**2026-08-24.** Finding 91 ruled that an attestation is meaningful only if its subject is the subject
the runtime later trusts, and closed it for the queue. Three more attestations then took their
subject from the caller's environment, one of them under **the exact variable name finding 91
deleted**, in a file whose header cites finding 91.

```
runtime reads                 the gate was told
[vars] R2_BUCKET              CD_R2_BUCKET            cases P, P2
[vars] PROVIDER_QUEUE         CD_QUEUE_NAME           case P2 — reintroduced
[[hyperdrive]] id             HYPERDRIVE_CONTROL_ID   case Q
[[hyperdrive]] id             HYPERDRIVE_JOBS_ID      case Q
```

MEASURED: change `[vars] R2_BUCKET` to a foreign bucket and every local gate stays green. So this is
reachable — the Worker writes to bucket B while P and P2 prove a perfect configuration for bucket A,
and every object lands **outside the accounting path**. Worse than a lost notification: there is no
anomaly counter, no DLQ, no retry, and the inventory pass enumerates the bucket it was told about.

> **AN ATTESTATION WHOSE SUBJECT IS CALLER-CHOSEN IS A CAPABILITY TO ATTEST THE WRONG SYSTEM.**
> **A LAW CLOSED FOR ONE RESOURCE IS NOT CLOSED.**

- **One derivation.** `scripts/deployment-subjects.mjs` reads `worker/wrangler.toml` and yields the
  Worker name, bucket, queue, DLQ and both Hyperdrive ids. P, P2 and Q take **only**
  `CF_ACCOUNT_ID` and `CF_API_TOKEN` from the environment — credentials, which are not subjects — and
  a retired subject variable is a **refusal**, not a silent override, so an operator who exports the
  old name is told rather than obeyed.
- **The expectations are a ruling too** (finding 106). `worker/topology.json` declares the R7 path:
  database, VPC service id, tunnel id, target, port. A gate handed both its subject and its
  expectation by the caller proves only that the caller was self-consistent.
- **The remaining gap is named.** The derivation reads what a deploy would be made FROM, not the
  deployed Worker's bindings, and reports `origin: "wrangler.toml"` so the difference is visible.
  When something is deployed it should read `GET /accounts/{a}/workers/scripts/{name}/bindings`, and
  a wrangler.toml that disagrees becomes its own refusal.

#### R7 is a claim about a PATH, not about a credential pair (finding 106)

Case Q proved two distinct configurations, two correct logins, one database, caching off — over
`host: "wrong-public-db.example"`. **A correct pair of credentials to the wrong architecture.** An
internet origin means Pigsty answers the public internet with a password, which is the thing §3's
Tunnel exists to make untrue.

So `vpc_service` is required and its `service_id` compared against the ruling — and then the **VPC
Service itself** is read, because the Hyperdrive names only a service_id and everything R7 rules
lives one level down: `type: "tcp"`, `tcp_port`, `app_protocol: "postgresql"`,
`host.network.tunnel_id` (or `resolver_network` for a hostname target), the target address, and
`tls_settings.cert_verification_mode`.

**Finding 102 is upgraded by this.** It recorded that TLS cannot be set on the Hyperdrive in this
topology and stopped there, as a note about something nobody asserted. It *can* be set on the VPC
Service, `verify_full` is the documented default, and `disabled` is legal — so it is exactly the
class of provider default that is correct until someone changes it and nothing notices, which is
what finding 101 was. Case Q refuses `disabled` and notes `verify_ca`.

#### And the evidence package must reproduce its own evidence (finding 104)

The shipped tar omitted two scripts its own tests import: README claimed 340/340, the artifact
produced 297 tests and two `ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND`. The implementation was fine; the **evidence** was
not. The copy list sat directly beneath a comment block stating that an evidence package which
cannot reproduce its own evidence is a claim — written after the same defect one round earlier.

> **A LESSON WRITTEN AS A COMMENT NEXT TO A HAND-MAINTAINED LIST DOES NOT MAINTAIN THE LIST.**

The shipped set is now derived from what the tests import, and the generator **extracts the tar it
just wrote and runs the suite and every shipped gate from that extraction** before publishing. It
went red on its first run, over a second hand-maintained staging list that had never carried
`worker/topology.json`.

### 6.12 The provider boundary is a layer, not a habit (findings 96, 98, 100, 103)

**2026-08-23.** The round that ruled *a fixture invented by the predicate's author tests the
invention* shipped `inventory.mjs` in the same breath, declaring its input as
`{ key, size, etag, uploaded }` with `uploaded` a string — a shape **no** documented R2 listing
interface returns. Thirteen tests passed against it; all three real surfaces were refused.

> **A LESSON LEARNED IN ONE FILE IS NOT LEARNED. IT HAS TO BECOME A SHAPE.**

```
                       normalizeR2ListingPage()  ->  beginSweep()/addPage()/finish()
provider response  ->     the ONLY function            the PROTOCOL that earns
   measured shape         that knows a provider        completeness (107), and
   pasted from CF         (96, 100)                    grants it via WeakSet (113)
                                                                |
                                                                v
                                                       reconciliationPlan()
                                                       pure semantics; cannot be
                                                       handed a provider object,
                                                       a page, or a forgery
```

- **The listing surface is chosen: S3-compatible `ListObjectsV2`.** Cloudflare's *Object Read only*
  token is bucket-scoped and grants list; object-scoped tokens **fail to authenticate** against the
  REST API, which would need an account-wide Admin token, and Cloudflare documents REST as rate
  limited and less suited to object operations. REST is **refused by name** so a future caller is told
  why. The Workers binding is normalized as a second named source — but note an `r2_bucket` binding
  carries write, so it is not the least-authority option.
- **The ETag spelling differs by surface** (finding 100). Cloudflare's schema: JSON list/get responses
  carry the **raw hex digest**; the HTTP `ETag` header follows RFC 7232 and **is quoted**. The
  notification body — where the ledger's etags come from — is raw. So the least-authority listing API
  is exactly the one whose etag does not compare equal, and unnormalized the first pass would report
  **every object divergent** and rewrite every etag to a quoted one. Stripping is idempotent and
  applied to all sources; the live case records which spelling actually arrived.
- **One object-key grammar** (finding 98). `src/objectkey.mjs`. The format had been written three
  times, and the third — `/^org\/[0-9a-f-]{36}\/world\/[0-9a-f-]{36}\/.+/`, in the file that decides
  which keys are ours — accepted a nil uuid and thirty-six dashes. Two implementations are
  unavoidable because one must be in SQL next to the constraint; **three is a choice.** Both
  JavaScript consumers now read one file and the existing shared fixture drives both.
- **Absence is only claimed from a complete listing** (finding 103). `ListObjectsV2` caps at 1000
  keys, and a missed continuation token would have produced a plan alleging an out-of-band delete of
  every object past page one — a false alarm large enough to train an operator to ignore the report
  whose entire job is noticing absence. Completeness is read from the provider's own truncation flag;
  an absent flag is a refusal, not a default.

### 6.3 Control-plane traffic uses a cache-disabled Hyperdrive binding

**R17.** Hyperdrive caches read queries by default. Everything in `cd` is authorization,
tenancy, membership, entitlement or billing state — exactly the class that must not be served from
an edge cache.

The sharper reason is that **the cache cannot see the thing that makes the query safe.** Hyperdrive
observes `SELECT * FROM cd.worlds`. It does not observe PostgreSQL rewriting that internally to
include `app.current_organization_id()`. Two different tenants issue a byte-identical query string
and the correct answers differ. Tenant isolation must not depend on an edge cache correctly
inferring that forever.

```
HYPERDRIVE_CONTROL   caching disabled   auth · permissions · worlds · billing · all of cd
HYPERDRIVE_CACHE     later, if earned   public, non-sensitive, read-mostly projections only
```

**Verify the current defaults first-party at the point of use** — §0.2's rule. This ruling is about
which binding the control plane uses, not about any particular TTL number.

### 6.2 An identity provider is a binding, not an identity

`principals` and `organizations` are provider-independent roots. Keycloak's `sub` and its
organization id live in `principal_identities` / `organization_identities`, with `status`,
`bound_at`, `unbound_at` — so an identity can be rebound without rewriting history.

A faithful restore of the same Keycloak database does preserve its ids; this is not defending
against backups. It is defending against a **clean realm rebuild, a realm migration, an IdP change,
or leaving Keycloak entirely** — any of which reissues subjects. Binding tables make that a rebind
instead of a data-loss event.

## 7. What is NOT in this round

Named so the gap stays visible, per `DOCTRINE.md`.

- **studbook holds nothing** (R15). Its own header says `spec` rung, no implementation, and §10.2 —
  where confidentiality comes from — is unruled. It has no query layer, no auth, no network surface
  and no cross-record transaction, so it cannot hold user state. Seams for pedigreed evidence, yes;
  storage, no.
- **TRVM governs nothing here yet.** Cloud behaviour that is Workers/Postgres/application
  convention gets called that. TRVM ownership is claimed only where the runtime actually checks the
  transition — `TRVM/governance/round-11-ledger.md` is P4's evidence, and none of it is wired to
  Cloud.
- **Remote execution is `SPEC`.** A Cloud request to a node is a *request*. The local runtime
  verifies independently and may refuse. Cloud holding a user's token never bypasses Super's machine
  authority boundary.
- **Presence** is a later substrate question (Durable Objects with WebSocket hibernation are the
  candidate). Not Phoenix Presence — see R7.

retracted in place: `CLAUDE.md` called R4 unruled six days after it was ruled;
`agents/C-infrastructure.md` ruled Keycloak onto Fly while budgeting its RAM onto Hetzner, and
justified PlanetScale against an alternative that no longer exists.

so M2 is no longer blocked on it. R24 moved storage admission ahead of M6 and **M1.5 is built, not
just ruled**. **R30's ruling stands and its mechanism was superseded the same day** — the advisory
lock it named is unsupported by Hyperdrive (§6.4). R33 targets PostgreSQL 17.x for v1.

**Open** — **R31** (write authority may not exceed its reservation) and **R32** (committed bytes are
provider-observed). Both are built against and neither is claimed: R31's byte-exactness is
`live-falsifier.mjs` case B, and R32 exists so the ruling can be made with a measured divergence

production transport does not document:

then `CD_PGBIN=/opt/pgsql-17/bin npm --prefix worker run test:all`.

(`cloud.computedriven.com/tools/render-status.mjs --verify`). The search that "proved" their absence

prove the absence of a constructed string** — and the duplicate was deleted before it became the

## 4.2 Schema — worker/migrations/

### `worker/migrations/0001_roles_and_schemas.sql`

```sql
-- 0001 — roles and schemas
--
-- Lane D owns this file. See CLOUD_V1.md §6.1 and agents/D-worker-auth.md.
--
-- These are the SAME migrations that run against Pigsty. There is no second
-- schema for local development (CLOUD_V1.md §4, M1). In Pigsty the roles are
-- normally created by the cluster provisioner; creating them here idempotently
-- means one file works on a bare cluster and on a provisioned one.
--
-- Role separation is load-bearing, not hygiene:
--   * the API role must NOT own the tables, because a table owner bypasses RLS
--     unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is also set. We set FORCE as well — belt
--     and braces — but the ownership split is the primary defence.
--   * the API role must NOT have BYPASSRLS. 0006 asserts this and the battery
--     re-checks it, because it is the single attribute that silently voids
--     every policy in this schema.

BEGIN;

DO $$
BEGIN
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'computedriven_migrations') THEN
    CREATE ROLE computedriven_migrations NOLOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;
  END IF;
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'computedriven_api') THEN
    CREATE ROLE computedriven_api NOLOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;
  END IF;
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'computedriven_jobs') THEN
    CREATE ROLE computedriven_jobs NOLOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;
  END IF;
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'computedriven_readonly') THEN
    CREATE ROLE computedriven_readonly NOLOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;
  END IF;
  -- Owns the three resolvers in 0005 and nothing else. See the note below.
  IF NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_roles WHERE rolname = 'computedriven_bootstrap') THEN
    CREATE ROLE computedriven_bootstrap NOLOGIN NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE;
  END IF;
END
$$;

-- Lets the migration runner hand ownership of the resolvers to the bootstrap
-- role in 0005 without needing superuser.
GRANT computedriven_bootstrap TO computedriven_migrations;

-- WHY A FOURTH ROLE EXISTS
--
-- Found by the battery, not by design: with FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY on, the
-- table OWNER is policed too -- and the SECURITY DEFINER resolvers in 0005 must
-- read cd.organizations BEFORE any tenant context exists, because deriving that
-- context is precisely their job. Running them as the owner made every login
-- path raise CD-TENANT-MISSING.
--
-- The fix is not to drop FORCE. It is to give the bootstrap path its own role
-- with its own NAMED, NARROW policies (0007). The rule that falls out is worth
-- stating on its own:
--
--     FORCE RLS stays on everywhere, and every exemption is a named policy.
--
-- Nothing bypasses invisibly. `SELECT * FROM pg_policies` is the complete list
-- of who can see across a tenant boundary, and it is short.

-- Defence in depth: even if a future migration forgets, these are never valid.
ALTER ROLE computedriven_api      NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS;
ALTER ROLE computedriven_jobs     NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS;
ALTER ROLE computedriven_readonly NOSUPERUSER NOBYPASSRLS;

-- app: the tenant-context contract and the three resolvers that are allowed to
--      run WITHOUT tenant context (see 0002).
-- cd:  ComputeDriven product truth. Every table here is either tenant-scoped
--      under RLS or unreachable by the API role.
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS app AUTHORIZATION computedriven_migrations;
CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS cd  AUTHORIZATION computedriven_migrations;

COMMENT ON SCHEMA app IS
  'Tenant-context contract. app.current_organization_id() raises rather than '
  'returning NULL — see CLOUD_V1.md 6.1.';
COMMENT ON SCHEMA cd IS
  'ComputeDriven product truth (R7). Pigsty owns this; studbook holds none of it (R15).';

GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA app, cd TO computedriven_api, computedriven_jobs, computedriven_readonly;

COMMIT;
```

### `worker/migrations/0002_tenant_context.sql`

```sql
-- 0002 — the tenant-context contract
--
-- R14: RLS fails closed by RAISING. A missing tenant context is an error, never
-- an empty result set.
--
-- WHY THIS FILE EXISTS AT ALL
--
-- PostgreSQL's current_setting(name, true) returns NULL when the setting is
-- absent, and an RLS USING clause that evaluates to NULL merely *hides the row*.
-- So the naive policy
--
--     USING (organization_id = current_setting('app.organization_id', true)::uuid)
--
-- turns "the server forgot to establish tenant context" into "this organization
-- has no worlds". That is a silent wrong answer in the direction that looks
-- normal, and no happy-path test will ever catch it.
--
-- Every policy in 0006 therefore goes through app.current_organization_id(),
-- whose contract is:
--
--     valid setting      ->  uuid
--     setting missing    ->  RAISE
--     setting malformed  ->  RAISE

BEGIN;

SET LOCAL ROLE computedriven_migrations;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION app.current_organization_id()
RETURNS uuid
LANGUAGE plpgsql
STABLE
AS $$
DECLARE
  raw text;
  val uuid;
BEGIN
  raw := current_setting('app.organization_id', true);

  IF raw IS NULL OR btrim(raw) = '' THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
      USING ERRCODE = '42501',
            MESSAGE = 'CD-TENANT-MISSING: app.organization_id is not set for this transaction',
            HINT    = 'Call app.set_organization_context(<uuid>) inside the transaction, '
                      'with a SERVER-DERIVED organization id. Never one the client sent.';
  END IF;

  BEGIN
    val := raw::uuid;
  EXCEPTION WHEN invalid_text_representation THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
      USING ERRCODE = '42501',
            MESSAGE = format('CD-TENANT-MALFORMED: app.organization_id is not a uuid (%L)', raw);
  END;

  RETURN val;
END;
$$;

COMMENT ON FUNCTION app.current_organization_id() IS
  'Returns the transaction-local tenant context, or RAISES. Never returns NULL. R14.';

-- Establishing context. is_local = true makes it transaction-scoped, which is
-- the correct primitive under a transaction pooler: Hyperdrive (and PgBouncer in
-- transaction mode) hand the connection back at COMMIT and reset transaction
-- state. A plain SET would survive into whichever request got the connection
-- next -- that is the leak this shape avoids, and the battery proves it rather
-- than assuming it.
--
-- The uuid parameter type is deliberate: a malformed id fails at bind time, on
-- the server, before it can reach a policy.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION app.set_organization_context(p_organization_id uuid)
RETURNS void
LANGUAGE plpgsql
VOLATILE
AS $$
BEGIN
  IF p_organization_id IS NULL THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
      USING ERRCODE = '42501',
            MESSAGE = 'CD-TENANT-NULL: refusing to establish a NULL tenant context';
  END IF;
  PERFORM set_config('app.organization_id', p_organization_id::text, true);
END;
$$;

COMMENT ON FUNCTION app.set_organization_context(uuid) IS
  'Transaction-local tenant context. The argument MUST be server-derived.';

COMMIT;
```

### `worker/migrations/0003_identity.sql`

```sql
-- 0003 — identity: provider-independent roots, external bindings beside them
--
-- R10. `principals` and `organizations` are ComputeDriven's own id space.
-- Keycloak's `sub` and its organization id are BINDINGS to that space, held in
-- `principal_identities` / `organization_identities` with status and history.
--
-- The failure this shape defends against is NOT backup/restore -- a faithful
-- restore of the same Keycloak database preserves its ids. It is:
--
--     a clean realm rebuild · a realm migration · an IdP change ·
--     leaving Keycloak entirely
--
-- any of which reissues subjects. With bindings, that is a rebind. With
-- `principals.keycloak_sub`, it is a data-loss event with no recovery path --
-- and CLOUD_V1.md's own release gate rehearses exactly those operations.

BEGIN;

SET LOCAL ROLE computedriven_migrations;

CREATE TABLE cd.principals (
  id         uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  status     text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
             CHECK (status IN ('active', 'suspended', 'closed')),
  created_at timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

COMMENT ON TABLE cd.principals IS
  'A ComputeDriven application identity. Holds no credential and no IdP id (R10).';

CREATE TABLE cd.principal_identities (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  principal_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES cd.principals(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  provider     text NOT NULL,                       -- 'keycloak'
  issuer       text NOT NULL,                       -- OIDC iss
  subject      text NOT NULL,                       -- OIDC sub
  status       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
               CHECK (status IN ('active', 'unbound')),
  bound_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  unbound_at   timestamptz,
  CONSTRAINT principal_identity_unbind_consistent CHECK (
    (status = 'active'  AND unbound_at IS NULL) OR
    (status = 'unbound' AND unbound_at IS NOT NULL)
  )
);

-- Partial-unique on ACTIVE only. Two consequences, both wanted:
--   * the same subject can never have two live bindings (idempotent login);
--   * an unbound row stays as history, and the subject can be rebound later.
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX principal_identities_active_uq
  ON cd.principal_identities (provider, issuer, subject)
  WHERE status = 'active';

CREATE INDEX principal_identities_principal_idx
  ON cd.principal_identities (principal_id);

COMMENT ON TABLE cd.principal_identities IS
  'External IdP bindings. Never store a password or a token here.';

CREATE TABLE cd.organizations (
  id           uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  slug         text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  display_name text NOT NULL,
  status       text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
               CHECK (status IN ('active', 'suspended', 'closed')),
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

COMMENT ON COLUMN cd.organizations.slug IS
  'Human-readable, for routing. NEVER the security boundary -- id is.';

CREATE TABLE cd.organization_identities (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  organization_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES cd.organizations(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  provider        text NOT NULL,
  issuer          text NOT NULL,
  provider_org_id text NOT NULL,
  provider_alias  text,
  status          text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                  CHECK (status IN ('active', 'unbound')),
  bound_at        timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  unbound_at      timestamptz,
  CONSTRAINT organization_identity_unbind_consistent CHECK (
    (status = 'active'  AND unbound_at IS NULL) OR
    (status = 'unbound' AND unbound_at IS NOT NULL)
  )
);

CREATE UNIQUE INDEX organization_identities_active_uq
  ON cd.organization_identities (provider, issuer, provider_org_id)
  WHERE status = 'active';

COMMENT ON COLUMN cd.organization_identities.provider_alias IS
  'The IdP-side human name. Recorded for debugging. Never matched against.';

-- The application shadow. Keycloak stays authoritative for authentication and
-- for who is in an organization; this table is what the product knows about that
-- membership -- app role, first/last seen, local status.
CREATE TABLE cd.organization_principals (
  organization_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES cd.organizations(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  principal_id    uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES cd.principals(id)    ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  app_role        text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'member'
                  CHECK (app_role IN ('owner', 'admin', 'member', 'viewer')),
  status          text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                  CHECK (status IN ('active', 'revoked')),
  first_seen_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  last_seen_at    timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (organization_id, principal_id)
);

COMMENT ON TABLE cd.organization_principals IS
  'Application membership shadow. NOT the auth source -- Keycloak is (R10).';

COMMIT;
```

### `worker/migrations/0004_worlds.sql`

```sql
-- 0004 — worlds, at three named sizes
--
-- R11 / CLOUD_V1.md §2. WORLD_SIZE.md §11 records this being got wrong once:
-- the world layer was measured at 247 KB realistic / 212.70 MB at the shell's
-- caps, and then reported as a conclusion about the product -- which is 100 GB
-- to 10 TB of the user's machine. 0.21% was mistaken for the whole.
--
--   WORLD         the persistent machine-sized environment      10 GB - 10 TB
--   WORLD VERSION a content-addressed root describing it        KB (a root)
--   WRL GRAPH     the semantic layer inside it                  247 KB - 212 MB
--
-- THERE IS NO `current_head` COLUMN ANYWHERE, and there must never be one. A
-- head is always qualified: `manifest_root` is the machine, `wrl_head` is the
-- graph. A column that could hold either is the relapse.

BEGIN;

SET LOCAL ROLE computedriven_migrations;

CREATE TABLE cd.worlds (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  organization_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES cd.organizations(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  name            text NOT NULL,
  status          text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active'
                  CHECK (status IN ('active', 'archived')),
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (organization_id, name),
  -- target for the composite FKs below
  CONSTRAINT worlds_id_org_uq UNIQUE (id, organization_id)
);

COMMENT ON TABLE cd.worlds IS
  'A WORLD is the machine-sized persistent environment (10 GB - 10 TB), not the '
  'shell graph. R11.';

-- One row per synced machine state. Immutable by convention: a new state is a
-- new version, never an UPDATE, so history cannot be rewritten.
CREATE TABLE cd.world_versions (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  world_id        uuid NOT NULL,
  organization_id uuid NOT NULL,
  manifest_root   text   NOT NULL,
  byte_size       bigint NOT NULL CHECK (byte_size  >= 0),
  chunk_count     integer NOT NULL CHECK (chunk_count >= 0),
  created_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  UNIQUE (world_id, manifest_root),
  -- The denormalised organization_id is what RLS filters on, so it must be
  -- impossible for it to disagree with the parent world's. This composite FK
  -- makes a cross-tenant row a CONSTRAINT VIOLATION rather than something a
  -- policy has to catch -- structure beats policy where structure can do it.
  FOREIGN KEY (world_id, organization_id)
    REFERENCES cd.worlds (id, organization_id) ON DELETE RESTRICT
);

CREATE INDEX world_versions_world_created_idx
  ON cd.world_versions (world_id, created_at DESC);

COMMENT ON COLUMN cd.world_versions.manifest_root IS
  'Content address of the MACHINE state. The manifest itself lives in R2; Pigsty '
  'holds refs only, never bytes.';
COMMENT ON COLUMN cd.world_versions.byte_size IS
  'Machine-sized. Expect values in the 1e10 - 1e13 range; bigint is not optional.';

-- The small one. Separate table, separate name, so it can never be confused with
-- a manifest root. ~0.2% of a backup at its ceiling -- it rides along free
-- inside a tier priced for the bulk (WORLD_SIZE.md §11.1).
CREATE TABLE cd.wrl_heads (
  world_id        uuid PRIMARY KEY,
  organization_id uuid NOT NULL,
  wrl_head        text,
  semantic_head   text,
  updated_at      timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  FOREIGN KEY (world_id, organization_id)
    REFERENCES cd.worlds (id, organization_id) ON DELETE RESTRICT
);

COMMENT ON TABLE cd.wrl_heads IS
  'The WRL GRAPH head -- the small semantic/topological layer INSIDE a world '
  '(247 KB - 212 MB). Not the machine state. R11.';

COMMIT;
```

### `worker/migrations/0005_resolvers.sql`

```sql
-- 0005 — the resolvers: the only code allowed to run without tenant context
--
-- Split out of 0002 because these reference tables created in 0003/0004, and a
-- LANGUAGE sql function is validated at CREATE time.

BEGIN;

SET LOCAL ROLE computedriven_migrations;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- The resolvers.
--
-- These are the ONLY functions permitted to run without tenant context, for a
-- reason that is easy to miss: the code that DERIVES tenant context cannot
-- itself require it. Login order is
--
--     verified OIDC token -> principal -> organization -> context -> queries
--
-- and the first three steps happen before there is a context to set.
--
-- They are SECURITY DEFINER and owned by computedriven_migrations, so they run
-- outside RLS. That is a deliberate, narrow escape hatch: three functions with
-- one job each, rather than granting the API role direct DML on the identity
-- tables. 0006 grants the API role EXECUTE on these and NO table privileges on
-- cd.principals / cd.principal_identities / cd.organization_identities.
--
-- search_path is pinned on each, because a SECURITY DEFINER function with a
-- caller-controlled search_path is a privilege-escalation primitive.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION app.resolve_principal(
  p_provider text,
  p_issuer   text,
  p_subject  text
)
RETURNS uuid
LANGUAGE plpgsql
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = cd, pg_temp
AS $$
DECLARE
  found uuid;
  fresh uuid;
BEGIN
  IF p_provider IS NULL OR p_issuer IS NULL OR p_subject IS NULL
     OR btrim(p_provider) = '' OR btrim(p_issuer) = '' OR btrim(p_subject) = '' THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
      USING ERRCODE = '22023',
            MESSAGE = 'CD-IDENTITY-INCOMPLETE: provider, issuer and subject are all required';
  END IF;

  SELECT pi.principal_id INTO found
  FROM cd.principal_identities pi
  WHERE pi.provider = p_provider
    AND pi.issuer   = p_issuer
    AND pi.subject  = p_subject
    AND pi.status   = 'active';

  IF found IS NOT NULL THEN
    RETURN found;                       -- idempotent: same subject, same principal
  END IF;

  INSERT INTO cd.principals DEFAULT VALUES RETURNING id INTO fresh;

  INSERT INTO cd.principal_identities (principal_id, provider, issuer, subject)
  VALUES (fresh, p_provider, p_issuer, p_subject);

  RETURN fresh;
END;
$$;

COMMENT ON FUNCTION app.resolve_principal(text, text, text) IS
  'Idempotently maps an external OIDC identity to a ComputeDriven principal. '
  'The IdP subject is a BINDING, not the identity (R10).';

-- Organizations are NOT auto-created. Provisioning one is a deliberate act with
-- billing consequences; a login that names an unknown organization is a refusal,
-- not an invitation to create it.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION app.resolve_organization(
  p_provider        text,
  p_issuer          text,
  p_provider_org_id text
)
RETURNS uuid
LANGUAGE plpgsql
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = cd, pg_temp
AS $$
DECLARE
  found uuid;
BEGIN
  SELECT oi.organization_id INTO found
  FROM cd.organization_identities oi
  JOIN cd.organizations o ON o.id = oi.organization_id
  WHERE oi.provider        = p_provider
    AND oi.issuer          = p_issuer
    AND oi.provider_org_id = p_provider_org_id
    AND oi.status          = 'active'
    AND o.status           = 'active';

  IF found IS NULL THEN
    RAISE EXCEPTION
      USING ERRCODE = '42501',
            MESSAGE = format('CD-ORG-UNBOUND: no active organization bound to %L/%L',
                             p_provider, p_provider_org_id);
  END IF;

  RETURN found;
END;
$$;

COMMENT ON FUNCTION app.resolve_organization(text, text, text) IS
  'Maps an external IdP organization id to an internal organization id. Refuses '
  'unknown organizations; does not create them.';

-- Membership. Holding a token that names an organization is not authority over
-- it -- CLOUD_V1.md, the core law. This is the check that turns identity into
-- permission, and it is the last gate before context is established.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION app.authorize_membership(
  p_principal_id    uuid,
  p_organization_id uuid
)
RETURNS boolean
LANGUAGE sql
SECURITY DEFINER
SET search_path = cd, pg_temp
STABLE
AS $$
  SELECT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM cd.organization_principals op
    WHERE op.principal_id    = p_principal_id
      AND op.organization_id = p_organization_id
      AND op.status          = 'active'
  );
$$;

COMMENT ON FUNCTION app.authorize_membership(uuid, uuid) IS
  'A valid token saying you belong to org A does not itself grant authority. This does.';

-- Ownership: these three run as computedriven_bootstrap, which holds exactly the
-- narrow policies in 0007 and nothing else. See 0001 for why this role exists.
--
-- Transferring ownership of a function requires the incoming owner to hold
-- CREATE on its schema. Granted for the transfer and revoked immediately, so at
-- rest the bootstrap role has USAGE and cannot create anything in app.
GRANT USAGE, CREATE ON SCHEMA app TO computedriven_bootstrap;

ALTER FUNCTION app.resolve_principal(text, text, text)    OWNER TO computedriven_bootstrap;
ALTER FUNCTION app.resolve_organization(text, text, text) OWNER TO computedriven_bootstrap;
ALTER FUNCTION app.authorize_membership(uuid, uuid)       OWNER TO computedriven_bootstrap;

REVOKE CREATE ON SCHEMA app FROM computedriven_bootstrap;

-- cd.principals and cd.principal_identities carry no RLS (a principal is not
-- tenant-owned -- one human can be in several organizations), so the bootstrap
-- role reaches them by grant rather than by policy.
GRANT USAGE ON SCHEMA cd TO computedriven_bootstrap;
GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON cd.principals, cd.principal_identities TO computedriven_bootstrap;
GRANT SELECT ON cd.organization_identities TO computedriven_bootstrap;

-- A policy admits; a GRANT is still required. The two are independent gates and
-- needing both is the point: 0007 gives this role a SELECT policy on these two
-- tables, and without the grant below the policy alone reaches nothing. Read-only
-- on purpose -- the bootstrap path resolves identity and never mutates a tenant.
GRANT SELECT ON cd.organizations, cd.organization_principals TO computedriven_bootstrap;

COMMIT;
```

### `worker/migrations/0006_audit.sql`

```sql
-- 0006 — audit events
--
-- Enough to make the M1 lifecycle visible: who did what, in which organization.
-- Not a receipt. A receipt names authority, placement and an executing node, and
-- none of those exist until M3/M4 -- calling this one would be an overclaim.

BEGIN;

SET LOCAL ROLE computedriven_migrations;

CREATE TABLE cd.audit_events (
  id              uuid PRIMARY KEY DEFAULT gen_random_uuid(),
  organization_id uuid NOT NULL REFERENCES cd.organizations(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  principal_id    uuid REFERENCES cd.principals(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT,
  action          text NOT NULL,
  subject_kind    text,
  subject_id      text,
  outcome         text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ok'
                  CHECK (outcome IN ('ok', 'refused', 'failed')),
  detail          jsonb NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}'::jsonb,
  occurred_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE INDEX audit_events_org_time_idx
  ON cd.audit_events (organization_id, occurred_at DESC);

COMMENT ON COLUMN cd.audit_events.outcome IS
  'refused and failed are DIFFERENT. A refusal is the system working.';

COMMIT;
```

### `worker/migrations/0007_rls.sql`

```sql
-- 0007 — row-level security, and the privilege split it rests on
--
-- Layering, per CLOUD_V1.md. RLS is the LAST line, never the only one:
--
--     1. verified OIDC identity
--     2. verified organization membership     app.authorize_membership()
--     3. application authorization            the Worker
--     4. resource ownership / grant
--     5. RLS                                  <- this file, defence in depth
--
-- Two things here are easy to get wrong and both are fatal in the quiet way:
--
--   FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY -- without it, the TABLE OWNER bypasses every
--   policy below. ENABLE alone is not enough. The battery asserts FORCE is on
--   for every tenant table, because "we enabled RLS" is exactly the sentence
--   people say right before a cross-tenant read.
--
--   NOBYPASSRLS on the API role -- the single role attribute that silently
--   voids this entire file. Asserted at the bottom, and re-checked by the
--   battery from a different angle.

BEGIN;

SET LOCAL ROLE computedriven_migrations;

-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
-- Tenant tables: RLS on, FORCEd, one policy each.
-- ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

ALTER TABLE cd.organizations           ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.organizations           FORCE  ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.organization_principals ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.organization_principals FORCE  ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.worlds                  ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.worlds                  FORCE  ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.world_versions          ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.world_versions          FORCE  ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.wrl_heads               ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.wrl_heads               FORCE  ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.audit_events            ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
ALTER TABLE cd.audit_events            FORCE  ROW LEVEL SECURITY;

-- Policies are scoped TO explicit roles rather than left at PUBLIC. A role with
```
