### `cloud.computedriven.com/tools/render-status.mjs`

```javascript
#!/usr/bin/env node
// Render status.json into the public pages, or verify they have not drifted.
//
//   node tools/render-status.mjs           write
//   node tools/render-status.mjs --verify  exit 1 if any page disagrees
//
// WHY THIS EXISTS
//
// Statuses hand-copied across pages drift, and they drift in the flattering
// direction. This tree has the receipts: a law count published as 116 while the
// suite derived 118, and a ladder rung that changed the day after it was
// written down. So no page hand-writes a rung. They are written between
// sentinels from one file, and --verify is a release gate.
//
// Zero dependencies on purpose -- a status renderer that needs an install step
// is a status renderer that stops being run.

import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { dirname, join } from "node:path";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";

const HERE = dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url));
const SITE = join(HERE, "..");
const VERIFY = process.argv.includes("--verify");

const status = JSON.parse(readFileSync(join(SITE, "status.json"), "utf8"));

const esc = (s) =>
  String(s).replace(/&/g, "&amp;").replace(/</g, "&lt;").replace(/>/g, "&gt;");

const RUNG_ORDER = ["live", "staged", "local", "spec"];
const byRung = (a, b) =>
  RUNG_ORDER.indexOf(a.rung) - RUNG_ORDER.indexOf(b.rung) ||
  a.label.localeCompare(b.label);

function counts() {
  const c = {};
  for (const r of Object.keys(status.rungs)) c[r] = 0;
  for (const cap of status.capabilities) c[cap.rung]++;
  return c;
}

// --- the blocks -------------------------------------------------------------

function renderBanner() {
  const c = counts();
  const total = status.capabilities.length;
  return `<p class="banner" role="status">
  <strong>Nothing here is deployed.</strong>
  Of ${total} capabilities, <b>${c.local}</b> run and are tested on a developer machine
  and <b>${c.spec}</b> are written down and not built.
  <b>${c.live}</b> are serving the public.
  <a href="/status">The full table</a> says which is which, as of ${esc(status.as_of)}.
</p>`;
}

function renderTable() {
  const rows = [...status.capabilities].sort(byRung).map(
    (c) => `    <tr>
      <th scope="row">${esc(c.label)}</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-${esc(c.rung)}">${esc(c.rung)}</span></td>
      <td>${esc(c.note)}</td>
      <td><code>${esc(c.evidence)}</code></td>
    </tr>`
  );
  return `<table class="status">
  <caption>Capability rungs, as of ${esc(status.as_of)} — ${esc(status.round)}</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Capability</th><th scope="col">Rung</th><th scope="col">What that means here</th><th scope="col">Where to check</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
${rows.join("\n")}
  </tbody>
</table>`;
}

function renderLegend() {
  const items = RUNG_ORDER.map(
    (r) =>
      `  <dt><span class="rung rung-${r}">${r}</span></dt>\n  <dd>${esc(status.rungs[r])}</dd>`
  );
  return `<dl class="legend">\n${items.join("\n")}\n</dl>`;
}

function renderBattery() {
  const b = status.battery;
  return `<table>
  <caption><code>${esc(b.command)}</code> — ${b.total} checks, mostly negative, as of ${esc(b.as_of)}</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Run</th><th scope="col">Passed</th><th scope="col">Failed</th><th scope="col">What it demonstrates</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Normal</th>
      <td class="num">${b.normal_passed}</td>
      <td class="num">${b.normal_failed}</td>
      <td>Cross-tenant reads, writes, updates and deletes all refuse.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Sabotaged</th>
      <td class="num">${b.sabotage_passed}</td>
      <td class="num">${b.sabotage_failed}</td>
      <td>With the naive function installed, an unscoped query returns <code>0</code> rows and reports success. The battery catches it.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Regression proof</th>
      <td class="num">${b.total - b.regression_failed}</td>
      <td class="num">${b.regression_failed}</td>
      <td>With migrations ${esc(b.regression_removed)} removed, the checks added for those defects fail — so they are load-bearing, not decorative.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Concurrency</th>
      <td class="num">${b.concurrency_passed ?? "—"}</td>
      <td class="num">${b.concurrency_failed ?? "—"}</td>
      <td>Two real sessions, hand-stepped to a deliberate interleaving — <code>${esc(b.concurrency_command ?? "")}</code>. Simultaneous first logins resolve to one principal; simultaneous quota requests cannot oversubscribe. Serial correctness is not concurrent correctness.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Worker suite</th>
      <td class="num">${b.worker_tests}</td>
      <td class="num">${b.worker_failed}</td>
      <td>Token verification, tenant context, credential scoping, provider refinement and storage admission — <code>${esc(b.worker_command)}</code>. No account, no network, no dependencies.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Worker mutations</th>
      <td class="num">${b.worker_mutations_caught}</td>
      <td class="num">${b.worker_mutations_total - b.worker_mutations_caught}</td>
      <td>Each vector breaks one security decision in a copy of the source and re-runs the unmodified suite. A surviving mutation is an untested decision.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>`;
}

// --- the auth surface -------------------------------------------------------
//
// Sign-in is the one control a visitor tries before reading anything, so it is
// the worst possible place for a hand-written status. It appears in the header
// of every page and in the foot of every page -- fourteen copies of one fact --
// and the fact is `portal_login`'s rung. So the header tag and the footer note
// are generated from status.json like everything else, and the day portal
// sign-in leaves `spec` they change on every page in one command rather than in
// fourteen edits, thirteen of which would be made and one of which would not.

function cap(key) {
  const c = status.capabilities.find((c) => c.key === key);
  if (!c) throw new Error(`status.json has no capability "${key}" — the auth blocks name it`);
  return c;
}

// The chain a sign-in actually has to walk. Listed by key so a relabelled
// capability follows its label here instead of silently dropping out.
const SIGNIN_CHAIN = [
  "keycloak_realm",
  "portal_login",
  "token_verification",
  "identity_mapping",
  "stable_org_identity",
];

function renderAuthCta(page) {
  const c = cap("portal_login");
  const tag = c.rung === "live" ? "" : ` <span class="tag">${esc(c.rung)}</span>`;
  const current = page === "auth.html" ? ' aria-current="page"' : "";
  return `<a class="site-auth" href="/auth"${current}>Sign in${tag}</a>`;
}

function renderFootAuth() {
  const c = cap("portal_login");
  const note =
    c.rung === "live"
      ? "Accounts, organizations, and enrolling a machine into a fleet."
      : `There is no sign-in yet — <code>portal_login</code> stands at <b>${esc(c.rung)}</b>. The auth page says what has to exist before there is a door here, and <a href="/status">the status table</a> carries the rung.`;
  return `<div class="foot-auth">
  <a class="foot-auth-cta" href="/auth">Sign in &rarr;</a>
  <p class="foot-auth-note">${note}</p>
</div>`;
}

function renderSignin() {
  const rows = SIGNIN_CHAIN.map(cap).map(
    (c) => `    <tr>
      <th scope="row">${esc(c.label)}</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-${esc(c.rung)}">${esc(c.rung)}</span></td>
      <td>${esc(c.note)}</td>
    </tr>`
  );
  return `<table>
  <caption>What a sign-in has to walk through, and where each part stands as of ${esc(status.as_of)}</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Part</th><th scope="col">Rung</th><th scope="col">What that means here</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
${rows.join("\n")}
  </tbody>
</table>`;
}

const BLOCKS = {
  banner: renderBanner,
  table: renderTable,
  legend: renderLegend,
  battery: renderBattery,
  authcta: renderAuthCta,
  footauth: renderFootAuth,
  signin: renderSignin,
};

// --- apply ------------------------------------------------------------------

// 404.html and auth.html carry no rung table, but they do carry the header's
// auth control and the footer's, so they are in the gate for the same reason
// the others are: a page the renderer does not know about is a page that drifts.
const PAGES = [
  "index.html",
  "architecture.html",
  "security.html",
  "pricing.html",
  "status.html",
  "auth.html",
  "404.html",
];

let drifted = 0;
let wrote = 0;

for (const page of PAGES) {
  const path = join(SITE, page);
  let html;
  try {
    html = readFileSync(path, "utf8");
  } catch {
    console.error(`  missing  ${page}`);
    drifted++;
    continue;
  }

  let next = html;
  for (const [name, render] of Object.entries(BLOCKS)) {
    const re = new RegExp(
      `(<!-- STATUS:${name}:BEGIN -->)([\\s\\S]*?)(<!-- STATUS:${name}:END -->)`,
      "g"
    );
    // Renderers take the page name so a block can mark itself current on the
    // page it points at. Most ignore it; the header's auth control does not.
    next = next.replace(re, (_m, open, _body, close) => `${open}\n${render(page)}\n${close}`);
  }

  if (next === html) continue;
  if (VERIFY) {
    console.error(`  DRIFT    ${page} — regenerate with: node tools/render-status.mjs`);
    drifted++;
  } else {
    writeFileSync(path, next);
    console.log(`  wrote    ${page}`);
    wrote++;
  }
}

if (VERIFY) {
  if (drifted) {
    console.error(`\n  ${drifted} page(s) disagree with status.json\n`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  console.log(`  ok       ${PAGES.length} pages agree with status.json`);
} else {
  console.log(`  ok       ${wrote} page(s) updated from status.json`);
}
```

### `cloud.computedriven.com/tools/check-assets.mjs`

```javascript
#!/usr/bin/env node
// M0 acceptance check: every locally-referenced asset actually exists on disk.
//
//   node tools/check-assets.mjs
//
// WHY
//
// An outside reviewer noticed the review tarball referenced `/amp-nav.js` and
// `/fonts/*.woff2` without containing them, and could not tell whether the site
// was deployable or whether the nav would render as an empty custom element.
// The files were present in the repo -- the tarball excludes them deliberately
// to save 120 KB -- but "I checked once by hand" is not an acceptance criterion.
//
// The failure this guards against is specific and quiet: a missing amp-nav.js
// does not break the page. `<amp-nav>` is an unregistered custom element, so it
// renders as an empty inline box and the site looks fine while the portfolio
// navigation is simply gone.
//
// Exit code is the number of missing assets, so it works as a gate.

import { readFileSync, existsSync, readdirSync, statSync } from "node:fs";
import { dirname, join, resolve } from "node:path";
import { fileURLToPath } from "node:url";

const SITE = resolve(dirname(fileURLToPath(import.meta.url)), "..");

function walk(dir) {
  return readdirSync(dir).flatMap((e) => {
    const p = join(dir, e);
    if (e === "fonts" || e === "tools" || e.startsWith(".")) return [];
    return statSync(p).isDirectory() ? walk(p) : [p];
  });
}

const sources = walk(SITE).filter((p) => /\.(html|css)$/.test(p));

// Local, root-relative references only. External URLs are a different question
// and a strict CSP problem, not a packaging one.
const PATTERNS = [
  /(?:href|src)\s*=\s*["'](\/[^"'#?]+)["']/g,
  /url\(\s*["']?(\/[^"')?#]+)["']?\s*\)/g,
];

const refs = new Map(); // asset path -> [referrers]
for (const file of sources) {
  const text = readFileSync(file, "utf8");
  for (const re of PATTERNS) {
    for (const m of text.matchAll(re)) {
      const p = m[1];
      // Extensionless routes are Pages' own rewriting, not files on disk.
      if (!/\.[a-z0-9]+$/i.test(p)) continue;
      if (!refs.has(p)) refs.set(p, []);
      refs.get(p).push(file.slice(SITE.length + 1));
    }
  }
}

let missing = 0;
const rows = [...refs.entries()].sort();
for (const [asset, referrers] of rows) {
  const onDisk = join(SITE, asset);
  const ok = existsSync(onDisk);
  const size = ok ? `${(statSync(onDisk).size / 1024).toFixed(1)} KB` : "—";
  if (!ok) missing++;
  console.log(
    `  ${ok ? "ok  " : "MISS"}  ${asset.padEnd(34)} ${size.padStart(9)}   ${
      [...new Set(referrers)].length
    } page(s)`
  );
}

console.log("");
if (missing) {
  console.error(`  ${missing} referenced asset(s) missing — the site is NOT deployable\n`);
  process.exit(missing);
}
console.log(`  ok       ${rows.length} referenced assets all present\n`);
```

```html
            <section class="hero">
                <div class="ht" data-ht>
                    <canvas class="ht-canvas" aria-hidden="true"></canvas>

                        <h1>One world.<br />Any machine.</h1>

<p class="banner" role="status">
  <strong>Nothing here is deployed.</strong>

  <a href="/status">The full table</a> says which is which, as of 2026-08-22.
</p>
<!-- STATUS:banner:END -->
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>What the product actually claims</h2>
                <figure class="fig">
                    <pre>
LOCAL ──┐
        │
FLEET ──┼── WORLD ── authority ── run ── receipt
        │
CLOUD ──┘</pre
                    >
                    <figcaption>
                        One placement model, three kinds of machine. Not three products.
                        <span class="dim"
                            >(A scheduler that acts on this is M4 — see
                            <a href="/status">status</a>.)</span
                        >
                    </figcaption>
                </figure>
                <p>
                    A world moves between machines. <strong>Authority does not travel with
                    it.</strong> A restored world on a second machine is not the first machine
                    wearing its clothes — it is a new machine that has been <em>granted</em>
                    the world, and the grant is a separate act that can be refused.
                </p>
                <p>
                    That distinction is the whole product, and it is why the sync-and-restore
                    round ships before the hosted-compute round. A machine we rent you proves
                    nothing that a machine you already own does not prove better.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>A world is bigger than you think, and the interesting part is free</h2>
                <p>
                    "World" gets used for two things whose sizes differ by four orders of
                    magnitude, so here both have their own name and neither borrows the
                    other's.
                </p>
                <div class="scroll">
                    <table>
                        <thead>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="col">Term</th>
                                <th scope="col">What it is</th>
                                <th scope="col">Size</th>
                            </tr>
                        </thead>
                        <tbody>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">World</th>
                                <td>the persistent machine-sized environment</td>
                                <td class="num">10 GB – 10 TB</td>
                            </tr>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">World version</th>
                                <td>a content-addressed root describing it at one instant</td>
                                <td class="num">a hash</td>
                            </tr>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">WRL graph</th>
                                <td>the semantic and topological layer inside it</td>
                                <td class="num">247 KB – 213 MB</td>
                            </tr>
                        </tbody>
                    </table>
                </div>
                <p>
                    Measured, not estimated: the graph is <strong>0.21%</strong> of a 100 GB
                    backup at its enforced ceiling, and 0.0002% in ordinary use. So the
                    differentiated part — the provenance, the tracks, the history of every
                    attempt — <strong>rides along nearly free inside a tier priced for the
                    bulk.</strong> You pay for the machine-sized state; the WRL graph beside it
                    costs almost nothing to carry.
                </p>
            </section>

                        <h3><a href="https://traaviis.com/">TRAAVIIS</a></h3>
```

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8" />
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
        <title>Architecture — [World] Cloud</title>
        <meta
            name="description"
            content="Keycloak identifies the subject. Pigsty owns ComputeDriven truth. The node key identifies the machine. Where each part runs, and the three identities that must never collapse into one."
        />
        <link rel="canonical" href="https://cloud.computedriven.com/architecture" />
        <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/site.css" />
    </head>
    <body>
        <header class="site">
            <div class="site-bar">
                <a class="site-logo" href="https://computedriven.com" aria-label="ComputeDriven — the studio [World] Cloud is one of three properties of"><b>[World]</b> Cloud<span class="bto" aria-hidden="true">&#8599;</span><span class="bto bto-w" aria-hidden="true">computedriven.com</span></a>
                <nav class="site-links" aria-label="Primary">
                    <a href="/">Overview</a>
                    <a href="/architecture" aria-current="page">Architecture</a>
                    <a href="/security">Security</a>
                    <a href="/pricing">Pricing</a>
                    <a href="/status">Status</a>
                </nav>
                <!-- STATUS:authcta:BEGIN -->
<a class="site-auth" href="/auth">Sign in <span class="tag">spec</span></a>
<!-- STATUS:authcta:END -->
            </div>
        </header>
        <main>
            <section>
                <h1>Architecture</h1>
                <p class="lede">
                    One sentence carries most of it:
                    <span class="thesis"
                        >Keycloak identifies the subject. Pigsty owns ComputeDriven truth. The
                        node key identifies the machine.</span
                    >
                </p>

                <!-- STATUS:banner:BEGIN -->
<p class="banner" role="status">
  <strong>Nothing here is deployed.</strong>
  Of 40 capabilities, <b>24</b> run and are tested on a developer machine
  and <b>16</b> are written down and not built.
  <b>0</b> are serving the public.
  <a href="/status">The full table</a> says which is which, as of 2026-08-22.
</p>
<!-- STATUS:banner:END -->
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>Where things run</h2>
                <figure class="fig">
                    <pre>
                    IDENTITY
              Keycloak  ·  Fly iad
                       │
              PlanetScale PS-5 HA
              KEYCLOAK DATABASE ONLY
                       │
                       ▼
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
                  CLOUDFLARE
    marketing · portal BFF · API · authorization
      R2 credential minting · presence (later)
                       │
                   Hyperdrive
                       │
                  Workers VPC
                       │
                Cloudflare Tunnel
                       │
                       ▼
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
                    HETZNER
                   PIGSTY PG
           queryable ComputeDriven truth
                       │
                       │ refs only — never bytes
                       ▼
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
                       R2
              machine-sized worlds
            chunks · manifests · data
 ──────────────────────────────────────────────
                       ▲
                       │  direct transfer, scoped credential
                       │
              SUPER / USER MACHINES
           compute + local authority</pre
                    >
                    <figcaption>
                        Three assertions, each of which was nearly lost — see below.
                    </figcaption>
                </figure>

                <h3>The control plane runs on Workers, not on a server</h3>
                <p>
                    Cloudflare Workers are V8 isolates: JavaScript and WebAssembly, no BEAM.
                    Our own runtime, Super (CD), is Elixir/OTP — and that is
                    <em>not</em> a reason for the cloud to be. Super being Elixir is a fact
                    about the user's machine. Hyperdrive lets a Worker reach a private
                    PostgreSQL over a Workers VPC and a Cloudflare Tunnel, so Pigsty keeps its
                    guarantees without exposing a Postgres port to the internet.
                </p>

                <h3>Bytes never pass through the Worker</h3>
                <figure class="fig">
                    <pre>
Super / client
      │  authenticate  ───────────►  Worker
      │                                ├── resolve principal + organization
      │                                ├── consult Pigsty
      │                                ├── authorize the requested object scope
      │                                └── mint a scoped, short-lived credential
      │  ◄──────────────────────────────┘
      │
      └──────────── chunks ───────────►  R2      direct</pre
                    >
                    <figcaption>
                        Not <code>client → Worker → 400 GB → R2</code>. The credential already
                        carries the authorization; a proxy in the byte path buys nothing and
                        costs everything.
                    </figcaption>
                </figure>

                <h3>Pigsty holds references, never payloads</h3>
                <p>
                    Bytes in Postgres cost roughly 18.7× what they cost in object storage. The
                    database holds the hash, the size, the ownership and the linkage; R2 holds
                    the chunks. That split is what makes a 10 TB customer arithmetic rather
                    than a catastrophe.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>Three identities that must never collapse</h2>
                <p>
                    The failure this prevents is mundane and expensive: someone rebuilds a
                    virtual machine and history quietly rewrites itself.
                </p>
                <figure class="fig">
                    <pre>
principal_id       the human or service asking
node_id            the ComputeDriven execution identity
provider_id        the infrastructure incarnation  (e.g. a Hetzner server id)</pre
                    >
                    <figcaption>
                        A provider's server id, an IP address, a hostname or an IdP alias is
                        never the authority identity.
                    </figcaption>
                </figure>
                <p>
                    So a hosted allocation — "keep one 16-core runner available" — is durable
                    customer intent, and the machine currently serving it is an
                    <em>incarnation</em> of that intent. Destroy and rebuild the machine and
                    the allocation survives with a new incarnation. The receipts that named
                    the old one stay true, because they named something that really did exist.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>An identity provider is a binding, not an identity</h2>
                <p>
                    <code>principals</code> and <code>organizations</code> are ComputeDriven's
                    own id space. Keycloak's subject and its organization id live beside them
                    in <code>principal_identities</code> and
                    <code>organization_identities</code>, each with a status and a history.
                </p>
                <p>
                    This is not a defence against backups — a faithful restore of the same
                    Keycloak database keeps its ids. It is a defence against a clean realm
                    rebuild, a realm migration, an identity-provider change, or leaving
                    Keycloak entirely. With bindings, each of those is a rebind. With a
                    <code>keycloak_sub</code> column on the user row, each is a data-loss event
                    with no recovery path.
                </p>
            </section>

            <nav class="pages" aria-label="Sections">
                <a href="/">Overview</a>
                <a href="/architecture" aria-current="page">Architecture</a>
                <a href="/security">Security</a>
                <a href="/pricing">Pricing</a>
                <a href="/status">Status</a>
            </nav>
        </main>

        <footer>
            <!-- STATUS:footauth:BEGIN -->
<div class="foot-auth">
  <a class="foot-auth-cta" href="/auth">Sign in &rarr;</a>
  <p class="foot-auth-note">There is no sign-in yet — <code>portal_login</code> stands at <b>spec</b>. The auth page says what has to exist before there is a door here, and <a href="/status">the status table</a> carries the rung.</p>
</div>
<!-- STATUS:footauth:END -->
            <p>Every rung on this page is generated from <code>status.json</code>.</p>
            <div class="foot-fam">
                <span>One system, three ways in</span>
                <span class="ff-links">
                    <a href="https://tr.computedriven.com/">T&amp;R</a>
                    <a href="https://super.computedriven.com">Super (CD)</a>
                    <b>[World] Cloud</b>
                    <a href="https://computedriven.com">computedriven.com <span aria-hidden="true">&#8599;</span></a>
```

### `cloud.computedriven.com/security.html`

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
    <head>
        <meta charset="UTF-8" />
        <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0" />
        <title>Security — [World] Cloud</title>
        <meta
            name="description"
            content="How tenants are kept apart, why a missing tenant context raises instead of returning nothing, and what this does not solve. Includes the negative-control result for the isolation battery."
        />
        <link rel="canonical" href="https://cloud.computedriven.com/security" />
        <link rel="stylesheet" href="/assets/site.css" />
    </head>
    <body>
        <header class="site">
            <div class="site-bar">
                <a class="site-logo" href="https://computedriven.com" aria-label="ComputeDriven — the studio [World] Cloud is one of three properties of"><b>[World]</b> Cloud<span class="bto" aria-hidden="true">&#8599;</span><span class="bto bto-w" aria-hidden="true">computedriven.com</span></a>
                <nav class="site-links" aria-label="Primary">
                    <a href="/">Overview</a>
                    <a href="/architecture">Architecture</a>
                    <a href="/security" aria-current="page">Security</a>
                    <a href="/pricing">Pricing</a>
                    <a href="/status">Status</a>
                </nav>
                <!-- STATUS:authcta:BEGIN -->
<a class="site-auth" href="/auth">Sign in <span class="tag">spec</span></a>
<!-- STATUS:authcta:END -->
            </div>
        </header>
        <main>
            <section>
                <h1>Security</h1>
                <p class="lede">
                    Two claims here are worth more than a page of assurances: what the
                    isolation tests do when we deliberately break the code, and what this
                    design explicitly does not protect you from.
                </p>

                <!-- STATUS:banner:BEGIN -->
<p class="banner" role="status">
  <strong>Nothing here is deployed.</strong>
  Of 40 capabilities, <b>24</b> run and are tested on a developer machine
  and <b>16</b> are written down and not built.
  <b>0</b> are serving the public.
  <a href="/status">The full table</a> says which is which, as of 2026-08-22.
</p>
<!-- STATUS:banner:END -->
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>Authorization is layered. Row-level security is the last layer, never the only one.</h2>
                <figure class="fig">
                    <pre>
1.  verified OIDC identity
2.  verified organization membership
3.  application authorization
4.  resource ownership / grant
5.  PostgreSQL row-level security      ← defence in depth</pre
                    >
                    <figcaption>
                        A system that relies on step 5 alone has one bug between a customer and
                        someone else's data.
                    </figcaption>
                </figure>
                <p>
                    Tenant context is derived on the server from a verified token. An
                    organization id supplied by a browser is never trusted, and it is not the
                    thing the database is told.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>A missing tenant context is an error, not an empty result</h2>
                <p>
                    This is the subtle one. PostgreSQL's
                    <code>current_setting(name, true)</code> returns <code>NULL</code> when a
                    setting is absent, and a security policy that evaluates to NULL merely
                    <em>hides the row</em>. So the obvious implementation turns "the server
                    forgot to establish tenant context" into "this organization has no data" —
                    a silent wrong answer, in the direction that looks perfectly normal, that
                    no ordinary test will ever catch.
                </p>
                <figure class="fig">
                    <pre>
valid context      →  uuid
context missing    →  RAISE
context malformed  →  RAISE</pre
                    >
                    <figcaption>
                        Every policy in the schema goes through one function with this
                        contract. It has no code path that returns nothing.
                    </figcaption>
                </figure>

                <h3>The exact boundary, because the first version of this claim was too broad</h3>
                <p>
                    A policy expression is evaluated per row. So a statement the query planner
                    can prove scans nothing never reaches that function and never raises. We
                    measured where the line actually falls, and it is narrower than we first
                    assumed — an <em>empty table</em> still raises, because the scan is still
                    planned. Only a constant-false qualifier removes it:
                </p>
                <figure class="fig">
                    <pre>
SELECT ... FROM cd.worlds WHERE false     no raise, returns 0   ← the whole gap
SELECT ... FROM cd.audit_events (empty)   RAISES
SELECT ... FROM cd.worlds LIMIT 0         RAISES
SELECT ... FROM cd.worlds                 RAISES</pre
                    >
                    <figcaption>
                        Asserted as a known limit in the battery, so it cannot be quietly
                        rediscovered later.
                    </figcaption>
                </figure>
                <p>
                    So the guarantee the database makes is
                    <strong>no row may pass without a valid tenant context</strong> — not "every
                    statement raises". The difference does not weaken the isolation, since a
                    statement that returns no rows leaks nothing. It does mean the raise is a
                    loud backstop rather than the primary control, and the application
                    establishes tenant context on entering a transaction rather than relying on
                    a policy to notice later.
                </p>
                <p>
                    Row-level security is enabled <em>and forced</em> on every tenant table, so
                    the table owner is policed too. Every exemption from that is a named,
                    listable policy — there are exactly two, both read-only, both belonging to
                    the login path that resolves an identity before a tenant context can exist.
                    Nothing bypasses invisibly.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>The negative control</h2>
                <p>
                    A test suite that passes is not evidence until you know it can fail. The
                    isolation battery has a sabotage mode that swaps the fail-closed function
                    for the naive version described above, and re-runs unchanged.
                </p>
                <div class="scroll">
                    <!-- STATUS:battery:BEGIN -->
<table>
  <caption><code>./worker/test/tenant-isolation.sh</code> — 196 checks, mostly negative, as of 2026-08-25</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Run</th><th scope="col">Passed</th><th scope="col">Failed</th><th scope="col">What it demonstrates</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Normal</th>
      <td class="num">196</td>
      <td class="num">0</td>
      <td>Cross-tenant reads, writes, updates and deletes all refuse.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Sabotaged</th>
      <td class="num">186</td>
      <td class="num">10</td>
      <td>With the naive function installed, an unscoped query returns <code>0</code> rows and reports success. The battery catches it.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Regression proof</th>
      <td class="num">76</td>
      <td class="num">120</td>
      <td>With migrations 0008 + 0009 + 0010 + 0011 + 0014 + 0016 + 0017 + 0018 + 0019 + 0020 + 0021 + 0022 + 0023 + 0024 + 0025 + 0026 + 0027 removed, the checks added for those defects fail — so they are load-bearing, not decorative.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Concurrency</th>
      <td class="num">34</td>
      <td class="num">0</td>
      <td>Two real sessions, hand-stepped to a deliberate interleaving — <code>./worker/test/concurrency.sh</code>. Simultaneous first logins resolve to one principal; simultaneous quota requests cannot oversubscribe. Serial correctness is not concurrent correctness.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Worker suite</th>
      <td class="num">486</td>
      <td class="num">0</td>
      <td>Token verification, tenant context, credential scoping, provider refinement and storage admission — <code>npm test --prefix worker</code>. No account, no network, no dependencies.</td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Worker mutations</th>
      <td class="num">139</td>
      <td class="num">0</td>
      <td>Each vector breaks one security decision in a copy of the source and re-runs the unmodified suite. A surviving mutation is an untested decision.</td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
<!-- STATUS:battery:END -->
                </div>
                <p class="dim">
                    The battery also covers connection re-use, because the production path is
                    transaction-pooled: a context established in one transaction must not
                    survive onto the next request that lands on the same backend.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>What this does not solve</h2>
                <p>
                    Collapsing these two questions is a category error, and calling the first
                    one by the second one's name would be a lie.
                </p>
                <div class="scroll">
                    <table>
                        <thead>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="col">Question</th>
                                <th scope="col">Answered by</th>
                            </tr>
                        </thead>
                        <tbody>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">Who are you, and are you entitled?</th>
                                <td>Everything on this page.</td>
                            </tr>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">Why can the storage provider not read your data?</th>
                                <td>
                                    Client-side keys. <strong>Nothing on this page touches it.</strong>
                                </td>
                            </tr>
                        </tbody>
                    </table>
                </div>
                <p>
                    So: <strong>this is authorization, not confidentiality.</strong> Nothing
                    here is described as end-to-end encrypted, because nothing here makes it so.
                    Content addressing is actively hostile to access control — if the key is
                    the hash of the content, then knowing the content is knowing the key — and
                    the question of where confidentiality comes from is open and recorded as
                    open rather than quietly assumed away.
                </p>
            </section>

            <nav class="pages" aria-label="Sections">
                <a href="/">Overview</a>
                <a href="/architecture">Architecture</a>
                <a href="/security" aria-current="page">Security</a>
```

```html
        <main>
            <section>
                <h1>Pricing</h1>
                <p class="lede">
                    Planned packaging, published early so it can be argued with.
                    <strong>Nothing on this page is purchasable</strong> — billing is not
                    built, and there is no checkout to hide behind a button.
                </p>

                <!-- STATUS:banner:BEGIN -->
<p class="banner" role="status">
  <strong>Nothing here is deployed.</strong>
  Of 40 capabilities, <b>24</b> run and are tested on a developer machine
  and <b>16</b> are written down and not built.
  <b>0</b> are serving the public.
  <a href="/status">The full table</a> says which is which, as of 2026-08-22.
</p>
<!-- STATUS:banner:END -->
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>Plans</h2>
                <div class="scroll">
                    <!--
                        COGS and gross-margin columns were removed 2026-08-21 on outside
                        review. They were measured, first-party and dated -- good internal
                        validation, and they stay in STACK_HUB.md 0.6 where they belong. On a
                        public page they are the wrong artifact: a customer needs price,
                        capacity, capability and limits, and a competitor needs nothing at all.
                        This is a positioning judgement, not a correction; the numbers were
                        never wrong.
                    -->
                    <table>
                        <caption>
                            Capacity figures are the machine-sized state under management.
                            Prices are planned and not yet chargeable.
                        </caption>
                        <thead>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="col">Plan</th>
                                <th scope="col">Price</th>
                                <th scope="col">Machine state</th>
                                <th scope="col">WRL graph history</th>
                            </tr>
                        </thead>
                        <tbody>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">Free</th>
                                <td class="num">$0</td>
                                <td class="num">10 GB</td>
                                <td class="num">unlimited</td>
                            </tr>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">Driver</th>
                                <td class="num">$6/mo</td>
                                <td class="num">100 GB</td>
                                <td class="num">unlimited</td>
                            </tr>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">Fleet</th>
                                <td class="num">$19/mo</td>
                                <td class="num">500 GB</td>
                                <td class="num">unlimited</td>
                            </tr>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">Factory</th>
                                <td class="num">$69/mo</td>
                                <td class="num">2 TB</td>
                                <td class="num">unlimited</td>
                            </tr>
                            <tr>
                                <th scope="row">Enterprise</th>
                                <td class="num">custom</td>
                                <td class="num">dedicated</td>
                                <td class="num">unlimited</td>
                            </tr>
                        </tbody>
                    </table>
                </div>
                <p>
                    Every plan includes <strong>unlimited WRL graph history</strong> — the
                    provenance, the tracks, every attempt your agents ever made. That is not
                    generosity: the graph is
                    <a href="/">about 0.2% of a backup at its ceiling</a>, so keeping every
                    version of it costs us approximately nothing and there would be no honest
                    reason to meter it.
                </p>
                <p class="dim">
                    <strong>Machine state is a different thing and is metered.</strong> Retained
                    unique bytes — chunks and snapshots of the machine itself — count against
                    the quota above. Under content addressing an unchanged chunk is stored once
                    however many versions reference it, so history is far cheaper than a naive
                    full-copy backup; it is not free. Saying otherwise would collapse the two
                    world sizes back together, which is the one distinction this product rests
                    on.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>These plans do not include a machine</h2>
                <p>
                    Stated plainly because the opposite assumption is easy and would be
                    ruinous. Driver, Fleet and Factory buy
                    <strong>persistence, sync, restore and fleet control</strong> for machines
                    you already have. They do not include hosted CPU, memory or GPU.
                </p>
                <p>
                    The arithmetic is not close. A single permanent 16-core hosted runner costs
                    a multiple of Factory's entire price — so a storage tier cannot absorb one
                    without inverting its own margin. Hosted capacity will therefore be metered
                    separately:
                </p>
                <figure class="fig">
                    <pre>
COMPUTEDRIVEN CAPACITY

  CPU        $ / compute-hour
  memory     $ / GB-hour
  GPU        $ / GPU-hour
  storage    ephemeral disk
  egress     where applicable</pre
                    >
                    <figcaption>
                        <code>Factory $69 + $143.82 capacity</code> is a legitimate invoice.
                        "Factory includes a runner" is a bankrupt one.
                    </figcaption>
                </figure>
                <p class="dim">
                    Those rates are not set. When they are, they will appear here with the date
                    they were measured — not before.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>Why there is no sign-up button</h2>
                <p>
                    Because taking money for something requires it to exist. Provisioning,
                    billing and entitlements are the last milestone in the plan, not the first,
                    and a checkout flow in front of unbuilt capacity is just a way of borrowing
                    from a customer. <a href="/status">The status page</a> lists what runs
                    today, and it is generated from the same file the rest of this site reads.
                </p>
            </section>
```

```html
<!-- STATUS:authcta:END -->
            </div>
        </header>
        <main>
            <section>
                <h1>Status</h1>
                <p class="lede">
                    What is built, what is written down, and what is serving anyone. This page
                    and every claim elsewhere on the site are generated from
                    <a href="/status.json"><code>status.json</code></a> — no page hand-writes a
                    rung, and a build check fails if one drifts.
                </p>

                <!-- STATUS:banner:BEGIN -->
<p class="banner" role="status">
  <strong>Nothing here is deployed.</strong>
  Of 40 capabilities, <b>24</b> run and are tested on a developer machine
  and <b>16</b> are written down and not built.
  <b>0</b> are serving the public.
  <a href="/status">The full table</a> says which is which, as of 2026-08-22.
</p>
<!-- STATUS:banner:END -->
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>What the rungs mean</h2>
                <!-- STATUS:legend:BEGIN -->
<dl class="legend">
  <dt><span class="rung rung-live">live</span></dt>
  <dd>Serving the public.</dd>
  <dt><span class="rung rung-staged">staged</span></dt>
  <dd>Deployed somewhere non-public.</dd>
  <dt><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></dt>
  <dd>Implemented, and its tests run on a developer machine.</dd>
  <dt><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></dt>
  <dd>Written down. No code.</dd>
</dl>
<!-- STATUS:legend:END -->
                <p class="dim">
                    A capability cannot be described anywhere on this site as more than its
                    rung here. That constraint is the point of the file: it is easier to keep
                    one manifest honest than five pages consistent.
                </p>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>Capabilities</h2>
                <div class="scroll">
                    <!-- STATUS:table:BEGIN -->
<table class="status">
  <caption>Capability rungs, as of 2026-08-22 — Cloud v1 — M0 / M1-local / M1.5-local / M2 shape</caption>
  <thead>
    <tr><th scope="col">Capability</th><th scope="col">Rung</th><th scope="col">What that means here</th><th scope="col">Where to check</th></tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Append-only world versions and audit</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>0004 called world_versions immutable while 0007 granted UPDATE and DELETE on it. Now enforced by the verb matrix, proven by attempting the write and witnessing the row survived.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0011_verb_matrix.sql · battery group I · CD_SABOTAGE=verbs</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Column-level authority on mutable tables</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>0011 granted table-wide UPDATE on memberships while its own comment said last-seen only; a viewer promoted itself to owner. Authority-bearing columns are now separately granted.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0012_column_authority.sql · battery group J · CD_SABOTAGE=columns</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">ComputeDriven → provider action translation</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>The translation is a declared table checked in BOTH directions against a closed provider vocabulary, so a correct R2 grant (ListObjectsV1 + ListObjectsV2 for one ComputeDriven ListObjects) conforms and half of one is refused as an under-grant. R2's own words were verified first-party against Cloudflare's documentation, not recalled.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/r2native.mjs · worker/test/r2native.test.mjs</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Concurrency battery (two real sessions)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>A separate battery, because tenant-isolation.sh runs one session on one connection and every property it can express is sequential. Hand-steps two sessions to a deterministic interleaving rather than racing and hoping, and judges its sabotage modes PER GROUP so a control that fires for the wrong reason reports MISDIRECTED.</td>
      <td><code>./worker/test/concurrency.sh · CD_SABOTAGE=lock · CD_SABOTAGE=quota</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Entitlement + storage quota admission</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>M1.5 (R24). Entitlement, a two-number byte ledger, and an expiring reservation with exactly-once finalize/abort/expiry. Admission is ONE statement: 20 simultaneous 100-byte requests against a 1000-byte limit admit exactly 10. Round 7 made it REQUEST-idempotent rather than merely accounting-idempotent (four concurrent retries all succeed with one reservation and zero errors), moved authority checks ABOVE replay, and bound the idempotency key to the whole request tuple. It is admission-safe and NOT hard-quota-safe — see byte_enforced_quota.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0014 + 0016 · worker/src/admission.mjs · battery group K · concurrency.sh group P</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Entrypoint composition battery</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Drives the real fetch handler, not modules. Exists because a JWKS rate-cap that passed its own module test did not hold at the entrypoint.</td>
      <td><code>worker/test/entrypoint.test.mjs</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Function-level privilege separation</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>PUBLIC holds EXECUTE on nothing; only the api role may call a resolver. Fixed after a review found readonly could mint principals.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0009_function_acl.sql · battery D12-D17</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Marketing + status surface</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>These pages. Built, not served.</td>
      <td><code>cloud.computedriven.com/</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Object-scoped write authority (M2 shape)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>One exact object key, not a prefix: a credential for .../chunk/abc cannot reach .../chunk/def. PutObject only. The intent carries expected bytes and a content digest and cannot over-commit its reservation CONCURRENTLY -- serialized on the reservation row with FOR UPDATE, the same lock finalize_storage() and abort_storage() have taken since 0014. An object key binds the whole promise {reservation, key, bytes, digest} (R43). THE STATE MACHINE IS THREE STATES AND ONE IS TERMINAL: offered, observed, client_abandoned. `observed` is provider truth and no local transition may walk it back (R54); `client_abandoned` is a DECLARATION that releases nothing, because abandoning a row in our database does not revoke a presigned URL already in the clients hands (R55). Only the reservation dying releases bytes, which is why the byte arithmetic has no state predicate at all.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0019 + 0022 · concurrency groups Q and R · CD_SABOTAGE=offer · CD_SABOTAGE=observe</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">OIDC subject → principal → organization</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Resolvers are implemented and tested, and idempotent under CONCURRENCY as well as in sequence. The mechanism CHANGED this round: 0013 used a PostgreSQL advisory lock, which Hyperdrive lists as unsupported — correct PostgreSQL that the production wire refuses. 0015 serializes on the unique partial index instead. No Keycloak has issued a real token to them.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0015_provider_safe_identity.sql · battery groups F and L · ./worker/test/concurrency.sh group N</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">OIDC token verification (RS256, pinned)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Algorithm pinned, never read from the token; iat required, crit refused, forced JWKS refresh rate-capped. No realm has issued it a real token.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/jwt.mjs · worker/test/jwt.test.mjs</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Organizations resolved by stable IdP id</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Alias is for selection only. A token carrying aliases without ids is refused as a realm misconfiguration.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/authz.mjs organizationEntries() · battery group F</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Pigsty schema + migrations</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Applies clean, with a working negative control and a regression proof. THE VERSION IT WAS MEASURED ON IS A FACT ABOUT THE RUN, NOT ABOUT THIS SENTENCE: the battery block below records the migration count, the PostgreSQL major it ran against, and whether anything warned. R33 targets 17.x because Hyperdrive documents known support for 9.0-17.x, and the batteries now default to the target build when it is installed rather than to whatever the box happens to have. This note used to carry its own copy of all three numbers and went stale while every gate stayed green -- scripts/check-status-prose.mjs is why it cannot again.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/ · ./worker/test/tenant-isolation.sh</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Principal / organization suspension</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>suspended and closed now refuse by name. They were decorative until 2026-08-21.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0008_principal_status.sql · battery group G</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Provider authority may not exceed scope</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Two laws, not one: no widening (safety) AND no under-granting (functionality). Checked against the PROVIDER-NATIVE grant through a declared translation table, because comparing R2's action names to ComputeDriven's directly made a correct R2 adapter fail its own law. Closed vocabulary: an action R2 does not define is refused as unknown. No provider is bound to it yet.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/r2creds.mjs assertRefines() · worker/src/r2native.mjs · worker/test/r2native.test.mjs</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Provider-observed storage accounting (R32)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>R32 is PROPOSED, not ruled, and is built anyway so it can be ruled with a number. THREE THINGS EARLIER ROUNDS GOT WRONG HERE. The consumer was UNREACHABLE -- it runs as computedriven_ledger and cd.organizations had no policy admitting that role, so every event including every valid one was refused (measured: count returns 0 with a row present). An append-only log is not an inventory (R41): R2 fires object-create on OVERWRITE, so summing the log charged a replaced body twice. And the queue consumer sat OUTSIDE the lock protocol, so a provider observation could be overwritten by a request-path replay -- measured, group R: fresh write authority handed out for an object R2 already held. DELIVERY identity is the queue message id, read from the ENVELOPE so a producer cannot choose it; (bucket, key) is object identity; etag and event_time are object state (R57). PROVIDER-EVENT identity is not exposed at all -- R2's notification body carries account, action, bucket, object and eventTime and no event id -- so what we have is exactly-once processing of a queue MESSAGE, and this note called that 'event identity' for a day after R57 was narrowed. Still runs against FIXTURE events -- no bucket, no queue, no notification rule.</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0021 + 0022 · worker/src/reconcile.mjs · battery groups M and O · concurrency group R</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">R2 credential scope computation</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>The prefix is BUILT from the organization id rather than validated against it, so no argument combination reaches another tenant. A scope also carries an unforgeable provenance brand: grantForScope() used to accept any object with a string `prefix`, so a hand-built whole-bucket scope produced a signable grant.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/r2creds.mjs</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Request path is Hyperdrive-compatible</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Battery group L asks the DATABASE which functions the API role may execute and reads their bodies, so advisory locks, LISTEN/NOTIFY and PREPARE/DEALLOCATE on the request path fail a check rather than a deployment. Exists because a ruled fix went green locally and Hyperdrive refuses the mechanism it used. It proves the schema is compatible; it CANNOT prove Hyperdrive accepts it — that needs a real binding.</td>
      <td><code>./worker/test/tenant-isolation.sh group L · worker/test/live-falsifier.mjs cases F, G, H</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Server-derived object permission</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>The client requests an operation; ROLE and WORLD STATUS decide what it may become. A viewer asking to write is refused, not downgraded. Entitlement and quota are now part of the decision too — a write permission requires a storage admission (R24).</td>
      <td><code>worker/migrations/0010_membership_role.sql · worker/src/authz.mjs permissionFor()</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">status.json battery numbers are derived, not typed</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Runs all five battery invocations and refuses to agree with a stale number. Exists because this file said “10 migrations” against a tree of twelve, and published a sabotage control (66/8) and a regression proof (28) from four migrations earlier — control results nobody re-runs casually are the ones that go stale. The RUNGS were already generated into the pages by tools/render-status.mjs --verify; this covers the counts, which were not.</td>
      <td><code>scripts/cloud-status-counts.mjs · cloud.computedriven.com/tools/render-status.mjs --verify</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Tenant isolation (fail-closed RLS)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Clean, with a working negative control and a regression proof against migrations 0008-0010 removed. Counts in the battery block.</td>
      <td><code>./worker/test/tenant-isolation.sh · CD_SABOTAGE=1 for the control</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Transaction-entry tenant context</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>Context is established on entering the transaction. The brand proves a tenant was minted by deriveTenant() and not hand-built — it does NOT prove the id came from a successful authentication, since deriveTenant() is exported and trusted code could misuse it.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/tenant.mjs · worker/test/worker.test.mjs</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Unforgeable verified-claims brand</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>verifyToken brands its result in a module-private WeakSet. Nothing exported can add to it, so a structural clone of verified claims is still refused.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/jwt.mjs assertVerified()</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Verified claims are frozen, not just branded</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-local">local</span></td>
      <td>The brand proved an object WAS ONCE verified; mutating it kept the brand. Deep-frozen before branding, including the nested organization claim.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/jwt.mjs deepFreeze() · battery</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Commerce — checkout, payment, subscriptions</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>M6, and now ONLY commerce. Entitlement and quota are authorization and moved ahead of M2 (R24); they are built and local — see storage_admission. What is missing here is checkout, payment and subscription lifecycle, plus the metered compute SKU that a storage tier cannot absorb.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §5</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">ComputeDriven-hosted capacity (Hetzner)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>M5. No paid infrastructure has been provisioned.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §4</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Control-plane API surface</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>Routes and refusal mapping exist and parse, and the credential route now takes the world lookup and the storage reservation in ONE transaction. connect() throws by design — no Hyperdrive driver adapter has been written.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/index.mjs · worker/wrangler.toml</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Cross-request JWKS refresh admission</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>The module-scope cache is best-effort in-isolate only. A durable limit needs a cross-request mechanism and is NOT claimed.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/index.mjs jwksFor()</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Keycloak realm on Fly</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>Ruled (R4) to Fly iad, database on PlanetScale. Not provisioned.</td>
      <td><code>agents/C-infrastructure.md §3</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Live-provider falsifier (plan only)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>Questions no local test can answer — see falsifier_cases for how many — each written down with what it would falsify and what we would do about it BEFORE it is run, so a negative result stays informative instead of becoming something to explain away. It PROVISIONS NOTHING and refuses to run without real bindings. Creating the account, bucket and queue is a spend decision. The count is DERIVED as of round 7.3: this note said “Eight” against an array of nine for a full round, and the prose gate could not see it because a fact that lives only in prose has nothing to disagree with.</td>
      <td><code>worker/test/live-falsifier.mjs --plan</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">LOCAL / FLEET placement</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>M4.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §4</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Minting real R2 credentials</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>The scope logic is local; the provider is not. No bucket, no account. FakeR2Provider is the only implementation and its keys say so.</td>
      <td><code>worker/src/r2creds.mjs R2Provider · agents/D-worker-auth.md</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Portal sign-in (BFF, server session)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>No portal exists.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §4 M1</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Provider-enforced byte ceiling on a write credential (R31)</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>OPEN, AND DELIBERATELY NOT CLAIMED. R2 temporary credentials constrain bucket, operations, prefixes/objects and TTL and document no maximum byte count; presigned URLs document Content-Type as signed and ENFORCED and say nothing about Content-Length. So reserving 1 MB does not stop R2 accepting 500 MB — the database refusal at finalize is correct and too late. THE EXPERIMENT HAS BEEN RE-AIMED: the S3-compatibility page documents neither Content-Length nor x-amz-checksum-sha256 for PutObject, so the old case B would have measured our header choice rather than R2. It does document Content-MD5, which binds CONTENT and is strictly stronger than a byte ceiling — a bound digest refuses a longer body, a shorter body and a same-length different body alike. Two questions hide in one: does the signature bind the header, and does R2 verify the digest against the body.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §6.5 · worker/test/live-falsifier.mjs case B</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Remote execution on a node</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>A Cloud request is a request. The local runtime verifies and may refuse.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §7</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Restore onto a second machine</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>M2. R23 is RULED: machine authority is NOT restored — data access is separately reacquired through a client-held User Recovery Key that unwraps the World Data Key. Revocation governs future Cloud access; it is not retroactive erasure, and we say so.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §6.2b · REVISION_REGISTER.md R23</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Super node identity + Fleet + revoke</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>M3.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §4</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">TRVM-governed Cloud transitions</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>TRVM P4 is proven in its own tree and is wired to nothing here. Cloud behaviour is Postgres and application convention, and is called that.</td>
      <td><code>TRVM/governance/round-11-ledger.md</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">Worker → Pigsty over Hyperdrive</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>Ruled (R7). No binding exists; the schema has only ever been reached over a local socket.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §3</code></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th scope="row">World sync — chunk, hash, upload</th>
      <td><span class="rung rung-spec">spec</span></td>
      <td>M2. The WRITE SHAPE is decided (R31 work): one bounded content-addressed chunk, one reservation, one EXACT object key, one short-lived artifact — so the session can last days while each grant lasts minutes. Multipart is NOT authorized; the claim that M2 would need it is retracted, because a 2 TB world is not a 2 TB object. No chunking implementation exists.</td>
      <td><code>CLOUD_V1.md §6.6 · worker/migrations/0017 · worker/src/r2native.mjs</code></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
<!-- STATUS:table:END -->
                </div>
            </section>

            <section>
                <h2>What "not deployed" means here</h2>
                <p>
                    No account has been created and no infrastructure has been provisioned by
                    this work. There is no Keycloak realm, no Hyperdrive binding, no object
                    bucket and no hosted machine. The schema has only ever been reached over a
                    local socket, by a test that builds a throwaway database and destroys it
                    again.
                </p>
                <p>
                    Where a subsystem is unavailable it is named <code>spec</code> rather than
                    stubbed out behind a mock that would report success. A mock that passes for
                    production is worse than a missing feature, because only one of the two
                    tells you the truth.
                </p>
            </section>

            <nav class="pages" aria-label="Sections">
                <a href="/">Overview</a>
                <a href="/architecture">Architecture</a>
                <a href="/security">Security</a>
                <a href="/pricing">Pricing</a>
                <a href="/status" aria-current="page">Status</a>
            </nav>
        </main>

        <footer>
            <!-- STATUS:footauth:BEGIN -->
<div class="foot-auth">
  <a class="foot-auth-cta" href="/auth">Sign in &rarr;</a>
  <p class="foot-auth-note">There is no sign-in yet — <code>portal_login</code> stands at <b>spec</b>. The auth page says what has to exist before there is a door here, and <a href="/status">the status table</a> carries the rung.</p>
</div>
<!-- STATUS:footauth:END -->
            <p>
                Regenerate with <code>node tools/render-status.mjs</code>; check with
                <code>--verify</code>.
            </p>
            <div class="foot-fam">
                <span>One system, three ways in</span>
                <span class="ff-links">
                    <a href="https://tr.computedriven.com/">T&amp;R</a>

        <amp-nav property="cloud"></amp-nav>
```
