  // ALL THE TARGETS".
  //
  // Cloudflare's host is a closed union: IPv4, IPv6, dual-stack (BOTH addresses),
  // or hostname + resolver_network. The old code read
  //
  //     target  = host.ipv4 ?? host.ipv6 ?? host.hostname
  //     network = host.network ?? host.resolver_network
  //
  // which takes the FIRST property present and never looks at the rest.
  // REPRODUCED: a dual-stack service carrying the expected ipv4 and an entirely
  // unreviewed ipv6 returned `ok: true`, reporting only the ipv4. And a mixed
  // object with `ipv4` + `hostname` and TWO DIFFERENT tunnels passed, silently
  // choosing the first of each.
  //
  //     A PREDICATE OVER A UNION MUST NAME THE VARIANT. `??` PICKS A WINNER AND
  //     CALLS THE REST UNSEEN.
  //
  // So the variant is declared by the ruling and matched exactly, and the target
  // set is compared as a SET — every address the service may route to has to be
  // one the ruling names.
  const host = service.host;
  if (host === null || typeof host !== "object") {
    refusals.push("the service states no host object, so neither the tunnel nor the target is known");
  } else {
    const present = HOST_ADDRESS_FIELDS.filter((f) => host[f] !== undefined && host[f] !== null);
    const variant = hostVariant(present);
    observed.hostVariant = variant;
    observed.targets = present.map((f) => host[f]);

    if (variant === null) {
      refusals.push(`the service's host carries ${JSON.stringify(present)}, which is not one of ` +
                    `Cloudflare's host variants (${Object.keys(HOST_VARIANTS).join(", ")}). An ` +
                    "unrecognised combination is not a recognised one with extras — the extras " +
                    "are routing targets nobody reviewed (finding 125)");
    } else if (variant !== expect.hostVariant) {
      refusals.push(`the service's host variant is ${JSON.stringify(variant)} and the ruling ` +
                    `names ${JSON.stringify(expect.hostVariant ?? null)}. A dual-stack service ` +
                    "reaches Pigsty over an address the ruling never mentioned, however correct " +
                    "the other one is");
    }

    // THE TARGET SET, both directions. Extra targets are unreviewed routes;
    // missing ones mean the ruling names something the service cannot reach.
    const want = new Set(expect.targets ?? []);
    const got = new Set(observed.targets);
    const extra = [...got].filter((t) => !want.has(t));
    const absent = [...want].filter((t) => !got.has(t));
    if (extra.length) {
      refusals.push(`the service also routes to ${JSON.stringify(extra)}, which the ruling does ` +
                    "not name. Proving one target matches is not proving these are all the targets");
    }
    if (absent.length) {
      refusals.push(`the ruling names ${JSON.stringify(absent)} and the service does not offer ` +
                    "it");
    }
    observed.target = observed.targets[0] ?? null;

    // THE TUNNEL. Exactly one network object, matching the variant: `network` for
    // an address target, `resolver_network` for a hostname. Both present is two
    // private networks and a silent choice between them.
    const nets = ["network", "resolver_network"].filter((f) => host[f] !== undefined && host[f] !== null);
    if (nets.length !== 1) {
      refusals.push(`the service's host states ${JSON.stringify(nets)}; exactly one of network / ` +
                    "resolver_network is expected, and two means the tunnel actually used is " +
                    "whichever this code happens to read first");
    } else {
      const wantNet = variant === "hostname" ? "resolver_network" : "network";
      if (variant !== null && nets[0] !== wantNet) {
        refusals.push(`a ${variant} target carries ${JSON.stringify(nets[0])}; Cloudflare pairs ` +
                      `that variant with ${JSON.stringify(wantNet)}`);
      }
      observed.tunnelId = host[nets[0]]?.tunnel_id ?? null;
      if (observed.tunnelId !== expect.tunnelId) {
        refusals.push(`the service routes through tunnel ${JSON.stringify(observed.tunnelId)}, ` +
                      `expected ${JSON.stringify(expect.tunnelId)} — a different tunnel is a ` +
                      "different private network, however correct everything above it is");
      }
    }

    // TLS. Finding 102 said this could not be set on the Hyperdrive and left it
    // there. It CAN be set here, `verify_full` is the documented default, and
    // `disabled` is legal — which makes it exactly the kind of provider default
    // that is correct until someone changes it and nothing notices (finding 101).
    //
    // FINDING 125, second half: the prose stated a condition the predicate did
    // not enforce. `verify_ca` verifies the chain and SKIPS THE HOSTNAME, and the
    // note said "acceptable for an IP target" while accepting it for a hostname
    // target too — REPRODUCED, `ok: true` for `pigsty.internal` + `verify_ca`.
    // The policy is now the ruling's to state, per variant.
    const mode = service.tls_settings?.cert_verification_mode ?? "verify_full";
    observed.certVerification = service.tls_settings?.cert_verification_mode
      ?? "(absent — provider default verify_full)";
    if (!TLS_MODES.includes(mode)) {
      refusals.push(`cert_verification_mode is ${JSON.stringify(mode)}, which is not one of ` +
                    TLS_MODES.join(" / "));
    } else if (mode === "disabled") {
      refusals.push("tls_settings.cert_verification_mode is \"disabled\": the connection to Pigsty " +
                    "would not verify the server certificate at all, inside the private path this " +
                    "whole gate exists to prove");
    } else if (mode !== expect.certVerification) {
      refusals.push(`cert_verification_mode is ${JSON.stringify(mode)} and the ruling requires ` +
                    `${JSON.stringify(expect.certVerification ?? "verify_full")}. This is a ` +
                    "ruling, not a preference: verify_ca skips HOSTNAME verification, which is " +
                    "defensible for an IP target with a private CA and is not defensible for a " +
                    "hostname target — so which one applies belongs in topology.json where it is " +
                    "reviewable (finding 125)");
    } else if (mode === "verify_ca" && variant === "hostname") {
      refusals.push("the ruling allows verify_ca and this service's target is a HOSTNAME. " +
                    "verify_ca verifies the chain and skips the hostname check, so the one " +
                    "property a hostname target most needs is the one it does not get");
    }
  }

  return { ok: refusals.length === 0, refusals, notes, observed };
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// The runner. Everything above is pure; everything below needs an account.

const PLAN = `
  CASE Q — HYPERDRIVE AUTHORITY + R7 TOPOLOGY (R7, R17, R80; findings 95/101/102/105/106)

  Needs, in the environment — CREDENTIALS ONLY (finding 105):
    CF_ACCOUNT_ID   the account
    CF_API_TOKEN    a token with Hyperdrive read and Connectivity Directory Read

  Takes its SUBJECTS from the ACTIVE WORKER VERSION, never the caller and never
  the manifest (findings 121, 127, 135). resolveLiveSubjects():

      GET .../workers/scripts/{name}/deployments   which version serves traffic
        -> require ONE version at 100%             (a split rollout is refused)
      GET .../workers/scripts/{name}/versions/{id} that version's bindings
        -> require exact agreement with worker/wrangler.toml
        -> return the DEPLOYED values, plus deploymentId and versionId

  So every assertion below is about the runtime, and says which one:
  *version V, which deployment D routes at 100%.*

  From the ruling (worker/topology.json):
    the two [[hyperdrive]] ids actually bound as HYPERDRIVE_CONTROL / HYPERDRIVE_JOBS

  Takes its EXPECTATIONS from the ruling (worker/topology.json):
    database, vpcServiceId, tunnelId, target, port

  Asserts, per Hyperdrive configuration:
    origin variant         == vpc_service       (finding 106: an internet origin PASSED before)
    origin.service_id      == the ruled VPC service
    origin.user            == ${EXPECTED.CONTROL.user} / ${EXPECTED.JOBS.user}
    origin.database        == the ruled database
    origin.scheme          in postgres, postgresql
    caching.disabled       === true             (absent means ON — finding 101)

  And across the pair:
    id                     CONTROL != JOBS
    origin.user            CONTROL != JOBS
    origin target          CONTROL == JOBS      (two authorities, ONE database)

  Then reads the VPC SERVICE ITSELF, because the Hyperdrive names only a
  service_id and everything R7 rules lives one level down:
    type                   == "tcp"
    tcp_port               == the ruled port
    app_protocol           == "postgresql"
    host.network.tunnel_id == the ruled tunnel   (or host.resolver_network for a hostname)
    host target            == the ruled address
    tls_settings           "disabled" REFUSED; "verify_ca" noted; default is verify_full

  Does NOT assert: that the two passwords differ. The API never returns them.
  The privilege witness — current_user; the request credential cannot EXECUTE
  app.observe_storage_object(); the jobs credential can — is Q's second half and
  needs the driver.
`;

async function main() {
  const argv = process.argv.slice(2);
  if (argv.includes("--plan")) { process.stdout.write(PLAN); process.exit(0); }

  const env = process.env;
  const missing = ["CF_ACCOUNT_ID", "CF_API_TOKEN"].filter((n) => !env[n]);
  if (missing.length) {
    process.stdout.write(PLAN);
    process.stderr.write(`\n  NOT RUN  missing: ${missing.join(", ")}\n` +
                         "           This is exit 2, not exit 0: an unrun check is not a passing " +
                         "one.\n\n");
    process.exit(2);
  }

  // Subjects from the deployment and expectations from the ruling; nothing that
  // decides WHAT is being proved comes from this process's environment (105/106).
  const retired = refuseRetiredSubjectEnv();
  if (retired) { process.stderr.write(`\n  REFUSED  ${retired}\n\n`); process.exit(1); }
  let ruled;
  try { ruled = ruledTopology(); }
  catch (e) { process.stderr.write(`\n  REFUSED  ${e.message}\n\n`); process.exit(1); }
  let deployment;
  try {
    // FINDING 127. THE SUBJECT IS RESOLVED HERE, AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT, NOW.
    // This used to be `requireSubjects()` — the FILE — on the reasoning that
    // case S had already compared the file to the deployment. But a prior check
    // is not a capability: S is separately invocable, `--run` does not exist to
    // sequence them, and the deployment can change in between. The subject has
    // to cross the boundary with the operation that uses it.
    deployment = await resolveLiveSubjects({
      accountId: env.CF_ACCOUNT_ID, apiToken: env.CF_API_TOKEN,
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (e.code === "CD-SUBJ-NOTDEPLOYED") {
      process.stderr.write("\n  NOT RUN  " + e.message + "\n           Exit 2: this gate attests a " +
        "DEPLOYED Worker and there is not one.\n\n");
      process.exit(2);
    }
    process.stderr.write(`\n  REFUSED  ${e.message}\n\n`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  const { hyperdriveControlId, hyperdriveJobsId } = deployment.subjects;
  process.stdout.write(`  subjects from ${deployment.origin}: CONTROL=${hyperdriveControlId} ` +
                       `JOBS=${hyperdriveJobsId}\n` +
                       `  ruling from worker/topology.json: db=${ruled.database} ` +
                       `vpc=${ruled.vpcServiceId} tunnel=${ruled.tunnelId}\n`);

  const get = async (path) => {
    const r = await fetch(`https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${env.CF_ACCOUNT_ID}${path}`,
                          { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${env.CF_API_TOKEN}` } });
    const body = await r.json().catch(() => null);
    if (!r.ok || body?.success !== true) {
      throw new Error(`GET ${path} -> ${r.status} ${JSON.stringify(body?.errors ?? null)}`);
    }
    return body.result;
  };

  Promise.all([
    get(`/hyperdrive/configs/${hyperdriveControlId}`),
    get(`/hyperdrive/configs/${hyperdriveJobsId}`),
    // FINDING 114. THIS WAS `/vpc/services/{id}`, WHICH IS NOT AN ENDPOINT.
    //
    // Round 8.2 shipped a guessed path with a comment saying it was a guess.
    // The real one — Cloudflare's own SDK, generated from their API schema:
    //
    //     GET /accounts/{account_id}/connectivity/directory/services/{service_id}
    //
    // A wrong path is a safe failure here (the catch below refuses rather than
    // skipping the topology half — finding 88's law applied to an endpoint), but
    // safe-failing forever is still never running the check. It runs now.
    get(`/connectivity/directory/services/${ruledTopologyServiceId(ruled)}`),
  ])
    .then(([control, jobs, service]) => {
      const v = hyperdriveAuthorityVerdict(control, jobs,
        { database: ruled.database, vpcServiceId: ruled.vpcServiceId });
      const sv = vpcServiceVerdict(service, {
        serviceId: ruled.vpcServiceId, tunnelId: ruled.tunnelId, port: ruled.port,
        hostVariant: ruled.hostVariant, targets: ruled.targets,
        certVerification: ruled.certVerification,
      });
      for (const [role, o] of Object.entries(v.observed)) {
        process.stdout.write(
          `  ${role.padEnd(8)} id=${o.id} user=${o.user} db=${o.database} ` +
          `origin=${o.variant} caching.disabled=${o.cachingDisabled}\n`);
      }
      const o = sv.observed;
      process.stdout.write(`  VPC      type=${o.type} port=${o.port} proto=${o.appProtocol} ` +
                           `tunnel=${o.tunnelId} variant=${o.hostVariant} ` +
                           `targets=${JSON.stringify(o.targets)} tls=${o.certVerification}\n`);
      for (const n of [...v.notes, ...sv.notes]) process.stdout.write(`  note     ${n}\n`);

      const refusals = [...v.refusals, ...sv.refusals];
      if (refusals.length) {
        process.stderr.write("\n  REFUSED  the ruled path from Worker to Pigsty is not proved:\n\n");
        for (const r of refusals) process.stderr.write(`     - ${r}\n`);
        process.stderr.write("\n");
        process.exit(1);
      }
      process.stdout.write("\n  ok       two configurations, two logins, one database, no SQL " +
                           "cache, through the ruled VPC service and tunnel\n");
    })
    .catch((e) => {
      // Cannot see -> refuse. An API error is not an absence of violations.
      process.stderr.write(`\n  REFUSED  could not read the configuration: ${e.message}\n\n`);
      process.exit(1);
    });
}

function ruledTopologyServiceId(ruled) { return ruled.vpcServiceId; }

if (import.meta.url === `file://${process.argv[1]}`) {
  main().catch((e) => {
    // An unhandled rejection would exit 0 on some runtimes, which is the one
    // outcome a gate must never produce by accident.
    process.stderr.write(`
  REFUSED  ${e?.stack ?? e}

`);
    process.exit(1);
  });
}
```

### `scripts/check-notification-coverage.mjs`

```javascript
#!/usr/bin/env node
// THE R2 RULE COVERS EVERY PROVIDER OBJECT-CREATE ACTION THAT CAN CHANGE M2.0
// OCCUPANCY.
//
// FINDING 112, 2026-08-24 — AND THAT WORDING IS THE FINDING. This file said
// "every ADMITTED write", which claims more than the system does: M2.0's
// credential minter authorizes PutObject-shaped uploads, and multipart is
// deliberately unearned. A rule covering CopyObject and CompleteMultipartUpload
// is therefore BROADER than what we authorize, and that is correct and
// deliberate — occupancy is a property of the bucket, not of our intentions.
//
//     WHAT WE AUTHORIZE AND WHAT CAN CHANGE OCCUPANCY ARE DIFFERENT SETS, AND
//     THE NOTIFICATION RULE MUST COVER THE SECOND.
//
// The distinction is load-bearing rather than pedantic. Under the old wording a
// CopyObject notification is "an admitted write arriving normally". Under this
// one it is an object created by an operation M2.0 never authorized — which is
// an ALARM, and the documentation no longer accidentally calls it intended
// authority. The check is unchanged; what it means is not.
//
//   node scripts/check-notification-coverage.mjs           check; exit 1 on a gap
//   node scripts/check-notification-coverage.mjs --plan    print what it would assert
//
// WHY (finding 99, 2026-08-23). Case P proves the queue is AUTHENTIC: exactly
// one producer, of type r2_bucket, being our bucket, with no unexpected
// consumer. What it does not read is the bucket's notification configuration, so
// this passes case P:
//
//     queue producer = OUR R2 bucket        <- case P is satisfied
//     consumer       = OUR observer
//     DLQ            = configured
//
// while the rule behind it is:
//
//     actions = [PutObject]
//     prefix  = "wrong-prefix/"
//
// and CopyObject, CompleteMultipartUpload, and every key outside that prefix are
// never sent at all. The channel is genuine and it carries a fraction of the
// truth.
//
//     AN AUTHENTIC CHANNEL IS NOT A COMPLETE ONE. CASE P ANSWERS "IS THIS R2
//     SPEAKING?"; NOTHING ANSWERED "IS R2 SPEAKING ABOUT EVERYTHING?"
//
// This is the SAME distinction that R79 drew one layer up — a notification
// channel minimizes latency, an R2 listing establishes recoverability — arriving
// at the provisioning layer. The queue side and the bucket side are separate
// configurations and each can be right while the other is wrong.
//
// The bundle already said, correctly, that overlapping or conflicting rules are
// OUR PROVISIONING OBLIGATION rather than a provider guarantee, and that it is
// "checked at provisioning". This is that check. A sentence in an architecture
// document is not a provisioning gate — that is exactly the complaint finding 84
// made about producer restriction, and it applies verbatim here.
//
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// WHAT THE PROVIDER ACTUALLY EXPOSES, from Cloudflare's own schema for
// GET /accounts/{account_id}/event_notifications/r2/{bucket_name}/configuration:
//
//     result.bucketName
//     result.queues[] { queueId, queueName, rules[] }
//     rule            { actions[] REQUIRED, description?, prefix?, suffix? }
//
// and the action vocabulary is a closed enum of exactly five:
//
//     PutObject  CopyObject  DeleteObject  CompleteMultipartUpload  LifecycleDeletion
//
// which is precisely reconcile.mjs's CREATE_ACTIONS (3) plus DELETE_ACTIONS (2).
// The event-notifications page states the same split: the `object-create` event
// type triggers on "PutObject CopyObject CompleteMultipartUpload".
//
// THAT MATCH IS WORTH SAYING OUT LOUD, because this tree has spent five rounds
// discovering places where its vocabulary and the provider's differed. Here they
// do not, and the assertion below is derived from reconcile.mjs's own constant
// rather than retyped — a hand-typed copy of a vocabulary is how the two come to
// disagree, which is finding 91 and R76 and finding 98, three times now.
//
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// PREFIX AND SUFFIX ARE OPTIONAL, AND ABSENT MEANS EVERYTHING.
//
// Cloudflare: "Notifications will be sent only for objects with this prefix" /
// "...this suffix"; a rule without them applies to all objects. So coverage of
// our namespace is exactly:
//
//     suffix   MUST be absent. Every key we mint ends in a content hash or a
//              manifest path; no suffix can cover them all, and a suffix that
//              seems to is a coincidence waiting to end.
//     prefix   absent, or a string every minted key starts with. `org/` is the
//              only non-empty prefix that qualifies, because scopeForWorld()
//              mints `org/<uuid>/world/<uuid>/...` and nothing else.
//
// Anything narrower is a gap; anything else entirely is a different namespace.
//
// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
// M2.0 IS APPEND-ONLY (R56), SO A DELETE RULE IS A REFUSAL, NOT A BONUS.
//
// If DeleteObject or LifecycleDeletion routes to this queue, deletions are
// arriving at an observer that has no delete path — reconcile.mjs's
// DELETE_ACTIONS exists to NAME them, not to apply them. Worse, it means
// something in the account believes deletes are expected here, which contradicts
// the premise the `extra` refusal in inventory.mjs rests on.
//
// IT PROVISIONS NOTHING. Creating a notification rule belongs to Travis
// (agents/C-infrastructure.md).

// IMPORTED, NOT RETYPED. reconcile.mjs is where the admitted-write vocabulary
// lives, and a hand-copied list here would be a second independent claim about
// the same fact — R76's law, which this tree has now broken three separate ways
// (a column, a config key, a regex). It costs one import and it means a fourth
// create action added to the consumer automatically becomes a coverage
// requirement on the rule.
import { CREATE_ACTIONS, DELETE_ACTIONS } from "../worker/src/reconcile.mjs";
// FINDING 105. This gate shipped with `CD_R2_BUCKET` and `CD_QUEUE_NAME` in its
// environment — and CD_QUEUE_NAME is the exact variable finding 91 DELETED one
// round earlier, reintroduced by a new gate that had read the ruling. So P2
// could prove a perfect notification configuration for queue A while the Worker
// consumed queue B, or for bucket A while the Worker wrote to bucket B.
//
//     A LAW CLOSED FOR ONE RESOURCE IS NOT CLOSED. Subjects come from the
//     deployment; the environment supplies credentials only.
import { refuseRetiredSubjectEnv, resolveLiveSubjects } from "./deployment-subjects.mjs";

/** Cloudflare's closed action enum. The union of ours, and it must stay so. */
export const PROVIDER_ACTIONS = Object.freeze([...CREATE_ACTIONS, ...DELETE_ACTIONS]);

/** The only non-empty prefix that covers every key scopeForWorld() mints. */
export const NAMESPACE_PREFIX = "org/";

/**
 * The whole judgement, as a pure function of the provider's response.
 *
 * @param config  result of GET .../event_notifications/r2/{bucket}/configuration
 * @param expect  { bucket, queue }  ALL REQUIRED — an attestation whose subject
 *                is unnamed proves nothing (R77, finding 91).
 * @returns { ok, refusals[], notes[], observed }
 */
export function notificationCoverageVerdict(config, expect = {}) {
  const refusals = [];
  const notes = [];
  const observed = { bucketName: null, queues: [], rulesToOurQueue: [] };

  for (const f of ["bucket", "queue"]) {
    if (typeof expect[f] !== "string" || expect[f].trim() === "") {
      refusals.push(`the check was not told which ${f} to expect`);
    }
  }
  if (refusals.length) return { ok: false, refusals, notes, observed };

  if (config === null || typeof config !== "object") {
    return { ok: false, notes, observed,
             refusals: ["the notification configuration response was not an object"] };
  }
  observed.bucketName = config.bucketName ?? null;

  // Cannot see -> refuse. Reporting an absent list as "no rules" would turn a
  // reshaped API into a clean bill of health, which is finding 88 exactly.
  if (!Array.isArray(config.queues)) {
    refusals.push("the response carried no enumerable queue list, so this check learned nothing " +
                  `(keys seen: ${Object.keys(config).join(", ") || "none"})`);
    return { ok: false, refusals, notes, observed };
  }
  observed.queues = config.queues;

  if (config.bucketName !== expect.bucket) {
    refusals.push(`the configuration describes bucket ${JSON.stringify(config.bucketName ?? null)}, ` +
                  `not ${JSON.stringify(expect.bucket)} — a correct answer about the wrong ` +
                  "bucket is the shape finding 91 was");
  }

  const ours = config.queues.filter((q) => q?.queueName === expect.queue);
  const others = config.queues.filter((q) => q?.queueName !== expect.queue);

  if (ours.length === 0) {
    refusals.push(`no rule on this bucket routes to ${JSON.stringify(expect.queue)}. The queue ` +
                  "can be authentic, dedicated and empty — case P would still pass");
    return { ok: false, refusals, notes, observed };
  }
  if (ours.length > 1) {
    // Cloudflare permits up to 100 rules per bucket and prohibits overlapping
    // rules that would fire twice for one event. Rather than trying to prove an
    // arbitrary collection equivalent to the intended one, M2.0 requires the
    // shape to be exact so drift is obvious.
    refusals.push(`${ours.length} separate queue entries route to ${JSON.stringify(expect.queue)}; ` +
                  "M2.0 requires exactly one, so that a rule change is a visible edit rather " +
                  "than an emergent property of a set");
  }

  const rules = ours.flatMap((q) => (Array.isArray(q.rules) ? q.rules : []));
  observed.rulesToOurQueue = rules;
  if (ours.some((q) => !Array.isArray(q.rules))) {
    refusals.push("a queue entry carried no enumerable rule list, so its coverage is unexamined");
  }
  if (rules.length === 0) {
    refusals.push(`the queue ${JSON.stringify(expect.queue)} is attached to this bucket with no ` +
                  "rules, so nothing is actually routed");
    return { ok: false, refusals, notes, observed };
  }
  if (rules.length > 1) {
    refusals.push(`${rules.length} rules route to this queue. Exactly one is required for M2.0: ` +
                  "proving that a set of overlapping rules covers the namespace without " +
                  "double-firing is a harder claim than provisioning one rule that plainly does");
  }

  // ---- the namespace ------------------------------------------------------
  for (const r of rules) {
    if (typeof r?.suffix === "string" && r.suffix !== "") {
      refusals.push(`a rule filters on suffix ${JSON.stringify(r.suffix)}. Keys are minted as ` +
                    "org/<uuid>/world/<uuid>/<path> and end in a content hash or a manifest " +
                    "path, so no suffix covers them and every non-matching write is silently " +
                    "unobserved");
    }
    const p = r?.prefix;
    if (p !== undefined && p !== null && p !== "" && !NAMESPACE_PREFIX.startsWith(p)) {
      // `org/` and its own prefixes (`o`, `or`, `org`) all cover the namespace.
      // Anything else — `org/x`, `chunks/`, `wrong-prefix/` — does not.
      refusals.push(`a rule filters on prefix ${JSON.stringify(p)}, which does not cover every ` +
                    `key this control plane mints (all of them begin ${JSON.stringify(NAMESPACE_PREFIX)})`);
    }

  // ---- the actions --------------------------------------------------------
  const declared = new Set();
  for (const r of rules) {
    if (!Array.isArray(r?.actions)) {
      refusals.push("a rule declares no action array; Cloudflare's schema marks `actions` " +
                    "required, so this is not a rule shape we can reason about");

    for (const a of r.actions) declared.add(a);
  }

  const unknown = [...declared].filter((a) => !PROVIDER_ACTIONS.includes(a));
  if (unknown.length) {
    refusals.push(`${unknown.length} action(s) outside Cloudflare's documented enum: ` +
                  `${unknown.map((a) => JSON.stringify(a)).join(", ")} — an action this gate ` +
                  "does not recognise is not one it may vouch for");
  }

  const missing = CREATE_ACTIONS.filter((a) => !declared.has(a));
  if (missing.length) {
    refusals.push(`the rule does not cover ${missing.join(", ")}. These are R2's object-create ` +
                  "actions — " + CREATE_ACTIONS.join(", ") + " — and EVERY one of them changes " +
                  "what is stored, whether or not M2.0 authorized it. That is deliberately " +
                  "broader than the credential minter, which is PutObject-shaped today: an " +
                  "uncovered action is occupancy that reaches R2 and never reaches the ledger " +
                  "(finding 65 from below the database, with no retry budget to exhaust because " +
                  "no message was ever produced), and a COVERED one we did not authorize is an " +
                  "alarm we would otherwise never see (finding 112)");
  }

  const deletes = DELETE_ACTIONS.filter((a) => declared.has(a));
  if (deletes.length) {
    refusals.push(`the rule routes ${deletes.join(", ")} to the observer. M2.0 is append-only ` +
                  "(R56) and the observer has no delete path — reconcile.mjs names these actions " +
                  "in order to REFUSE them. A delete rule here also contradicts the premise the " +
                  "`extra` refusal in inventory.mjs rests on");
  }

  // ---- what else this bucket feeds ---------------------------------------
  // Not a refusal. A second queue on the same bucket is a legitimate thing to
  // do (an analytics fan-out, a thumbnailer) and it takes no authority away
  // from ours. It is reported because a reader of this output should know the
  // bucket has other listeners.
  if (others.length) {
    notes.push(`this bucket also routes to ${others.length} other queue(s): ` +
               others.map((q) => JSON.stringify(q?.queueName ?? null)).join(", ") +
               " — not a violation, but they see every write we do");
  }

  return { ok: refusals.length === 0, refusals, notes, observed };
}

// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

const PLAN = `
  CASE P2 — R2 NOTIFICATION COVERAGE (R77, R79, finding 99)

  Needs, in the environment — CREDENTIALS ONLY (finding 105):
    CF_ACCOUNT_ID   the account
    CF_API_TOKEN    a token with R2 read

  Takes its SUBJECTS from the ACTIVE WORKER VERSION, never the caller and never
  the manifest (findings 121, 127, 135). resolveLiveSubjects():

      GET .../workers/scripts/{name}/deployments   which version serves traffic
        -> require ONE version at 100%             (a split rollout is refused)
      GET .../workers/scripts/{name}/versions/{id} that version's bindings
        -> require exact agreement with worker/wrangler.toml
        -> return the DEPLOYED values, plus deploymentId and versionId

  So every assertion below is about the runtime, and says which one:
  *version V, which deployment D routes at 100%.*

  Reads:
    GET /accounts/{account}/event_notifications/r2/{bucket}/configuration

  Asserts:
    bucketName            == the ACTIVE VERSION's R2_BUCKET binding
    exactly one queue entry for the ACTIVE VERSION's PROVIDER_QUEUE binding,
                          carrying exactly one rule
    rule.actions          covers ${CREATE_ACTIONS.join(", ")}
                          — every provider object-create action that can change occupancy,
                            which is BROADER than what M2.0 authorizes, on purpose (finding 112)
    rule.actions          contains NO delete action (M2.0 is append-only, R56)
    rule.actions          contains nothing outside Cloudflare's five-action enum
    rule.suffix           absent
    rule.prefix           absent, or a prefix of ${JSON.stringify(NAMESPACE_PREFIX)}

  Reports (not refusals): other queues this bucket also feeds.

  CASE P AND CASE P2 ARE BOTH REQUIRED AND NEITHER IMPLIES THE OTHER.
  P:  is the thing that speaks on this channel really R2?     (queue side)
  P2: does R2 speak about every write that can change occupancy?   (bucket side)
      NOT "every write we admit" (finding 112, and the wording survived it):
      the rule must cover all three provider create actions, which is BROADER
      than what M2.0 authorizes, precisely because an unadmitted write is the
      one we most need to hear about.
`;

async function main() {
  if (process.argv.slice(2).includes("--plan")) { process.stdout.write(PLAN); process.exit(0); }

  const env = process.env;
  const need = ["CF_ACCOUNT_ID", "CF_API_TOKEN"];
  const missing = need.filter((n) => !env[n]);
  if (missing.length) {
    process.stdout.write(PLAN);
    process.stderr.write(`\n  NOT RUN  missing: ${missing.join(", ")}\n` +
                         "           This is exit 2, not exit 0: an unrun check is not a passing " +
                         "one.\n\n");
    process.exit(2);
  }

  const retired = refuseRetiredSubjectEnv();
  if (retired) { process.stderr.write(`\n  REFUSED  ${retired}\n\n`); process.exit(1); }
  let deployment;
  try {
    // FINDING 127. THE SUBJECT IS RESOLVED HERE, AGAINST THE DEPLOYMENT, NOW.
    // This used to be `requireSubjects()` — the FILE — on the reasoning that
    // case S had already compared the file to the deployment. But a prior check
    // is not a capability: S is separately invocable, `--run` does not exist to
    // sequence them, and the deployment can change in between. The subject has
    // to cross the boundary with the operation that uses it.
    deployment = await resolveLiveSubjects({
      accountId: env.CF_ACCOUNT_ID, apiToken: env.CF_API_TOKEN,
    });
  } catch (e) {
    if (e.code === "CD-SUBJ-NOTDEPLOYED") {
      process.stderr.write("\n  NOT RUN  " + e.message + "\n           Exit 2: this gate attests a " +
        "DEPLOYED Worker and there is not one.\n\n");
      process.exit(2);
    }
    process.stderr.write(`\n  REFUSED  ${e.message}\n\n`);
    process.exit(1);
  }
  const { r2Bucket, providerQueue } = deployment.subjects;
  process.stdout.write(`  subjects from ${deployment.origin}: bucket=${r2Bucket} ` +
                       `queue=${providerQueue}\n`);

  fetch(`https://api.cloudflare.com/client/v4/accounts/${env.CF_ACCOUNT_ID}` +
        `/event_notifications/r2/${r2Bucket}/configuration`,
        { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${env.CF_API_TOKEN}` } })
    .then(async (r) => {
      const body = await r.json().catch(() => null);
      if (!r.ok || body?.success !== true) {
        throw new Error(`${r.status} ${JSON.stringify(body?.errors ?? null)}`);
      }
      return body.result;
    })
    .then((config) => {
      const v = notificationCoverageVerdict(config, { bucket: r2Bucket, queue: providerQueue });
      process.stdout.write(`  bucket   ${v.observed.bucketName}\n`);
      for (const r of v.observed.rulesToOurQueue) {
        process.stdout.write(`  rule     actions=[${(r.actions ?? []).join(", ")}] ` +
                             `prefix=${JSON.stringify(r.prefix ?? null)} ` +
                             `suffix=${JSON.stringify(r.suffix ?? null)}\n`);
      }
      for (const n of v.notes) process.stdout.write(`  note     ${n}\n`);
      if (!v.ok) {
        process.stderr.write("\n  REFUSED  the notification rule does not cover every admitted " +
                             "write:\n\n");
        for (const r of v.refusals) process.stderr.write(`     - ${r}\n`);
        process.stderr.write("\n");
        process.exit(1);
      }
      process.stdout.write("\n  ok       one rule, every create action, the whole key namespace, " +
                           "no deletes\n");
    })
    .catch((e) => {
      process.stderr.write(`\n  REFUSED  could not read the notification configuration: ${e.message}\n\n`);
      process.exit(1);
    });
}

if (import.meta.url === `file://${process.argv[1]}`) {
  main().catch((e) => {
    // An unhandled rejection would exit 0 on some runtimes, which is the one
    // outcome a gate must never produce by accident.
    process.stderr.write(`
  REFUSED  ${e?.stack ?? e}

`);
    process.exit(1);
  });
}
```

## 4.5 Ownership documents (reconciled this round)

### `agents/README.md`

```markdown
# Agent lanes — what can be worked on in parallel, and what will collide

**Written 2026-08-15.** Six lanes. Each has a brief in this directory. Start a session by pointing
it at its brief; the brief is written to be self-sufficient.

> **2026-08-16 — a second set exists: `agents/SITES.md`, lanes G–N**, covering the domain
> `index.html`s. It touches no A–F file. Two things in it bind every lane here too: **half the
> domains live in `/home/travis/Projects/`, not this tree**, and four names exist in both with only
> one copy live. See `SITES.md` §0.1 for the byte-count check that settles which.

> **`docs/` is the stackdocs aggregation site** and anything put there is swept into the atlas
> build. That is why these live in `agents/` at the root instead.

---

## The constraint that shapes everything: one working tree

**All your sessions share `/home/travis/ProjectAmp2`. There are no worktrees.** Two agents editing
the same file is not merge conflict — it is one silently overwriting the other, and it has cost
real work before.

**So the lanes are partitioned by file ownership, and the ownership is the contract.** Every brief
opens with what it owns and what it must not touch. If a lane needs a file another lane owns, it
says so and stops rather than reaching across.

**Do not run all six at once.** Three or four is the realistic ceiling on one tree.

---

## Can they start now?

| Lane | Owns | Ready? |
|---|---|---|
| **A — Shell wiring** | `RRABBIT/m2/`, `RRABBIT/test/` | ⚠️ **only if no other session is in `m2/`** |
| **B — studbook** | `studbook/` | ❌ blocked on two [TRAVIS] rulings |
| **C — Infrastructure** | no repo files; cloud accounts | ❌ needs you present — spend and credentials |
| **D — Worker / auth / control plane** | `worker/`, **incl. `worker/migrations/`** | ⚠️ **schema + RLS + token tests unblocked 2026-08-21**; cloud integration still on C |
| **E — Site** | `computedriven.com/` *(nav moved to lane N, 2026-08-16)* | ✅ **now** |
| **F — Docs reconciliation** | root `*.md` | ✅ **now** |
| **O — Cloud site** | `cloud.computedriven.com/` (new, 2026-08-21) | ✅ **now** — static; its claims read from `status.json` |

**Start today: D, E, F and O.** D's local half needs no cloud account at all — a local Postgres and
a locally generated keypair carry the schema, the tenant-isolation battery and token verification.

> **2026-08-21 — lanes D and O both touch the Cloud v1 round and must not be run in one session.**
> D owns the Worker and the schema; O owns the marketing/status surface. The seam between them is
> `cloud.computedriven.com/status.json`, which **O owns and D only reads**. If a capability's rung
> changes, D reports it and O edits the file — never both.

**A is the highest-value build work** and the only question is whether the tracks/reel session is
still live. Check `git log --oneline -3` in `RRABBIT/` — if the newest commit is `a4ea112`
("Somewhere to put a track…"), that was this session and the lane is free.

---

## What is blocking B, C and D — all of it is yours

None of these is a task. Each is a decision only you make.

1. **studbook §10.5 — does the identity ladder admit a `track-` prefix?** A track records a *live OS
   world*, not a sealed `sem-` world. The code already uses `track-` and marks it **provisional**;
   if the answer is no, that constant changes and every id changes with it. **Blocks B, and makes
   anything published before it disposable.**
2. **The index question** (`CONFIDENTIALITY.md` §4) — the operator-visible graph: accept it,
   minimise it, or encrypt it. Recommendation is *minimise* (ids, sizes, edges; no names, no paths).
   **Blocks B's schema.**
3. **The threat model** (`CONFIDENTIALITY.md` §1) — which of T1–T7 are in scope. Everything in
   class B (private data) is downstream. **Blocks B's crypto, not its index.**
4. **Spend approval** for Hetzner, Fly, PlanetScale, Cloudflare R2. **Blocks C.**
   **Amended 2026-08-21:** it no longer blocks all of D. D's local half — schema, RLS, tenant
   batteries, JWT verification against a generated keypair — runs with no account. Only the
   *integration* half waits on spend.
5. **The enterprise tier price.** **~$438/month** carries 65% on 10 TB; the *product* is dedicated
   infrastructure, not gigabytes. **Blocks E's pricing copy.**
   **Corrected 2026-08-16** — this said ~$236, which carries **35%**. $153.45 ÷ $236 = 65.02%, i.e.
   COGS÷price, the inverse of margin.
6. **`STACK_COMPLETION.md` §0/§6 re-rating** — the ruling changed an input those ratings read as
   strength. **Blocks nothing; it is just wrong until you do it.**

---

## What is already ruled — do not relitigate

Every brief repeats the ones it needs, but the whole set:

- **Cloudflare for everything; Fly for Keycloak alone.** Workers are V8 isolates and cannot run
  Java — the mirror of Firecracker being unable to boot FreeBSD.
- **Hetzner for the VM.** T&R and Pigsty both need a real machine.
- **PlanetScale PS-5 HA ($15/mo) for Keycloak's database.** Not Fly Managed Postgres ($38).
- **R2 for bulk objects** — zero egress is what makes the restore claim true.
- **Compute moves into the OS.** The ten Fly apps are being wound down, but **nothing is torn down
  before its OS-side replacement is `live_local`.**
- **T&R backs up the user's machine, 10 GB–10 TB.** Not just the shell's graph.
- **Confidentiality is four questions.** Published needs none (v0); enterprise is isolation;
  private-single-user is client-side keys; shared-private is deferred.
- **Convergent encryption is refused by name** — it restores the confirmation-of-a-file attack.

**Added 2026-08-21 — the Cloud v1 rulings (R7–R16, `REVISION_REGISTER.md`):**

- **No server-hosted BEAM in Cloud v1.** The control plane is Workers, reaching Pigsty over
  Hyperdrive → Workers VPC → Cloudflare Tunnel. Super stays Elixir/OTP *on the user's machine*.
- **The R2 credential minter survives** and is now the API surface. Bulk bytes go client ↔ R2
  **directly**; a Worker in the byte path is a design error, not an optimisation.
- **PlanetScale is Keycloak's database and nothing else** — for failure isolation, not for price.
- **Keycloak `sub` is not an identity.** It is a *binding* to one, in `principal_identities`.
- **Three world sizes, three names:** WORLD (the machine, 10 GB–10 TB) · WORLD VERSION (a manifest
  root in R2) · WRL GRAPH (the small semantic layer inside it). Never one `current_head`.
- **World sync + restore ships before hosted compute.** M2, not M5.
- **Driver/Fleet/Factory do not include a VM.** Hosted capacity is a separate metered SKU.
- **RLS raises on missing tenant context.** An empty result set is not a refusal.

---

## Read before any non-trivial work

`CLAUDE.md` (repo instructions, corrected 2026-08-15) → `REVISION_REGISTER.md` (what is still stale)
→ then the lane's brief.

**Do not trust an undated planning doc.** This tree had `CLAUDE.md` teaching an architecture
abandoned sixteen days earlier, and a rung table that was wrong one day after it was measured.

---

## The house rules every lane is held to

From `DOCTRINE.md`, which is entrenched and which Travis alone ratifies:

- **A check outranks an opinion.** If a command settles it, run the command.
- **Do not fabricate** counts, statuses or provenance. `?` is an acceptable answer.
- **Name the gap.** Say what is not built, in the same breath as what is.
- **Measure before you claim, and say how.**
- **Retract out loud**, by name, in the same place the claim was made.
- **Some decisions are Travis's.** Flag and stop.
- **Commit so work survives; verify so it is worth surviving.**

Every report ends with a `DOCTRINE:` section saying which of *advanced / contradicted / proposed /
none* applies. **`none` is common and correct** — do not manufacture a finding.

# Lane C — stand up the cloud

**Owns:** no repository files. Cloud accounts, and `PARKVPS/` for local VM work.
**Must not touch:** application code in any lane.

> ## ❌ NEEDS TRAVIS IN THE ROOM
>
> Every task here spends money or creates an account. **An agent must not provision paid
> infrastructure, enter payment details, or accept terms.** Prepare the commands, explain what each
> will cost, and let Travis run the ones that spend.
>
> Standing constraint: **this stack is built on a zero-budget assumption.** Do not casually add a
> line item.

---

## Read first

`STACK_HUB.md` §0.7 and §0.9–0.11 — the provider rulings and what each costs.

## What is ruled

| Piece | Where | Why that vendor |
|---|---|---|
| Keycloak | **Fly `iad`** | Workers are V8 isolates and cannot run Java |
| Keycloak's database | **PlanetScale PS-5 HA, $15/mo** | **Rationale replaced 2026-08-21 (R9) — see §3.** Failure isolation, not price |
| Control-plane API, portal BFF, credential minting | **Cloudflare Workers** | **R7** — §0.6's ruling holds. No server-hosted BEAM in Cloud v1 |
| Worker → Pigsty transport | **Hyperdrive → Workers VPC → Cloudflare Tunnel** | **R7** — Pigsty stays private on Hetzner with no Postgres port facing the internet |
| Pigsty Postgres — studbook index **and the Cloud control plane** | **Hetzner VM** | Pigsty needs systemd/sudo/sshd; Fly gives Firecracker containers |
| Bulk objects | **Cloudflare R2** | zero egress at any volume |

> **2026-08-21 — this table gained a row and lost an assumption.** A proposed Cloud brief put a
> Phoenix/Elixir API at the centre of the architecture, which silently reversed `STACK_HUB.md` §0.6
> (*"Workers cannot run Elixir, Phoenix, or the BEAM … that decision has to be revisited rather than
> patched"*). **R7 declines to reopen it.** The control plane is Workers; Pigsty is reached over
> Hyperdrive rather than by moving the application to the database. Super stays BEAM/OTP **on the
> user's machine** — Cloud does not mirror Super's implementation just because Super is Elixir.

---

## The four jobs

### 1. The Hetzner VM

**T&R is FreeBSD and Hetzner Cloud's API has no image upload.** The documented path is to boot the
**rescue system** and write the raw image straight to `/dev/sda` (`qemu-img convert`, or
`hcloud-upload-image` which automates it). FreeBSD-on-hcloud is independently documented, including
a 2026 Packer write-up.

**Snapshot after the first install** — that is the distribution path, and the workaround is not
repeated per machine.

**Budget a session, not an afternoon.** It is documented, not supported. Nothing is blocked
meanwhile: PARKVPS runs T&R locally today.

**Sizing: do not trust any euro figure you find.** Hetzner adjusted prices in June 2026 and CX32 is
deprecated, so published comparisons are stale. **Price it on Hetzner's own calculator.**

> **CORRECTED 2026-08-21.** This read *"Pigsty wants 1C2G, Keycloak wants 2 GB, so ~4 vCPU / 8 GB is
> the plausible floor for the shared box"* — which budgeted Keycloak's RAM onto Hetzner while the
> table two sections up ruled Keycloak onto **Fly**. The table is right and the sizing line was
> wrong. **Keycloak is not on this box.**
>
> What actually runs here under R7: **Pigsty** (Patroni, etcd, HAProxy, PgBouncer, pgBackRest,
> MinIO, Grafana, Nginx) and **`cloudflared`** for the Tunnel. No application server — R7 keeps the
> control plane on Workers, so nothing here serves HTTP to the public. Shape only, still to be
> priced first-party: Pigsty's own floor is 1C1G, 1C2G recommended, and the Tunnel daemon is small.

### 2. Pigsty

Ansible-driven, needs **systemd, sudo and sshd**, installs Patroni, etcd, HAProxy, PgBouncer,
pgBackRest, MinIO, Grafana and Nginx. Minimum 1C1G, 1C2G recommended. This is why it goes on the
Hetzner VM and not on Fly.

Serves **studbook's index** (lane B) — and *not* user bytes. Bytes in Postgres is 18.7× R2 and
would lose ~$2,867/month on a single 10 TB customer.

### 3. Keycloak on Fly + PlanetScale

- **Deploy Keycloak to Fly `iad`.** PlanetScale's pricing is AWS `us-east-1`, the same metro —
  single-digit milliseconds. Put it in a European region and every token issuance crosses the
  Atlantic. **The rule is co-locate, and co-location is about distance, not matching logos.**
- **Do not point it at the Hetzner Postgres.** It will look tidy. It puts the auth path — the one
  thing that must be up for anyone to do anything — on the longest wire in the architecture, and
  re-couples exactly what the split decoupled.

  > **R9, 2026-08-21 — this bullet is now the whole reason, and the recorded price argument is
  > retired.** The $15/mo was justified by beating **Fly Managed Postgres at $38**. That comparison
  > was correct when nothing else in the stack ran Postgres. It is not the live alternative any
  > more: Pigsty *is* Patroni plus streaming replicas, so the honest comparison became "$15/mo
  > versus another database on a cluster you are already paying for", and on price alone PlanetScale
  > loses that.
  >
  > **The ruling does not change, because price was never the load-bearing reason** — this bullet
  > was. What $15/mo buys is stated plainly so it can be re-decided later on its merits:
  >
  > ```
  > Pigsty trouble  ≠  Keycloak database trouble
  > ```
  >
  > Reconsider when product economics matter. Do not reconsider mid-implementation.
- **PS-5 is 1/16 vCPU and 512 MiB.** "HA" means redundant, not fast. If auth feels slow the answer
  is **PS-10 HA at $30**, still under Fly's $38.
- **PlanetScale Postgres is real Postgres, not Vitess** — the well-known no-foreign-keys caveat is
  about their MySQL product and does not apply. Keycloak's JPA schema is fine.
- **Connect directly, not through their optional PgBouncer.** Keycloak brings Agroal;
  transaction-mode pooling against JDBC prepared statements is a known trouble source.
- **SQLite is not an option.** Keycloak supports Postgres/MariaDB/MySQL/MSSQL/Oracle/Aurora/Azure
  SQL. H2 (`dev-file`) is explicitly *"not suitable for production use-cases."*

### 4. R2

A bucket for published track bundles. **Class A ops are $4.50/M** — the discipline is
content-addressed chunks, never re-PUT an unchanged chunk, ≥8 MB minimum, incremental by default.
Measured: naïve weekly fulls on 1 TB are $30.67/yr against **$4.30/yr** incremental.

**Public tracks need no credential** — class A data, world-readable, no Worker in front of them.
That is why this rung ships before lane D.

---

## Done means

- `trvs doctor` printing `status ready` on a Hetzner instance, and `trvs id` deriving the **same**
  `sem-` identity as the workstation. A **different** id is the more interesting result and should
  be reported loudly, not debugged into agreement.
- A Keycloak realm issuing a JWT, fetched from Fly `iad`, verifiable against its JWKS.
- A track bundle PUT to R2 and GET back **on a different machine**, verified by re-derived hash.
- **Every figure recorded with the date it was measured.** This tree has quoted stale storage prices
  three times; the rule now is quote first-party at the point of use, never from prose.

## Do not tear anything down yet

Ten Fly apps are `live_deployed` and are being wound down — but **nothing is torn down before its
OS-side replacement is `live_local`.** Deleting a working deployment to honour a plan is how a
portfolio loses a capability it had. `box-and-box-mcp` is first in the queue and even that can wait.
```

### `agents/D-worker-auth.md`

```markdown
# Lane D — the credential surface, and now the control plane

**Owns:** `worker/` (created 2026-08-21), including `worker/migrations/` — the Pigsty schema.
**Must not touch:** `RRABBIT/`, `studbook/`, root `*.md`, `cloud.computedriven.com/`.

> ## ⚠️ PARTIALLY UNBLOCKED — 2026-08-21, R7/R8
>
> **What is no longer blocked:** the schema, the RLS battery, the tenant-context contract and the
> token-verification unit tests. All of it runs against **local PostgreSQL** and a **locally
> generated keypair**. None of it needs a cloud account. That is most of M1.
>
> **What is still blocked on lane C:** integration against a real realm, a real Hyperdrive binding,
> and a real R2 bucket. Those stay `NOT DEPLOYED` and must be *named* so, never mocked into a
> production claim.
>
> **Not needed for v0 public tracks.** Public tracks are world-readable and need no credential at
> all, which is why lane A ships without this. This lane exists for **private** data.

---

## What changed on 2026-08-21

A proposed Cloud brief dropped this lane entirely — R2 objects and a Pigsty `storage ref` appeared
in its architecture with **no credential minter anywhere**. **R8 keeps the lane and widens it.**

This is now *two* jobs in one Worker, not one:

1. **the control-plane API** — the portal BFF and `api.computedriven.com`, reaching Pigsty over
   **Hyperdrive → Workers VPC → Cloudflare Tunnel** (R7);
2. **the credential minter** — unchanged in purpose, better in mechanism (below).

It stops being "small and stateless". Re-read the free-tier arithmetic below with that in mind: the
100k req/day ceiling now has to cover portal traffic, not just credential mints.

---

## Read first

`STACK_HUB.md` §0.7 (the shape) and §0.4.3 (the hole this fills) · `CONFIDENTIALITY.md` (what this
does **not** solve).

## The one job

```
Keycloak (Fly)      issues an OIDC JWT — who you are, which plan you hold
      ↓  JWKS
Worker (Cloudflare) verify signature · check entitlement ·
                    mint a SCOPED, SHORT-LIVED credential
      ↓
R2                  encrypted blobs — never sees a plaintext byte
```

**This closes the only hole in the compute-in-the-OS design:** an object store cannot decide who
deserves a credential. Everything else moved into the user's machine; this could not, because a
customer who could mint their own credential could mint their own subscription.

**Keep it small.** It is a stateless request/response handler and it fits inside the Workers **free**
plan — 100,000 requests/day, 10 ms CPU per invocation. If it grows past that, something has gone
wrong with the design rather than with the plan.

> **Amended 2026-08-21 (R8).** "Small" now means *the bytes never come through here*, not *the
> request count is tiny*. The rule that matters:
>
> ```
> Super / client
>       │  authenticate  ────────────►  Worker
>       │                                 ├── resolve principal + organization
>       │                                 ├── consult Pigsty (Hyperdrive)
>       │                                 ├── authorize the requested object scope
>       │                                 └── mint a scoped, short-lived R2 credential
>       │  ◄───────────────────────────────┘
>       │
>       └──────────── chunks ────────────►  R2      DIRECT. Never via the Worker.
> ```
>
> **Not** `client → Worker → 400 GB of machine backup → R2`. A Worker in the byte path would blow
> the CPU limit, the request duration and the cost model simultaneously, and it buys nothing: the
> credential already carries the authorization.
>
> **Mechanism:** use R2's **temporary-credentials** API for a chunk session — short-lived S3
> credentials scoped to a bucket, a set of operations, and an exact prefix or object path. Use a
> **presigned URL** where the operation is genuinely one object. The chunker does batches, so
> temporary credentials are the normal case and presigned URLs are the exception.
>
> **Verify both against Cloudflare's own docs at the point of use.** This tree has quoted stale
> provider facts three times; §0.2's rule applies to API shapes as much as to prices.

## What it must do

1. **Verify the JWT** against the realm's JWKS. Workers cannot use Node-native libraries — use
   `jose` or `cloudflare-worker-jwt`. Cache the JWKS briefly; rotate.
2. **Check `iss`, `aud`, `exp`** and the claims. A valid signature on a token for a different
   audience is not authorization.
3. **Check entitlement** — is this subscription current, and for which tier.

   > **SUPERSEDED 2026-08-21 (R7).** This said subscriber state lives in **D1**. It does not.
   > R7 makes **Pigsty the single owner of ComputeDriven truth**, and entitlements are that —
   > they are joined against organizations, worlds and usage, which is exactly the shape D1 is
   > wrong for. `entitlements` is a Pigsty table reached over Hyperdrive.
   >
   > D1 keeps no application state under this ruling. If it earns a job later it will be a cache
   > with a named invalidation rule, not a second source of truth.
4. **Mint a scoped, short-lived credential** — a presigned URL or scoped token, narrowed to that
   tenant's prefix. **Never hand out a broad credential because it is simpler.**
5. **Fail closed.** Anything unverifiable is a refusal, by name, with no fallback path.

## What this does NOT solve — do not let it drift

**This is authorization, not confidentiality.** They are different questions with different
mechanisms, and collapsing them is the same category error as conflating a `sem-` world with an OS
world:

| Question | Answered by |
|---|---|
| Who are you, and are you entitled? | **this lane** |
| Why can the storage provider not read your data? | **client-side keys** — nothing here touches it |

Keycloak controls *who may ask for a credential*. It has nothing to say about *why knowing a content
hash does not reveal content*. **Never describe this as making anything end-to-end encrypted.**

## Done means

- Unit tests against a locally generated keypair: valid token accepted, expired refused, wrong
  audience refused, bad signature refused, `alg: none` refused, a token for tenant A unable to
  obtain a credential for tenant B.
- Integration against a real Keycloak realm once lane C lands.
- A measured request cost showing it fits the free tier.

## Traps

- **`alg: none` and algorithm confusion.** Pin the expected algorithm; never take it from the token.
- **Clock skew** — allow a small leeway on `exp`/`nbf`, and say how much.
- **A JWKS fetch that fails must refuse, not fall back** to a cached key indefinitely.
- **Scope every credential to a tenant prefix.** The most likely real bug in this lane is a
  credential that works for more than it should, and it will not show up in a happy-path test.
- **Do not build auth by hand.** Verify tokens someone else issued; issue none yourself.
```

| R79 | **Queue notifications minimize convergence latency; R2 inventory establishes recoverability.** `max_retries = 5` with no dead letter queue, and Cloudflare documents the consequence: *without a DLQ configured, messages that reach the retry limit are deleted permanently.* A long enough Pigsty outage therefore reaches R2 holding the object, the notification deleted, and `committed_bytes` unmoved — **finding 65 arriving from BELOW the database instead of above it.** A transport with a finite retry budget is a buffer, not a durability theorem. A DLQ is configured and case P refuses a consumer without one, but a DLQ only *bounds* the loss (four days unconsumed); the closure is a reconciliation pass over the R2 listing, which is **strongly consistent** and therefore authoritative for an append-only M2.0 (R56). `worker/src/inventory.mjs` is a PURE planner — finding 88's lesson applied in advance — classifying `missing`/`divergent` as repairable and **REFUSING `extra`**, because auto-crediting bytes back on an out-of-band delete is worse than the divergence. ~~The pass is also the ambiguity resolver R75 left open.~~ **CORRECTED 2026-08-23 (finding 97): it is not.** An equal-time repair leaves `count(DISTINCT (etag,size_bytes)) > 1` unchanged, so the tie survives; the planner now REPORTS a resolution candidate and refuses to apply it, and case **J** decides whether a provenance-rank migration is ever needed. `CLOUD_V1.md` §6.9 | 2026-08-23 | DLQ behaviour documented first-party; the recovery half is PROPOSED until live case **N** |
| R80 | **Two authorities, two credentials.** A Hyperdrive configuration carries its own origin user and password, so one binding is one database credential — and `connect()`/`connectJobs()` both reading `HYPERDRIVE_CONTROL` would have made `computedriven_api` and `computedriven_jobs` one authority wearing two function names, silently, at the moment the driver was written, with both names still reading correctly. The request role deliberately holds no EXECUTE on `app.observe_storage_object()`; that is the boundary at stake. Two bindings, each with a LOGIN principal inheriting exactly one NOLOGIN role — provisioner work, not a migration. **The one-login-with-`SET ROLE` alternative is refused**: the credential then holds the union and the boundary is application convention. `scripts/check-channel-identity.mjs` fails the build if either helper reads the other's binding. **R80.1, 2026-08-23 (finding 95): that gate read binding NAMES.** Two bindings pointing at one configuration id exited 0 saying "two Hyperdrive authorities" — one credential wearing two names. Colliding ids are refused now; the rest is not in any file, because a Hyperdrive configuration's origin user and its SQL response cache are provider state (`wrangler hyperdrive create --caching-disabled` sets the cache on the CONFIGURATION). Live case **Q** attests them. `CLOUD_V1.md` §6.10 | 2026-08-23 | structural, gated locally; **the credential and the cache are unattested until case Q runs**, and `origin.password` is write-only so even Q proves the named user and not the secret |
| R79.2 | **A completed sweep is not a point-in-time snapshot, and R79 said it was.** Cloudflare guarantees that an object-list operation *"will list all objects at that point in time"* — for ONE list operation. A whole-bucket enumeration is many, and no first-party source says page 1 at T₁ and page 500 at T₅₀₀ share a snapshot, so an object created behind the cursor need not appear in the sweep that passed it. `CompletedScan` implied otherwise by its name. Renamed **`CompletedSweep`**, asserting only *every provider page traversed through a verified cursor chain from beginning to normal termination*, with `doesNotAssert` stated as a field beside it. R79's recoverability is therefore **eventual, through repeated authoritative sweeps**, not one-pass reconstruction under concurrent mutation. `CLOUD_V1.md` §6.9 | 2026-08-24 | Cloudflare consistency page read first-party; the multi-page question is **unanswered by the docs** and case **N** measures it (quiesce the bucket, or repeat until the delta converges to zero) |
| R81 | **Evidence used for a negative conclusion must be both unforgeable and immutable.** `reconciliationPlan()` admitted a completed enumeration on `scan?.__completeScan !== true` — a field, which a hand-typed literal supplies — and the planner then reported a known ledger object absent from R2, an alleged out-of-band delete from an enumeration that never ran. The second half is sharper: `Object.freeze()` freezes the POINTER, and `presentKeys` was a live `Set`, so on a genuinely protocol-built scan `Object.isFrozen(scan) === true` while `presentKeys.delete(key)` **succeeded** and moved the plan from 0 refusals to 1. Absence is this pass's strongest and least reversible conclusion, so its evidence gets the treatment the tree already gave JWT claims, admissions and R2 scopes: a module-private `WeakSet` granted only by the protocol that earns it, plus a collection with no reachable mutator. **A proof object is not proved because it contains the field that says it is proved.** `worker/src/inventory.mjs`, `CLOUD_V1.md` §6.9 | 2026-08-24 | MEASURED both halves against the shipped tree; **+6 tests, 2 mutation vectors**. The pattern was already in `jwt.mjs` / `admission.mjs` / `r2creds.mjs` — R76's shape, fourth round running |
| R82 | **A set-difference theorem requires completeness of both operands.** Rounds 8.2 and 8.3 spent themselves earning ONE: `CompletedSweep`, unforgeable, immutable, cursor-chain verified — and handed it to `reconciliationPlan(sweep, known)` where `known` was an ordinary `Array`. Nothing said those rows were every ledger object, were read by a role that can see every tenant, were untruncated, belonged to that bucket, or came from one snapshot. MEASURED in both directions: R2 {A,B} against a caller-passed `[A]` FABRICATES a missing repair; R2 {A} against a caller-passed `[A]` when the ledger really holds {A,B} **erases the out-of-band delete entirely** — the exact R56-impossible state the pass exists to catch. The likeliest cause is not carelessness but **RLS**: `computedriven_jobs` carries no tenant context by design, so a policied read returns a subset that is indistinguishable from a clean bucket. `beginLedgerInventory()` earns a `CompleteLedgerInventory` by the same keyset-chain protocol, brands it in a module-private WeakSet, and carries bucket, authority and snapshot; the planner takes two proofs or none. **The types were saying this out loud — `CompletedSweep` on one side, `Array` on the other — for two rounds.** `worker/src/inventory.mjs`, `CLOUD_V1.md` §6.9 | 2026-08-24 | MEASURED both directions; **+8 tests, 5 vectors**. No migration — this is an evidence protocol, not a schema |
| R83 | **Protocol-completeness and provider-authority are two facts and need two brands.** R81's WeakSet proves a value went through the sweep state machine. It does not prove the pages came from R2, because `sweepBucket()` takes its I/O from the caller. MEASURED with no R2 anywhere: `sweepBucket({ listPage: async () => ({Contents:[], KeyCount:0, IsTruncated:false}) })` produced a branded sweep that concluded absence. This is R27's boundary reached from the other side — **a WeakSet attestation is unforgeable by DATA and still forgeable by CODE** — so `AuthoritativeR2Sweep` is minted only when the pages arrived through `r2ListingAdapter()`, a bucket-scoped credentialed lister. Positive evidence (a repair) still computes from a merely protocol-complete sweep, because *R2 named this key* is true the moment it is read; **absence** yields `absenceUnknown` with its reasons. | R84 | **The deployment manifest is an intention. Once a deployment exists, the runtime deployment is the subject.** Finding 105 made `scripts/deployment-subjects.mjs` the single place a subject may come from and closed the caller-chosen half; the file itself then recorded, in a comment, that `origin: "wrangler.toml"` is *"correct today and wrong once deployment can drift"*. That moment is the next item on the schedule. If the adapter does not perform the authenticated act, it cannot attest that the act occurred.** R83 confined provider authority to a "credentialed adapter" — which took `{bucket, accessKeyId, secretAccessKey, endpoint, transport}`, checked the four strings were non-empty, and branded a closure calling the caller's `transport`. **There was no signing anywhere in it.** MEASURED with a fake key, a fake secret and a transport returning an object literal: `isAuthoritativeSweep()` **true**, with no R2 and no network. The defect did not close; it moved one wrapper deeper. `worker/src/s3sig.mjs` now implements AWS Signature Version 4 with no dependencies — **verified byte-equal against AWS's own published "Get Bucket (List Objects)" worked example**, because a signer checked against its author's expectations is finding 90 — and `r2ListingAdapter()` builds, signs and parses a real `ListObjectsV2`. Consequence stated plainly: **no authoritative sweep or ledger is reachable offline**, which is correct while the bundle says 0 live |

Completeness is the ADDITIONAL requirement for absence.** R83 modelled authority as something only negative evidence needed, on the reasoning that *R2 named this key* is true the moment it is read. It is — **but only if R2 named it.** MEASURED: a synthetic page claiming a 10 TB object produced a `missing` repair candidate for a key R2 never mentioned. Authority has two dimensions and R83 had one. The diff still computes without authority, because that is what keeps the set-difference algorithm exercisable with no account (round 4.1); what changes is that every repair carries `providerAuthoritative`, and a false one is a **blocker** in the same `applicationBlockers()` computation that finding 124 established — so it is printed and enforced by one code path rather than two. `worker/src/inventory.mjs` | 2026-08-24 | MEASURED; **+3 tests, 1 vector**. No migration |
| R87 | **A real network is not a provider. Provider authority requires authenticated I/O to the provider's RULED IDENTITY.** R85 made the adapter sign, and decided authority from `net === globalThis.fetch` while still taking `endpoint` from the caller. MEASURED by the reviewer and reproduced here with an ordinary local HTTP server and the REAL global fetch — nothing injected, nothing monkey-patched: `networkVerified: true`, `isAuthoritativeSweep: true`, signed host `127.0.0.1:39775`. **A signature authenticates the request to whoever owns the endpoint; it says nothing about who that is.** So round 8.5 shipped an acceptance theorem — *no R2 and no PostgreSQL means absence can never be established* — that was FALSE in the tree that published it, and my verification missed it because I tested the injected-transport attack and asserted the general case from one instance. | R88 | **A transaction id is not a snapshot, and an isolation level you EXPECT is not one you have.** R85's ledger adapter read `txid_current()` on every page, compared the values, called the result "one snapshot", and carried a comment saying *"the caller is expected to have opened a REPEATABLE READ transaction"* — precisely the external convention this system has spent rounds deleting. PostgreSQL, first-party: READ COMMITTED is the **default**, and under it *"two successive SELECT commands can see different data ... within a single transaction"*; a transaction id is stable across exactly that, so the equality check proved nothing it claimed. REPEATABLE READ is the level at which successive selects see one view. The adapter now issues `BEGIN TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY` itself, **reads back `current_setting('transaction_isolation')` rather than trusting what it asked for**, records `pg_current_snapshot()`, and commits so a pooled connection does not inherit the snapshot. ### 9. `AGENTS.md` — five errors, and one of them disabled the memory loop

Found in passing while writing the lane briefs; never swept. Audited line by line 2026-08-15:

1. **"WebHost.Systems (Convex + Vite/React/Clerk)."** False. `apps/web/package.json` depends on
   `@supabase/supabase-js`; **no Convex and no Clerk dependency exists anywhere in the monorepo**,
   and the root `package.json` still carries `supabase:start` / `supabase:stop` scripts.
2. **"EXLA is intentionally omitted from graphonomous."** False and backwards — `mix.exs:45` has
   `{:exla, "~> 0.9", runtime: false}`. `CLAUDE.md` had it right in both cases.
3. **The "Required context" list named 12 files and 11 do not exist.** It told every agent to load
   `AGENT_BOOTSTRAP_PROMPT.md` and `01_RETRIEVE_AND_REMEMBER.md` … `10_ANTI_PATTERNS.md`. Only
   `SKILLS.md` is real; the skills were renamed to phase-named files (`bootstrap.md`,
   `retrieve.md`, …). **This is the worst of the five**: an agent that cannot find its required
   reading concludes the memory loop is unavailable, and the policy silently stops running.
4. **The repo layout was four months stale** — no `RRABBIT/`, `TRVM/`, `WRL/`, `TRAAVIIS/`,
   `PARKVPS/`, `studbook/`, `workbench/`, `PRISM/`, `PULSE/`, `computedriven.com/`. It did not know
   about the operating system this portfolio is now built around.
5. **No data-layer section at all**, so an agent reading only this file got no warning about R1.

### 16. A published number did not re-derive — and it flattered us

**Found 2026-08-16 by an outside review of `computedriven.com`, not by us.**

`WORLD_SIZE.md` §11.1 asserts *"the world layer is ~0.1% of a 100 GB backup"*. It is not:

```
212.70 MB / 100 GB = 0.21%      (the enforced ceiling)
   247 KB / 100 GB = 0.0002%    (the realistic world)
```

Neither rounds to a tenth of a percent. **The likely origin is §1 of the same document**, which
uses "~0.1%" for something entirely different — *run-to-run variance* between measurements (246.8
vs 246.9 KB) — and the figure appears to have been carried across into a claim about proportion.

Two things make this the most instructive entry in this register:

1. **The error was in the flattering direction.** Every other drift recorded here (116/118, 2/4,
   35/40) was neutral — a stale count. This one made the product look better than the measurement
   supports, which is the specific failure doctrine rule 5 exists to catch.
2. **It survived being copied onto a public page and reviewed twice before anyone divided
   212.70 by 102400.** The measurement was correct, sourced and dated; only the ratio derived from
   it was wrong, and a correct measurement with a wrong conclusion attached reads as more
   trustworthy than either alone.

**Fixed** in `WORLD_SIZE.md` (retracted in place, conclusion unchanged and no weaker — a fifth of a
percent at a ceiling nobody reaches is still a layer that rides along free) and on the live page,
where the rung note now carries the retraction beside the corrected figure.

**This is the fourth typed-rather-than-derived number in this register**, and the first that was
not merely stale. The rule stands and now has a sharper form: *derive it, and then divide it out
loud.*

### 17. The page asserted a property it did not have

`computedriven.com`'s hero says **no telemetry**; the operating system it ships leads with **no
first-boot download**; and `computedriven.com/README.md` stated *"nothing else on the page calls out
at load."* All three were contradicted by a `fonts.googleapis.com` stylesheet in the document head,
which made every visitor fetch from Google — logging their IP — before a word rendered.

Nobody had checked. **The check is one line** —
`performance.getEntriesByType('resource').map(r => r.name)` — and it now returns zero off-origin
entries, with the fonts self-hosted at 53,720 bytes for both families.

The general lesson for this register: **a self-description in a README is a claim like any other,
and this one had never been tested against the document it describes.** Worth extending the next
sweep to cover README self-descriptions, not just planning docs.

### 14. Where "35 migrations across 11 schemas" came from

`CLAUDE.md` asserted it; `workbench/docs/spec/README.md` line 406 has
`"supabase_migration_count": 35` inside a JSON example. Counted in the tree instead:

```
ls ampersand-supabase/migrations/*.sql | wc -l                                    → 40
grep -hoE 'create schema if not exists [a-z_]+' …/*.sql | awk '{print $NF}' | sort -u | wc -l → 10
```

**40 migrations, 10 schemas** — `agentelic amp fleet geo govern kag orchestrate rune temporal
webhost`. This is the third derived number in this register to have drifted by being typed rather
than derived, after the law count (116 vs 118) and the sitemap occurrence count (2 vs 4). The rule
holds: quote the command.



**Two dated changelog entries were deliberately left carrying "116"** — the 2026-06-07 one (true when
written) and the 2026-08-13 one (wrong, and corrected at the top of the file instead). Doctrine rule
5: retract in place, do not edit history.

**R4 was ruled 2026-08-15** — Cloudflare for everything, Fly for Keycloak alone — which unblocked
item 2. **Still open, all [TRAVIS]:**

- **studbook §10.2** — where confidentiality comes from. **Analysed in `CONFIDENTIALITY.md`; still
  unruled.** It is **four questions, not one**: published data needs none, enterprise is answered by
  single-tenant isolation, private-single-user is client-side keys, and shared-private is the hard
  one and is not in v0. **Nothing is built and no E2EE exists today.** Two standing cautions: the
  index is **plaintext to the operator** even when blobs are encrypted (§4), so the phrase
  "end-to-end encrypted" is not currently earned; and **convergent encryption must be refused by
  name** (§5) because it restores the confirmation-of-a-file attack §6.2 identified.
- **The threat model has never been written.** `CONFIDENTIALITY.md` §1 lists T1–T7; every mechanism
  choice is downstream of which are in scope, and none are declared.
- ~~**The cloud-VM provider for T&R.**~~ **RULED 2026-08-15: Hetzner.** Confirmed workable — the
  image goes on via the rescue system (`hcloud-upload-image` / `qemu-img convert` to `/dev/sda`),
  since Hetzner's API has no image upload; snapshot it after the first install. `STACK_HUB.md` §0.9.
- ~~**Object store: R2 or Hetzner?**~~ **RULED: R2**, for the egress-heavy bulk path. Hetzner Object
  Storage is not needed — its free-operations advantage only mattered against *naïve full backups*
  ($306.71/yr); content-addressed incremental is **$4.30/yr on R2**, so that was a client-design
  problem, not a vendor one. One object store is the simpler system.
- ~~**Does Fly survive at all?**~~ **RULED: yes, for Keycloak**, on reliability grounds — restarts,
  health checks, independent scaling from the Hetzner database.
- **`STACK_HUB.md` §0.10 records one thing that cannot be built as asked: Keycloak does not support
  SQLite** (Postgres/MariaDB/MySQL/MSSQL/Oracle/Aurora/Azure SQL only; H2 is explicitly dev-only).
  The intent is satisfied by giving Keycloak **its own small Postgres co-located on Fly** — and the
  trap to avoid is pointing it at the Hetzner database, which would put the auth path across the
  public internet on every token issuance.
- ~~**Keycloak's database.**~~ **RULED: PlanetScale PS-5 HA, $15/month** — 1 primary + 2 replicas,
  10 GB storage and 100 GB egress included. Verified first-party. Replaces Fly Managed Postgres at
  $38 with **more** redundancy for **$23/month less**, and retires what had been the single largest
  line in the bill. `STACK_HUB.md` §0.11. Two conditions on it: **deploy Keycloak to Fly `iad`**,
  since PlanetScale's pricing is AWS `us-east-1` and the co-location rule is about distance, not
  vendor; and if auth ever feels slow, **PS-10 HA at $30** is still under Fly's $38 — PS-5 is
  1/16 vCPU and 512 MiB, which is redundant rather than fast.
- **§0/§6 re-rating** (item 8).
