### The outside review, 2026-08-21 — four defects the first pass shipped

The Cloud v1 bundle went to an outside reviewer. It came back with two security
findings, both real, both **reproduced on a throwaway cluster before being fixed**. Recorded here
because the first three are the kind of defect that would otherwise be found by a customer.

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 22 | **`SECURITY DEFINER` functions kept PostgreSQL's default `PUBLIC EXECUTE`.** 0007 wrote an explicit grant matrix and never revoked the implicit one, so the matrix documented an intent the database was not enforcing. Measured: all 5 `app.*` functions open to PUBLIC, and **`computedriven_readonly` successfully called `resolve_principal` and created a principal** — a read-only role performing an INSERT | **FIXED** — `0009_function_acl.sql`; battery D12–D17 |
| 23 | **`principal.status` was decorative.** A suspended principal resolved and `authorize_membership` returned `true`. Asymmetric and so easy to miss: `resolve_organization` already checked `o.status`, principals were checked nowhere | **FIXED** — `0008_principal_status.sql`; battery group G |
| 24 | **R14 was overclaimed.** "A missing tenant context always raises" is false: a policy is evaluated per row, so a constant-false qualifier never reaches it. Measured boundary is *narrower than either party predicted* — an **empty table still raises** | **NARROWED (R19)** — asserted as a known limit in A7 |
| 25 | **The pricing page relapsed into the `WORLD_SIZE.md` §11 error**, one round after R11 was ruled to prevent it. *"Every plan includes unlimited world history … costs approximately nothing"* — true of the WRL graph, ruinous if WORLD means the machine. The homepage had the matching slip: *"You are charged for the machine. The world costs nothing to carry"*, when after R11 the world **is** the machine | **FIXED** — both pages now say WRL graph history; machine bytes are metered |

**Why the battery missed 22 and 23.** Groups D and F asserted **table** privileges and never once
asked who could execute a **function**; nothing tested a status column at all. The lesson is not
"add two checks" — it is that a battery inherits the blind spots of whoever wrote it, which is the
argument for outside review rather than more of the same author's tests.

**The checks are load-bearing, not decorative.** Re-run against a migration set with 0008 and 0009
removed — `CD_MIGRATIONS=<dir>` — **9 of the 55 fail**, including D16 reproducing the escalation.
A check added after a fix means nothing until it is shown to fail before it.

### The round-7 review, 2026-08-22 — the provider boundary, and a claim the database never honoured

**The theme changed again and this time it left the tree.** Every finding through round 6 was
something a local battery could have caught. The headline finding here is one it *structurally
cannot*: a fix that is correct PostgreSQL, passes every check, and the production transport refuses.

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 47 | 🔴 **R30's advisory lock cannot reach production.** Cloudflare's Hyperdrive compatibility page lists, verbatim, *"Advisory locks, LISTEN and NOTIFY, PREPARE and DEALLOCATE, any modification to per-session state not explicitly documented as supported elsewhere."* R7 puts every control-plane query through Hyperdrive. So `0013` went green on a mechanism the wire refuses | **AMENDED (R30)** — `0015`; the unique partial index is the serialization primitive; battery group L reads function bodies from `pg_proc` so this cannot recur silently |
| 48 | 🔴 **P4 proved accounting idempotence, not request idempotence** — and it was round 6's own mistake, reproduced inside the check written to fix it. It asserted "one reservation, 50 bytes" while accepting a duplicate-key error from a losing caller. Four retrying clients, one 500 | **FIXED** — `0016`; P4 now demands 4 successes / 1 reservation / 50 bytes / **0 errors** |
| 49 | 🔴 **Replay happened before authority.** `reserve_storage()`'s own comment said it "must not depend on having been called politely" — and returned an existing reservation *above* the membership, role and world checks. A demoted viewer could still retrieve a live hold by presenting its key | **FIXED** — `0016`; authority is unconditional, replay is a cheaper answer to the same question |
| 50 | 🔴 **An idempotency key was a name, not a promise.** Reuse with different bytes/world/principal returned the original reservation and ignored what was asked | **FIXED** — `0016`; the key binds `{organization, principal, world, bytes}`, mismatch is `CD-RESERVE-IDEMPOTENCY-MISMATCH` |
| 51 | 🔴 **`0009`'s PUBLIC-EXECUTE safety net has never existed.** Found while fixing a smaller version of it. Measured on PG 18.4: `ALTER DEFAULT PRIVILEGES … REVOKE EXECUTE ON FUNCTIONS FROM PUBLIC` stores **zero rows** and a function created afterwards is **PUBLIC-executable**. Two rounds of that sentence reading as a guarantee, carried entirely by later migrations remembering to `REVOKE` by hand — 0010/0011/0014/0017 did, **0016 did not** | **FIXED** — `0018` installs a `ddl_command_end` event trigger, per *database* rather than per role, and proves it with a canary. `0009`'s claim is retracted in place; D18 is now empirical |
| 52 | 🟠 **The battery runs on PostgreSQL 18.4; Hyperdrive documents 9.0–17.x** | **RULED (R33)** + `CD_PGBIN`; check L7 **WARNs** on every run |
| 53 | 🟡 **"M2 chunking will need multipart" was an assumption wearing the clothes of a plan** | **RETRACTED** — a 2 TB world is not a 2 TB object |

### The round-7.1 closure, 2026-08-22 — the same bug, one layer up, three times

**The theme is repetition.** Round 6 fixed read-check-write for quota. Round 7 built the upload-intent
layer on top and reproduced it exactly, along with the two idempotence defects 0016 had just closed.
Nothing here is a new *kind* of mistake; all of it is the previous round's law failing to travel to
the layer built next.

```text
M1.5, before 0014      read quota   -> decide -> write
M2 shape, in 0017      sum offers   -> decide -> insert
```

Every row below was **reproduced before it was fixed**. Concurrency group Q against the unfixed
`0017`: `OVERSUBSCRIBED: 160 > 100`.

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 54 | 🔴 **`offer_upload()` reintroduced the read/check/write race.** Two 80-byte offers for *different* keys against one 100-byte reservation both admitted — 160 bytes of authority against a 100-byte hold. The unique constraint on `object_key` cannot help, because the keys differ, which is the point of a chunked upload. `finalize_storage()` and `abort_storage()` have taken `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on that row since 0014; `offer_upload` was the only member of the family that read it unlocked | **FIXED** — `0019`; the reservation row is the serialization boundary. Group Q + `CD_SABOTAGE=offer` |
| 55 | 🔴 **Upload-intent idempotence was sequential again.** Two callers offering one fresh chunk both miss the opening SELECT; the loser gets `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "upload_intents_key_uq"` — the retrying client is the one that 500s | **FIXED** — `0019`; reservation lock + `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` for the cross-reservation case the lock cannot order |
| 56 | 🔴 **An object key was becoming an idempotency key that bound no reservation.** The replay path checked organization, bytes and digest, then returned `existing.reservation_id` — whatever it was. A dead hold's write authority was handed to a live reservation asking about the same chunk | **FIXED (R43)** — `0019`; the promise is `{reservation, key, bytes, digest}`, and an already-written object returns `already_observed` with no authority instead of reviving anything |
| 57 | 🟠 **0018 found a real leak and blamed the wrong clause.** It generalized one measurement into "REVOKE-from-PUBLIC default privileges store nothing". Measured on 17.10 *and* 18.4: the **`IN SCHEMA`** form stores nothing; the global form stores `{r=X/r}` and protects new routines, covers procedures, reaches schemas it never named, and needs **no superuser** | **CORRECTED (R42)** — `0020`. The trigger is **kept**, because measurement `J` shows per-role defaults do not cover a role added later and a canary created only as the migration role cannot see that. A second canary, created by a rule-less role, now can |
| 58 | 🟠 **`storage_divergence()` summed an event log and called it occupancy.** R2 fires object-create on overwrite, so a replaced body was charged twice: log 22, actual 12 | **FIXED (R41)** — `0021`; `cd.storage_objects` is the inventory, `cd.storage_observations` stays the log. Check O4 requires the two numbers to **differ**, so repointing divergence back at the log turns it red |
| 59 | 🔴 **THE ENTIRE R32 CONSUMER PATH WAS UNREACHABLE, and no review found it — writing the accept-path test did.** `observe_storage_object()` runs as `computedriven_ledger` and asks whether the organization exists. `cd.organizations` has FORCE RLS and three policies — tenant, owner, bootstrap — and **none names the ledger**. 0014 granted the ledger SELECT and gave `cd.worlds` a matching policy; `cd.organizations` never got one. Measured: as the ledger, `SELECT count(*) FROM cd.organizations` returns **0** with a row present. Every R2 event, including every valid one, would have been refused with *"the key names an organization that does not exist"*. 137 SQL checks and 226 Worker tests tested the **refusal** paths and never once called it with an organization that exists | **FIXED** — `0021` adds `organizations_ledger`. Check **O0** generalizes it: any row-secured table the ledger holds a GRANT on must also have a policy admitting it |

> **A GRANT WITHOUT A POLICY IS NOT A NARROW PERMISSION. IT IS A PERMISSION THAT SILENTLY RETURNS
> NOTHING, AND EVERY QUERY BUILT ON IT IS WRONG IN THE DIRECTION THAT LOOKS LIKE ABSENCE.**

### The round-7.2 closure, 2026-08-22 — time passing differently on two edges

**Groups N, P and Q each race one subsystem against itself.** Two logins, two reservations, two
offers; every fix was "serialize that function". Round 7.2 is the first round where the two sides are
**different subsystems** — a tenant-scoped HTTP request and a cross-tenant queue consumer — and the
reservation row turned out to be a boundary only one of them had ever agreed to.

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 60 | 🔴 **The queue observer was outside the lock protocol.** `offer_upload()` took the reservation row; `observe_storage_object()` took nothing. So the observer could commit `observed` between the offer's read and its UPDATE — and that UPDATE carried no state predicate, so a blocked statement had nothing to re-evaluate when it woke. MEASURED, group R: `state=offered` and `disposition=replayed`, i.e. **fresh write authority for an object R2 already holds** | **FIXED (R54)** — `0022`; `app.lock_intent()` is the one lock order, reservation → intent → decide, and every transition is CAS-shaped under it. Group **R** + `CD_SABOTAGE=observe` |
| 61 | 🔴 **`abandon_upload()` spent authority it had already given away**, and this one needs no concurrency at all. R40 released an intent's bytes on abandon; abandon is a row in our database and a presigned URL authorizes its holder until it expires. `reserve 100 → offer A → get URL → abandon A → offer B → use A's still-live URL` = **200 bytes stored against a 100-byte reservation**, which is exactly what R31 forbids. Separately, abandon read the intent BEFORE taking the lock, so it decided from a snapshot older than the wait (MEASURED: `observed` → `abandoned`) | **AMENDED (R55)** — `0022`; the state is `client_abandoned`, it releases nothing, and the reservation dying is the only release path left. The remaining question — whether OUR expiry is a fence against a PUT R2 already admitted — is falsifier case **I** |
| 62 | 🟠 **`(bucket, key, etag)` was answering three different questions.** A genuine second PUT of identical bytes produces the same three, so it was dismissed as a queue redelivery and vanished from the append-only provenance log. Harmless for occupancy today; correctness-sensitive the moment deletes exist | **FIXED (R57)** — `0022`; the Cloudflare queue **message id** is event identity, read from the envelope so a producer cannot choose its own. Check **O2b** is the positive case |
| 63 | 🟠 **The status system had a second drift boundary nobody was watching.** The derived battery block said 21 migrations / PG17 / 0 warned while a capability note still said *"18 migrations apply clean … to PostgreSQL 18.4 … L7 WARNs on every run"* — and the renderer faithfully synchronized the stale sentence onto the public page. Every gate was green | **FIXED** — `scripts/check-status-prose.mjs`. Historical strings are exempted **by exact match** in `$prose_exemptions`, because a sweep that "updated" them would rewrite a true account of a past defect into a false one |
| 64 | 🟡 **A ghost state and a wrong ruling number.** `upload_intents.expired` was in the CHECK constraint and in the observer's WHERE clause and **nothing ever set it**; `0019` labelled the expiry rule R34 throughout, which belongs to the parallel box-and-box session | **FIXED** — `0022` removes the state (under R55 nothing would be released by reaching it, so it was a second name for `offered`); R34→R40 corrected in place in `0019` |

> **SINGLE-SOURCE RENDERING DOES NOT HELP IF THE SINGLE SOURCE ITSELF CONTAINS DUPLICATED FACTS.**

### The round-7.3 settlement pass, 2026-08-22 — one lesson in five places

Round 7.2 ruled **R54** — provider-observed truth is monotonic, `observed` is a fact about the world
and not a stage in our workflow — and applied it to the intent STATE. It did not apply it to the
BYTE LEDGER, which is where the money is. Everything below is that one gap.

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 65 | 🔴 **The provider said the bytes landed, and expiry made them free.** `reserve 100 → offer → R2 event arrives and COMMITS → client crashes before finalize → TTL passes → expire_storage_reservations()` and the ledger reads `committed 0, reserved 0` while R2 holds 100. No race, nothing in flight, no clock skew. MEASURED, and the reproduction found the worse half: **after expiry there is no path left to ever charge them** — `finalize_storage()` refuses a terminal reservation with `CD-FINALIZE-STATE`, and finalize was the only writer of `committed_bytes`. The drift is permanent, not a lag. `storage_divergence()` reported `delta=100` throughout; the system had the number and nothing was wired to act on it | **FIXED (R68 + R69)** — `0023`; the observer writes the ledger, expiry releases nothing, the hold is derived. Checks **K29–K31**, **K35** |
| 66 | 🟠 **`client_abandoned` and `observed` are independent facts that one enum was making destroy each other.** "The client abandoned at T1" and "R2 accepted a write at T2" are both true, and the second is the most interesting anomaly this table can hold; 0022 transitioned `client_abandoned → observed` and overwrote the single `settled_at` | **FIXED (R71)** — `0023`; two timestamps, and `state` is a GENERATED projection of them and therefore unassignable. Checks **O12–O15** |
| 67 | 🟠 **R57 called a Queue message id an R2 event identity.** Cloudflare documents `Message.id` as "a unique, system-generated ID for the message"; the R2 notification BODY carries `account`/`action`/`bucket`/`object{key,size,eTag}`/`eventTime` and **no event id at all**. What we possess is exactly-once processing of a QUEUE MESSAGE. Falsifier case **E** still described the `(bucket, key, etag)` mechanism R57 replaced, so it would have tested a dedupe key the code no longer uses | **FIXED** — R57 narrowed in place; case **E** rewritten to exercise real retry semantics. **And a hole neither review saw:** `message_id` absorbs redelivery only if the id is STABLE across attempts, which Cloudflare does not document — and because R2 is the producer, the documented remedy ("generate a unique ID when writing the message") is unavailable to us. Case E now measures it |
| 68 | 🟠 **An unattributed write could become attributed by a LATER intent.** `storage_divergence()` joined `storage_objects` to `upload_intents` on `object_key`, so creating an intent for a key an out-of-band write already occupied retroactively claimed 70 bytes for a reservation that had never had anything to do with it. MEASURED: `T1 → 0 divergence rows, T3 → 1`, while the observation row still correctly said `intent_id IS NULL` — the provenance log was right and the query went around it | **FIXED (R70)** — `0023`; `current_observation_id`, and every join runs through it. Checks **O10/O10b** |
| 69 | 🟡 **`overwrite_count` depended on delivery order.** The same three provider events scored 1 or 2 overwrites depending on arrival sequence, and Queues does not guarantee order. **0021's own backfill computed it correctly** (`count(DISTINCT etag) - 1`, read from the append-only log) and the incremental path installed in the same file did not | **FIXED** — `0023` uses the backfill's expression. Check **O11** |
| 70 | 🟡 **The review bundle could not reproduce its own evidence.** It presented `check-status-prose.mjs`'s green result as the finding-63 mechanism and shipped a tar with **no `scripts/` directory**. Separately: the generator's prose said "PostgreSQL 18.4" eight lines above a captured run saying 17.10; `status.json` said "Eight questions" against nine; `0019` cited **R51** for the abandon amendment, which is a binding/authentication ruling — the amendment is R55 | **FIXED** — gates ship in the tar; the PG major comes from the run's own banner; `falsifier_cases` is now DERIVED. **Why the prose gate missed the count:** it compares prose against the derived block, so *a fact that lives only in prose has nothing to disagree with* |
| 71 | 🔴 **`abort_storage()` was R55 at the reservation level, and R55 was ruled as a general principle and applied at one call site.** `reserve 100 → offer → R2 event lands → abort_storage()` and the hold drops to 0 while R2 holds 100; the next 100-byte reservation is admitted in the same second. No clock, no race, one synchronous client call. MEASURED. Found by reproducing 65 and reading what else wrote `reserved_bytes` — **not** raised by either review | **FIXED (R69)** — `0023`; abort records a declaration and releases nothing. Checks **K15/K16** |

> **THE FIX FOR A CLASS OF DEFECT IS NOT APPLIED UNTIL EVERY MEMBER OF THE CLASS HAS BEEN LOOKED AT.**

### M2.0 round 2, 2026-08-23 — capability closure

The settlement round shipped a **cross-tenant read**, a **caller-chosen safety constant**, and **two
clocks under one name**. All four findings below reproduced against 0023 before 0024 was written.

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 72 | 🔴 **A SECURITY DEFINER function that takes a tenant id is a cross-tenant capability, whatever its name says.** 0023 gave `computedriven_api` three functions accepting an organization uuid, owned by `computedriven_ledger` — the role with `USING (true)` policies *by design*. MEASURED from org A's connection: `storage_ledger(B)` → `outstanding=777`; `storage_divergence(B)` → B's row; **`storage_divergence(NULL)` → every tenant's rows**, and NULL was the most convenient call a caller could write. The control that makes it a finding: the direct read of the same data returned **0 rows**, so RLS worked and the definer was the only door | **FIXED** — `0024`; the interface splits by NAME. `storage_ledger()`/`storage_divergence()` take **no argument** and derive the tenant; `_for(uuid)` variants are jobs-only; `storage_outstanding` loses its API grant outright. Checks **K37–K41**, and **O0c** is the derived gate |
| 73 | 🔴 **The only release path let its caller choose the safety constant.** `settle_storage_reservations(org, p_quiet)` had no lower bound. MEASURED: a reservation one second past expiry, against a one-hour quiet period — default call released 0, `interval '0'` released it and took the hold 500 → 0. R69 made settlement the single release path *because* our clock is not the provider's, and case I exists because the right period is unknown | **FIXED** — `0024`; `p_quiet` is **removed**, not validated: a floor check still leaves a knob whose safe range nobody has measured. Tests move `expires_at`. Checks **K42/K42b** |
| 74 | 🟠 **R70 closed database order and left provider order open.** The observer found its intent by key alone, so a notification delayed in the queue was attributed to whatever intent held that key on arrival. MEASURED: an event **three hours older** than the intent, credited to it. O10/O10b could not see this — they vary the order rows are INSERTED; this varies the order the PROVIDER's events arrive | **FIXED (R72)** — `0024`; causal attribution against `eventTime`, with a named skew allowance. Checks **O16/O16b** |
| 76 | 🟠 **Two clocks under one name.** `provider_observed_at` was set to `now()` — ours, at consume time — while R2's own `eventTime` sat unused in the same function's arguments. MEASURED three hours apart on a delayed message, so the anomaly record R71 exists to preserve was storing *queue-consumed-at* and calling it the write. Separately, R57's narrowing to *queue-message* identity did not propagate: `0022`, `CLOUD_V1.md` and `status.json` went on saying "event identity" | **FIXED** — `0024` adds `provider_event_at`, write-once like its sibling; terminology corrected in all three. Checks **O17/O18** |
| 75 | 🟡 **A claim of ours that was too strong, corrected by the review.** This tree's case E said an unstable queue message id would double-charge `committed_bytes`. It does not: the second observation passes the message-id index, but the charge is `v_after - v_prior` read under the inventory row lock, and 100 → 100 is a delta of **zero**. MEASURED | **CORRECTED** — case E keeps the experiment and drops the consequence; it now ranks below I, B, F and G for M2.0 and rises again in M2.1. Check **K43** pins the no-double-charge property so the claim cannot drift back |

> **THE REQUEST SUPPLIES INTENT, NOT AUTHORITY** — `reserve_storage()` has taken no organization
> argument since 0014 for exactly this reason, and the round that hardened the ledger added three
> read paths that did.

**Two things this round changed about the gates.**

- **O0b cannot see a capability nobody realised they created.** It enumerates *known* cross-tenant
  capabilities from a hand-maintained list and requires an accept witness for each; it passed on
  0023 throughout. **O0c** asks the catalog instead — any storage-surface definer owned by the
  cross-tenant role, taking a uuid, reachable by a request role. The same assertion runs at apply
  time, and **it refused the first draft of 0024**, naming `storage_outstanding`: `REVOKE … FROM
  PUBLIC` does nothing to a grant held by a named role, and that function was not dropped and
  recreated like the ones around it.
- **A fixture's constants encode the relationships the code happened to care about when they were
  written.** The O group used three fixed `2026-08-22` timestamps — stable and correctly ordered
  relative to each other, unrelated to when their intent was created. R72 compares exactly that, so
  on the first day after, every O-group event correctly became unattributed and O6 returned no rows.
  The base is now read from the database once, after the intents exist.
- **The bundle guard was itself a class-fix applied to one member.** Finding 70's remedy —
  `require_tally()` — covered the TEST captures and left `VERIFY`/`ASSETS`/`PROSE` on bare
  `|| true`. The very next bundle inlined *"1 page(s) disagree with status.json"* as evidence,
  because `cloud-status-counts.mjs --write` had updated `status.json` after the pages were last
  rendered. `require_green()` now covers the gates, and the requirement is stronger than "produced
  output": a bundle is a claim that the tree passes its own checks. **This tree wrote
  "the fix for a class of defect is not applied until every member has been looked at" down in the
  round immediately before, and then did it again.**
### M2.0 round 3, 2026-08-23 — observation coherence

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 79 | 🟠 **A duplicate delivery recomputed its answer from today's world.** The observer derived attribution from current state, then on conflict reported *that* rather than the stored row. MEASURED: `RETURNED attributed=true` against `PERSISTED intent_id IS NULL` — the database was right and the function narrated it differently, to a consumer that uses the bit operationally. Sibling: the fallback unique index is `(bucket, key, etag, event_time)` and the duplicate LOOKUP omitted `event_time` | **FIXED (R73)** — `0025`; the replay check runs FIRST and every returned field comes from the recorded row. Checks **O19/O20** |
| 78 | 🟠 **The backfill paired two clocks from two different events.** `provider_event_at` was backfilled `ORDER BY event_time ASC` while `provider_observed_at` had been written by the first notification *consumed*. MEASURED under out-of-order delivery: earliest-event and first-consumed are different rows. The runtime path was already correct — it writes both from one event — so this affected only rows 0024 migrated, and the reason it was *possible* is structural | **FIXED (R74)** — `0025`; `observing_observation_id` is the fact, the timestamps are its projection, and a CHECK refuses a row where they disagree about whether an observation happened at all. Checks **O21/O22** |
| 77 | 🟠 **R72 was recorded as measured while resting on an unmeasured constant**, and `0024` cited "case D writes the real number" for a case that contains no clock experiment. The falsifier also has no execution path yet, so the citation pointed at a measurement nobody was going to take | **CORRECTED** — R72 is now explicitly half-measured, half-**PROPOSED**; case **D2** is split out to measure the skew distribution and its worst legitimate tail. The **upper** bound is named too: once case I lands, R72 should become an interval, not a lower bound |
| 80 | 🟡 **There were two O0c's and they disagreed.** The bundle said the same assertion ran at apply time; `0024`'s copy checked only `computedriven_api` and **exempted every `_for` name** — precisely the cross-tenant doors the round exists to keep shut | **FIXED** — `0025` uses the battery's predicate verbatim. *A suffix that marks a function as dangerous is not a reason for the gate to skip it* |
| 81 | 🟡 **R57's narrowing never reached the executable sources.** `reconcile.mjs`, its call site, `sabotage.sh` and a test name still said "EVENT identity" | **FIXED** — swept repo-wide rather than in the three files `0024` happened to name |

> **A CONTROL THAT BREAKS FOR THE WRONG REASON IS A FALSE GREEN ABOUT ITS OWN MEANING.** R74's new
> CHECK made the `CD_SABOTAGE=observe` body raise, so the mode went from 2 failures to 6 and still
> printed `CAUGHT` and isolated — while measuring "the naive observer violates a constraint" instead
> of "the naive observer takes no lock". Fixed by giving the sabotage all three columns; it is back

and **D2** would have published **9** against an array of 10 — silently, in the field that exists

number that takes longer to notice.

- **"Ship every gate the bundle cites" is not "ship every gate named in it."** `check-doc-claims.mjs`
  was added to the tar and then removed: its only appearance is inside the inlined register
  describing R66 — a box-and-box ruling — and it scans `AmpersandBoxDesign/` files the bundle does
  not contain. From the extracted tar it reported **0 documents scanned** and a green tick. *A gate
  with nothing to check passes*, which in an evidence package is worse than its absence.

**Three things this round changed about how the work is checked.**

- **A test that asserts the old ruling fails loudly, and that is the signal.** Seven SQL checks and
  three concurrency checks broke on 0023 — K10 had asserted *"finalize moves reserved bytes to
  committed, exactly"* and been green for six rounds. Each was rewritten to assert the **ruling**,
  not the code; where one protected something real (K19's privilege split, K24's negative-byte
  constraint) the replacement protects the equivalent, and where the invariant stopped needing a
  constraint (**K24b**) the check says so rather than disappearing.
- **The battery's own fixture was relying on the defect.** Group P reset itself between checks with
  `state='aborted'`, which under R69 releases nothing — so the reset silently stopped resetting and
  P5 failed with a quota error inherited from P1. A fixture shortcut is a claim about semantics.
- **`CREATE OR REPLACE` overwrites whatever is there.** 0023's `reserve_storage()` was first written
  from **0014**'s body — the version that introduced the ledger arithmetic — silently reverting
  everything **0016** added: authority checked before the replay branch, the mismatch assertion, and
  the `ON CONFLICT` that lets four simultaneous retries all succeed. Nothing about the byte
  accounting looked wrong. **Group P caught it: 1 success, 3 errors.** The base for an edit is the
  latest definition, not the one that introduced the part being changed.

**Two things this round changed about how the batteries are written.**

- **A reproduction that depends on the bug's mechanism stops being a test the moment the bug is
  fixed.** R2's first draft held the reservation row from a third session so abandon would block
  after its read — which worked because the observer needed no reservation lock. Under `0022` the
  observer queues at that lock too, so the check **deadlocked the battery** on a foreground psql with
  no timeout. It had to be rebuilt to reproduce through something both versions do.
- **O0 was widened from one role to a shape.** It named `computedriven_ledger`, so it proved a fact
  about the role that had already been caught. It now enumerates every `SECURITY DEFINER` owner from
  `pg_proc` — **not by parsing `prosrc`**, which is a static-analysis problem that would produce a
  gate confident and wrong. **O0b** is the behavioural half: every cross-tenant capability must have
  at least one *positive accept witness*, recorded by the check that exercises it and only on a pass.

**Three checks that were green while measuring nothing**, all found by running them rather than
reading them, and all fixed:

- **Q2 passed against the broken function** because four racing processes usually do not overlap —
  three find the winner's committed row and take the replay path. Hand-stepped, it fails every time.
  *A race you cannot step is a race you cannot claim to have closed.*
- **Q2a passed** because writing to a session's FIFO is not the session executing; S1's `COMMIT`
  landed first and the race was never constructed. The ordering gate is load-bearing.
- **Truncating `out1`/`out2` to reuse them** does not rewind a psql that still holds them open — it
  leaves a hole, the hole reads back as NUL, grep calls the file binary and every content assertion
  silently stops matching. Baselines now, never truncation.

**Two rulings PROPOSED, deliberately built against rather than assumed:**

> **R31 (OPEN) — storage authority may never authorize more bytes than the reservation that
> produced it.**

M1.5 is **admission-safe and not hard-quota-safe**, and the gap is real:

```text
reserve 1 MB → receive PutObject authority → upload 500 MB
     → R2 HAS ALREADY ACCEPTED IT → finalize(500 MB) refused, too late
```

Verified first-party: R2 temporary credentials constrain bucket, operations, prefixes/objects and
TTL, with **no documented byte ceiling**; presigned URLs document `Content-Type` as signed *and
enforced* and say nothing about `Content-Length`. **So byte-exactness is not claimed** — it is case B
of `worker/test/live-falsifier.mjs`. If it fails, that is the architectural result:

> hard pre-write quota and fully direct client→R2 uploads cannot **both** be claimed with the
> current grant primitive

and the choice between a small controlled data plane and softer asynchronous quota becomes conscious
rather than accidental.

> **R32 (OPEN) — committed storage is provider-observed, never client-asserted.**

R2 event notifications carry `object.size` and `object.eTag` on `PutObject` / `CopyObject` /
`CompleteMultipartUpload`, over Queues. **Queues is at-least-once**, so exactly-once accounting comes
from a unique constraint on `(bucket, object_key, etag)` — never from delivery. Built with fixtures
(`0017`, `src/reconcile.mjs`), and `app.storage_divergence()` reports where the client and the
provider disagree, **so R32 can be ruled with a number instead of an argument**.

**R33 — Pigsty targets PostgreSQL 17.x for v1.** Hyperdrive documents known support for 9.0–17.x. PG18
is not refused; it is **unproven through the transport**, and proving it is live-falsifier case H.
Until then every green battery line is measured on a major the wire does not claim, and L7 says so on
every run. Installing a 17.x build needs one command and is Travis's to run:

```bash
sudo pacman -S postgresql-old-upgrade
```

**The M2 write shape, decided this round.** One bounded content-addressed chunk → one reservation →
one **exact** object key → one short-lived write artifact. R2 recommends ordinary `PutObject` below
~100 MB and supports single PUT to 5 GiB, so tens of thousands of ordinary puts carry a
multi-terabyte world. This dissolves round 6's unanswerable question about whether a reservation
should last an hour or a week — it was unanswerable because it asked one object to be both:

> **The session can live for days; a chunk grant does not.**

Multipart stays unauthorized. Granting `CreateMultipartUpload`/`UploadPart`/`ListParts`/`Complete`/
`Abort` is five capabilities nothing has measured a need for.

**THE LAW THIS ROUND EARNED**

> **A local battery proves the database's behaviour, not the transport's.**

And its companion, from #51, which is the round-5 law arriving from a direction reading cannot cover:

> Every earlier instance was prose describing a restriction **the code** did not implement. This one
> was prose describing a restriction **the database** does not implement. Reading the migration
> carefully would not have revealed it. Only running it does.

### The round-6 review, 2026-08-22 — refinement, provenance, temporal authority, concurrency

The theme changed again, and the reviewer named the change better than I would have: the findings
are no longer "this claim is false". They are **refinement, provenance, concurrency and temporal
authority** — the class of error that appears when a coherent architecture starts becoming a real
system.

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 40 | **A correct R2 adapter failed its own conformance law.** `r2creds.mjs` said in capitals that its permission names are ComputeDriven capability names and that "a provider adapter MAPS these"; `assertProviderConformance()` then compared provider actions against those same words literally. So `ListObjects → ListObjectsV1, ListObjectsV2` — the correct translation — returned **CD-CRED-WIDENED**. The module was demanding a translation and forbidding one at the same time | **FIXED** — `src/r2native.mjs`; `test/r2native.test.mjs`; mutation `r2-list-half-translated` |
| 41 | **`grantForScope()` could not tell an authorized scope from a forgery.** Its comment said it needed a scope from `scopeForWorld()`; its check was `typeof scope.prefix === "string"`. A hand-built `{prefix: "", expiresAt: "2099-…"}` — the entire bucket, every tenant, for 73 years — produced a signable grant, and conformance accepted the pair because the forgery agreed with itself. Third instance of this exact defect: verified claims (round 4), scopes, admissions | **FIXED** — module-private `WeakSet`, same mechanism as `verifyToken()`; a structural clone is still refused |
| 42 | **Expiry was validated as a string.** `Date.parse("not-a-date")` is `NaN`, `NaN > authorized` is `false`, and **every malformed timestamp conformed** — including an already-expired one. A comparison that returns false for garbage fails in the permissive direction and reads as a pass | **FIXED** — the comparison primitive is an integer of epoch seconds; malformed, non-finite and out-of-range values refuse by name |
| 43 | **`resolve_principal()` was sequentially idempotent, not concurrently idempotent.** Survived five rounds because F1 calls it twice *in one session*, which cannot construct the state that matters. Reproduced by hand-stepping two sessions, and unstructured: **6 of 12 rounds diverged**, the loser getting a duplicate-key error. One of two simultaneous first logins 500s | **FIXED (R30)** — `0013_concurrent_identity.sql`, xact advisory lock on the identity triple; `test/concurrency.sh` group N; `CD_SABOTAGE=lock` |
| 44 | **M1.5 was ruled and empty** — status.json said "NO TABLE EXISTS YET" | **BUILT** — `0014_storage_admission.sql`, `src/admission.mjs`, battery group K, concurrency group P |
| 45 | **A hand-typed count went stale the moment the schema grew.** D4 asserted `= 6` tenant tables with FORCE RLS. 0014 added three — all three correct — and the check failed. It was measuring the *number of tables*, which is not a security property, and would have failed identically for a table added right and a table added wrong | **FIXED** — D4 is now derived: *no* tenant table may lack ENABLE+FORCE, so a table added next year is covered on the day it is created. Same law as the box-and-box law counts, different suite |
| 46 | **`status.json` said "10 migrations apply clean"** while the tree had 12. Its `sabotage_passed` (66/8) and `regression_failed` (28) were from four migrations ago — control results nobody re-runs casually, which is what makes them the ones that go stale | **FIXED** — every number in `battery` is now produced by `scripts/cloud-status-counts.mjs`, which runs all five battery invocations and exits 1 rather than agree with a stale one |

**And one finding retracted, because the rule here is retract out loud.** I recorded a #47 — that
`status.html`'s claim *"no page hand-writes a rung, and a build check fails if one drifts"* had
sentinels but no generator and no gate — and wrote a second renderer on that premise. **It was
wrong.** Both exist, at `cloud.computedriven.com/tools/render-status.mjs --verify`. The search that
"proved" their absence grepped for the literal string `STATUS:banner`, and the tool builds its
sentinel as `` `STATUS:${name}:BEGIN` `` — so the pages matched and the thing that writes them did
not. The duplicate was deleted before it could become the second source of truth it was accusing the
tree of lacking, and the one genuine improvement in it — a concurrency row in the battery table —
was moved into the real renderer.

**The general shape, worth keeping:** *a grep for a literal cannot prove the absence of a
constructed string.* The same reasoning would fail for a route table built from segments, a SQL
identifier built with `format(%I)`, or a class name assembled at runtime — and this tree has already
been bitten by the last one (`project_rrabbit_shell`: class-name checks die under minification).

**Two things the review got right that are worth keeping as sentences.**

> **Refinement between capability vocabularies must itself be explicit and testable.**

The translation is now a declared table (`R2_TRANSLATION`) checked in **both directions** against a
**closed vocabulary** — an action R2 does not define is refused as *unknown*, which is stronger than
a deny-list because it catches the action nobody thought to forbid. And the ComputeDriven name was
changed from `ListBucket` to `ListObjects`, because `ListBucket` is AWS IAM's action name: a reader
could not tell whose word it was, and the code beneath it had already decided it was a provider's.
**A name no provider uses cannot be accidentally passed through as one.**

> **Serial correctness is not concurrent correctness.**

`test/concurrency.sh` exists because `tenant-isolation.sh` runs one session on one connection, so
every property it can express is sequential. The new file hand-steps two sessions to a deterministic
interleaving rather than racing and hoping. Its two sabotage modes are checked **per group** — a
mode that breaks the *other* group prints `MISDIRECTED`, because a control that fires for the wrong
reason is not a control.

**What M1.5 actually earns.** The property, stated the way `CLOUD_V1.md` states it, and measured:

```
limit 1000 · 20 simultaneous requests for 100 each
        →  exactly 10 admitted, 10 refused        (group P1)
900 used · two simultaneous requests for 80
        →  exactly one admitted                   (group P3)
```

and under `CD_SABOTAGE=quota`, which restores the read-then-write form the design refuses, the same
battery measures **2000 bytes reserved against a 1000-byte limit**. The atomicity is one statement —
`UPDATE … WHERE committed + reserved + n <= limit` — because a check followed by a write has a
window and two Workers both read the same number. The rest of the module is a typed wrapper.

Three design decisions in 0014 worth naming, each of which is a rule already earned elsewhere
applied to money instead of to rows:

- **`reserve_storage()` takes no organization argument.** It reads `app.current_organization_id()`.
  Reserving against another tenant is not rejected, it is **unspeakable** — the same shape as
  `scopeForWorld()` building its prefix from the org id rather than validating one.
- **The API role holds `SELECT` on the ledger and nothing else.** There is no `UPDATE` grant to
  revoke a column of. Round 5's law — a comment is not an enforcement mechanism — read forward
  instead of backward.
- **Credential authority is the output of admission, not an input to minting.** A write scope cannot
  be constructed without a branded `StorageAdmission` whose organization, world and expiry all match
  the credential being minted.

### The round-5 review, 2026-08-22 — and a pattern worth naming as a law

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 37 | **A `viewer` could promote itself to `owner`.** 0011's own comment said the API "may read membership and record last-seen; it may not enrol or remove" — and granted table-level UPDATE, which reaches every column. Measured: `SET app_role='owner'` **succeeded**, and a `revoked` membership **un-revoked itself**. It composes with 0010, since `permissionFor()` derives R2 write authority from that role | **FIXED** — `0012_column_authority.sql`; battery group J; `CD_SABOTAGE=columns` |
| 38 | **Provider conformance checked one dimension of four.** A grant with identical actions but `prefixes: [""]` and a seven-day expiry passed — unrestricted reach across every tenant, for a week | **FIXED** — bucket, prefixes, actions and expiry are all checked, and `grantForScope()` is the only constructor so the object checked is the object signed |
| 39 | R24 was ruled while the milestone table and status manifest still said "Billing + entitlements — M6" | **FIXED** — storage admission is **M1.5**; M6 is commerce only |

**Found by the harness, not by a reviewer:** deleting the `assertSatisfies()` call from
`assertProviderConformance()` changed nothing, because the two laws were tested separately and their
composition never was. The mutation battery reported MISSED and the test now asserts the composition.

### THE LAW THIS ROUND EARNED

Three rounds running, a comment described a restriction the code beside it did not implement:

| Where | The comment said | What was granted |
|---|---|---|
| `0003_identity.sql:78` | *"provider_alias … Never matched against."* | the Worker matched on it |
| `0004_worlds.sql` | *"Immutable by convention"* | 0007 granted UPDATE **and** DELETE |
| `0011_verb_matrix.sql` | *"may only record last-seen"* | table-wide UPDATE |

> **A comment is not an enforcement mechanism.** Every restriction a comment claims must be
> expressed as a privilege, a policy or a constraint — or the comment must say
> *"by convention, not enforced"* in those words.

Prose sitting next to a `GRANT` reads as though it were part of it. All three defects were invisible
to review for exactly that reason, and all three were found by someone reading the grant instead of
the sentence.

**The authority ladder, now complete:**

```
RLS                answers  WHOSE row.
verb matrix        answers  WHAT operation.        0011
column authority   answers  WHICH FACTS it may change.   0012
```

### The round-4 review, 2026-08-22 — composition, and a defect in the evidence itself

The theme changed. Every finding this round was a **module law that held, and a composition that
broke it anyway** — which is a better class of problem than the last three rounds, and a worse one
to find by reading.

| # | Defect | Status |
|---|---|---|
| 30 | **The mutation harness's baseline gate was vacuous again.** It made a grep for `ℹ fail [1-9]` the truth condition; Node's TAP reporter prints `# fail 1` for the same failure, which that pattern does not match. A genuinely broken baseline would pass the gate and all vectors would then score CAUGHT against an already-failing suite | **FIXED** — the test process **exit code** is now the truth condition; output parsing is display only and understands both reporter formats |
| 31 | **Two mutation vectors were silently mangled by a delimiter collision.** The vector table used `\|` as its field separator and JS `\|\|` is everywhere, so `IFS='\|' read` truncated any anchor containing a logical-or. The mangled source failed every test and **scored CAUGHT for the wrong reason** | **FIXED** — delimiter is now `:::`, split with literal string expansion rather than `IFS`; a **parse gate** scores unloadable mutations as INVALID instead of crediting them |
| 32 | **The JWKS refresh cap did not exist at the entrypoint.** `index.mjs` constructed a fresh `JwksCache` inside `fetch()`, so every request began with `forcedAt = 0` and R22's cooldown — correct in its own module test — protected nothing | **FIXED** — module-scope cache registry, plus `test/entrypoint.test.mjs`, a suite that drives the real `default.fetch`. The claim is narrowed: this is best-effort in-isolate, **not** a durable global limit |
| 33 | **`authorizeClaims()` could not tell verified claims from a fabricated object.** Its check tested that `sub` and `iss` were strings — so the test named *"claims that were never verified are refused"* passed because `iss` was missing, not because provenance was proven | **FIXED** — `verifyToken()` brands its return in a module-private `WeakSet`; nothing exported can add to it, so even a structural clone is refused |
| 34 | **A naive R2 adapter would widen authority.** Our `object-write` permits upload and read and forbids deletion; the provider's coarse `object-read-write` preset bundles deletion. Mapping one onto the other silently grants more than the control plane decided | **FIXED** — `assertProviderConformance()`: effective authority may never exceed the scope, and an adapter that cannot express a scope exactly must refuse rather than approximate upward |
| 35 | **Entitlement was scheduled behind the thing it authorizes.** M2 issues direct-to-R2 write credentials; quota lived in M6 | **RULED (R24)** — storage admission is authorization and moves ahead of M2; commerce stays at M6 |
| 36 | **The review tarball could not reproduce its own asset gate** — it excluded `amp-nav.js` and the fonts to save ~120 KB, so `check-assets.mjs` run against the extraction reported three missing files | **FIXED** — the artifact now ships them |

### R23 — **RULED by Travis, 2026-08-22**, with the revocation caveat added

Ruled after the round-6 review recommended ratifying it with one sentence added. The added sentence
is the last paragraph below, and it exists because "revoke" means two different things and only one
of them is achievable:

> Once an authorized machine has recovered a WDK or plaintext, later Cloud revocation cannot make
> that machine forget information it already obtained. **Revocation governs future Cloud access; key
> rotation governs future encrypted state. ComputeDriven does not claim retroactive cryptographic
> erasure.**

Saying so in the ruling is the point. A product that lets a customer believe "revoked" means
"unreadable everywhere, retroactively" has sold a guarantee no cryptosystem delivers, and the
discovery would come at the worst possible moment.

**M2 is unblocked.** The remaining M2 prerequisite is M1.5, which this round built.

The ruled text:

> A private world owns a random **World Data Key (WDK)**, used only to encrypt world content. It
> is never derived from content, never a node identity, and never grants execution authority. It is
> stored only wrapped under a separately generated **User Recovery Key**, held client-side;
> ComputeDriven, Pigsty, R2 and Keycloak never see either in plaintext.
>
> Restoring onto machine B requires **two independent admissions**: ComputeDriven authorizes access
> to the *ciphertext*, and the user locally unwraps the WDK. Success transfers **data state only** —
> not A's node key, credentials, sessions or execution grants. B stays unenrolled until M3.
>
> **Keycloak authentication alone is insufficient to decrypt a private world.** If the user loses
> all recovery material the plaintext is unrecoverable, and ComputeDriven says so rather than
> quietly keeping a server-side copy.
>
> Shared-private distribution stays deferred. Convergent encryption stays refused.
>
> Once an authorized machine has recovered a WDK or plaintext, later Cloud revocation cannot make
> that machine forget information it already obtained. Revocation governs future Cloud access; key
> rotation governs future encrypted state. ComputeDriven does not claim retroactive cryptographic
> erasure.

The sentence it buys: **Cloud authorization gets the ciphertext; user recovery authority gets the
plaintext; node authority gets to act.**

The authority stack it leaves, and these stay different forever:

```
Cloud identity + storage admission   →  may obtain CIPHERTEXT
User Recovery Key                    →  may unwrap the WDK
World Data Key                       →  may decrypt world state
Node key                             →  may identify a machine
Execution grant                      →  may cause an effect
```

Never matched against."* — and the Worker matched on it. A rename orphans the binding; a reused alias silently resolves to the previous organization | **FIXED (R20)** — `organizationEntries()` returns `{alias, providerOrgId}`; alias never leaves the selection step |

### What the review got wrong, recorded because the rule is retract out loud

The review's PlanetScale finding was presented as an unexamined $180/yr line item. **It was
examined** — `agents/C-infrastructure.md` §3 already refuses pointing Keycloak at the Hetzner
Postgres, by name and with a reason:

> *"It will look tidy. It puts the auth path — the one thing that must be up for anyone to do
> anything — on the longest wire in the architecture, and re-couples exactly what the split
> decoupled."*

The economic half of the finding stands: that reason is about **latency and coupling**, and the
recorded *cost* justification did compare against the wrong alternative. But the decision was not
unconsidered, and the review implied it was. R9 keeps the ruling and fixes only the rationale.

## DOCTRINE:

- **contradicted** — `CLAUDE.md`, the file injected into every session in this repository, taught the
  Supabase data layer as current architecture for **sixteen days** after Travis abandoned it, with
  working commands. Every session in that window began from a false premise. Fixed in this pass.
- **contradicted** — `RECONCILIATION_LEDGER.md` D2 reported the `STACK_SITEMAP.md` law-count drift as
  **two** occurrences. It is **four**, and `STACK_COMPLETION.md` carries **two more** that D2 did not
  mention at all. The audit undercounted the thing it was auditing.
- **proposed** — that a **revision register is worth keeping as a standing document** rather than
  rebuilt per session, because the failure it catches is silent and cumulative: a ruling is made,
  the documents are not swept, and the next session builds on the pre-ruling state. What would test
  it: check at the next ruling whether anything in this file moved.

### Added by the 2026-08-15 lane-F pass

- **advanced** — the proposal above **passed its own test on the first try.** Every item in the
  "Not checked" list has been checked, by the next session, because the list existed. Three of the
  four found something. The register is doing the job it was proposed for.
- **contradicted** — `AGENTS.md` told every agent that read it to load **11 files that do not
  exist**, and named the wrong backend for WebHost.Systems, and denied a dependency the mix file
  declares. Nobody had audited it. `CLAUDE.md` was found wrong on 2026-08-15 after sixteen days;
  this file had been wrong for months and was found only because a lane brief happened to quote it.
- **contradicted** — the register's own framing looked for the abandoned data layer leaking to the
  public. **It is not leaking.** What is public is a *different* wrong claim — `webhost.systems`
  advertising a Convex backend it does not have — which the search would have missed if `convex`
  had not been added to the grep on a hunch. **A sweep finds what it greps for.** The next one
  should read a page, not scan it.
- **proposed** — that **a derived number must never be typed** is now evidenced three times in this
  one document: the law count (116 vs a derived 118), the sitemap occurrence count (2 reported vs 4
  actual), and the migration count (35 vs 40, from a JSON example in a spec). All three were
  copied from another document rather than re-derived. What would test it: whether the next drift
  is also a copied number, or a genuinely new failure mode.

### Added 2026-08-16, after an outside review

- **contradicted** — the "0.1% of a 100 GB backup" claim (items 16) was **wrong, published, and
  flattering**. 212.70 MB against 100 GB is 0.21%. The measurement underneath it was correct,
  sourced and dated; only the ratio was wrong — which is worse than a bad measurement, because a
  correct measurement with a wrong conclusion attached reads as *more* trustworthy than either
  alone. It survived two internal passes and was caught by a reviewer doing the division.
- **contradicted** — `computedriven.com` asserted **no telemetry** in its hero and *"nothing else
  on the page calls out at load"* in its README while loading fonts from Google on every visit
  (item 17). The page did not have the property it was claiming, and the check that settles it is
  a single line nobody had run.
- **advanced** — the previous entry proposed that the register earns its keep because the failure
  it catches is silent and cumulative. **Both findings above came from outside this tree.** That is
  the register's limit, stated plainly: it catches what a ruling contradicts, and it does not catch
  arithmetic nobody re-ran or a self-description nobody tested. **Extend the next sweep to README
  self-descriptions and to every published ratio**, which are the two shapes it just missed.
```

## 4.7 Prior context a reviewer will want

These are pre-existing files, included because the rulings above are
measured against them.

### `studbook/docs/spec/README.md`

```markdown
# Studbook

**Status: draft spec. No implementation. `spec` rung.**
**Nothing in §7 or §10 has been ruled. Do not build from this yet.**

The data layer for the [&] stack, built on the substrate the stack already owns instead
of on a hosted Postgres it does not.

A studbook is a pedigree register: every animal in it is recorded with its ancestry, and
a record whose parentage cannot be shown is not a record. That is the whole design goal
here. A record in studbook carries where it came from, and a record that cannot show its
provenance is refused rather than stored.

---

## 1. What is decided, and by whom

Decided by Travis, 2026-07-30:

- The shared-Supabase route is **abandoned**. `ampersand-supabase` is archived, not
  failed — the 35 migrations across 11 schemas still apply and the code running against
  them still runs. The route changed, not the verdict on the code.
- The replacement is called **studbook**.
- It lives in **core**, not substrate and not compose. Core is the layer that rests on
  substrate and that compose consumes, and a database is exactly that shape.

Everything from §5 onward is derived from reading the substrate code or from published
prior art, and is marked as such. It is a proposal. §10 lists what has to be ruled
before any of it is built.

## 2. Why the Supabase route was abandoned

Not because it did not work. It worked locally. Three reasons it was the wrong shape for
this stack:

1. **It could not carry a certificate.** Core's job is that the dark factory closes as
   one pass with a certificate at every step. Postgres stores a row. It does not store
   *why the row is that row*, and nothing in the migration layer could refuse a row whose
   provenance did not check out. The stack's central claim — that a divergence is
   refusable rather than silent — stopped at the database boundary.
2. **It was a dependency the stack does not control.** `live_deployed` against a hosted
   instance is partly a claim about somebody else's uptime.
3. **The substrate grew the capability underneath it.** See §5.

## 3. What studbook is

A record store where the identity of a record **is** the hash of its content, and where a
record's ancestry is part of what is hashed.

Three properties, in the order they matter:

- **Content-addressed.** The key is the hash of the canonical bytes. Writing the same
  content twice is one record, not two.
- **Verified on read.** Every read re-derives the id from the bytes and refuses to return
  a record that no longer matches its key. Bit-rot and tampering surface as a named
  refusal, never as plausible-looking bad data.
- **Pedigreed.** A record names its parents by their ids. Because ids are content hashes,
  a lineage cannot be edited after the fact without changing every id downstream of the
  edit.

## 4. Where this sits, and the three questions

substrate → **core** → compose.

Studbook may depend on substrate. It may not depend on any product in compose. Products
in compose may consume it. If studbook reimplements something substrate already proves,
that is a finding, not a shortcut.

The component test applies to core too:

1. **What does it consume?** From substrate: content-addressed durable storage,
   hash-verified reads, atomic write, exact-CAS, closure-verified bundles (§5).
2. **What one service does it offer?** A queryable pedigree register — given a record,
   its ancestry; given two states, what changed between them; given a claim, the evidence
   chain that produced it, with every link re-derivable.
3. **What does it connect to on either side?** Beneath: `TRVM/forge/`. Above: KILN's
   manifest and audit lineage first, then any compose lane that needs provenance it can
   show. It connects to nothing that has a user in it until §10.2 is answered.

## 5. What substrate already provides

Evidence, not assertion — running code with batteries behind it:

| Capability | Where | Guarantee |
|---|---|---|
| Content-addressed object store | `TRVM/forge/wrl_store.py` `_ContentStore` | key IS `sha(bytes)`; put refuses mislabeled content (`WRL_STORE_ID_MISMATCH`) |
| Verified read | `wrl_store.py` `_get_bytes` | re-hashes every read; `WRL_STORE_CORRUPT` on mismatch, `WRL_STORE_MISSING` on absence |
| Durable write | `wrl_store.py` `_atomic_write` | temp → flush+fsync → `os.replace` → dir fsync; a crash leaves a `.tmp-*` stub, never a torn record |
| Idempotent write | `_put_bytes` | same content → same id → same file; reorder- and label-equivalent inputs collapse to one file |
| Mutable named documents | `TRVM/forge/wrl_project.py` | named docs over the immutable substrate |
| Optimistic concurrency | `wrl_project.py` | per-document exact-CAS: `WRL_PROJECT_STALE`, `WRL_PROJECT_EXISTS`, `WRL_PROJECT_MISSING` |
| Verified export/import | `TRVM/forge/wrl_bundle.py` | closure (`WRL_BUNDLE_UNRESOLVED`), identity re-derivation (`WRL_BUNDLE_IDENTITY`), corruption (`WRL_BUNDLE_CORRUPT`) |
| Crash recovery | `RecoveryJournalV1` (v0.6-0) | separate, atomic, non-authoritative checkpoint; never auto-applied on reopen |

That is values, references, per-document transactions, integrity-checked backup and
restore, and a crash journal. A from-scratch storage engine would spend its first two
milestones earning most of this. **Studbook does not rebuild it.**

## 6. What substrate does NOT provide

The honest half. Supabase was not only Postgres — it was PostgREST, Auth and row-level
security. Dropping it drops all four.

1. **No query layer and no index.** `wrl_store.py` says it outright: *"The stores hold NO
   in-memory index."* `ids()` is a `listdir` and a sort. Everything is get-by-id. Any
   access pattern that is not "I already know the hash" has no answer today.
   **This is the largest gap.** §7.3 is a candidate answer to it.
2. **No authentication and no row-level security.** Nothing in substrate has any concept
   of a user, and content addressing is actively *hostile* to access control: if the key
   is the hash of the content, then knowing the content is knowing the key.
   Confidentiality has to come from somewhere else entirely. WebHost.Systems and
   FleetPrompt use Supabase Auth and RLS **today**, so until §10.2 is answered studbook
   is not their replacement.
3. **No network surface.** The stores are library objects over an explicit filesystem
   root. No server, no wire protocol, no pooling.
4. **No cross-record transaction.** CAS is per-document. Two records that must move
   together have no mechanism today.
5. **Keys are tied to the frozen identity ladder.** The stores are keyed by `sem-`,
   `scen-` and `replay-` prefixes. A general record type is new work — and the identity
   spine is **frozen**, so touching it is a ruling to be asked for, never a task to be
   done. See §7.2.

## 7. Proposed design — NOT RULED

### 7.1 The record

A studbook record is canonical bytes plus a declared ancestry, sealed together so that
the ancestry is inside the hash rather than beside it. Sketch, not a schema:

- `content` — canonical bytes, serialized by the same discipline `wrl_canonical.py`
  already uses (sorted keys, exact types, no floats where an int will do).
- `parents` — an ordered list of studbook ids. Order is part of the canonical form,
  because a claim derived from A-then-B is not the claim derived from B-then-A.
- `kind` — what sort of record this is, so a reader can refuse a record it does not
  understand rather than half-read it.

The seal is the existing one: identity is the hash of the canonical bytes, a write of
mismatched content is refused, and every read re-derives. That is `_put_bytes` and
`_get_bytes` behaviour, unchanged.

Two consequences worth stating before they are discovered:

- **A record cannot be written before its parents.** A store that admits a record naming
  an absent parent has stopped being a pedigree register. The refusal already has a
  shape — `wrl_bundle.py` calls it `WRL_BUNDLE_UNRESOLVED`.
- **Editing history is not possible, only forking it.** Changing any ancestor changes
  every id beneath it. This is the property; it is not a limitation to be worked around.

### 7.2 Identity — what studbook must ask for

Studbook needs at least one new key prefix, because §6.5 says the three existing stores
are keyed to the WRL ladder and a general record is not a `sem-`, `scen-` or `replay-`.

**That is a ruling request, not a design decision, and it is listed as §10.5.** This
section exists to make the request precise rather than to pre-empt it:

- one prefix, for the record itself;
- no second rung for ancestry — ancestry is *inside* the record, so it is not a separate
  identity;
- nothing that requires re-deriving an existing `sem-`, `scen-` or `replay-` id.

If the answer is no, studbook lives inside an existing rung or does not exist. Either is
a legitimate outcome and neither is a reason to widen the ladder quietly.

### 7.3 The index problem, and the candidate answer

Gap §6.1 is the one that decides whether studbook is weeks or years. Substrate has
content addressing and no index. A B+tree gives an index and gives up content addressing
as the storage primitive — which is the property the stack's whole claim rests on.

A **prolly tree** (probabilistic B-tree; invented by the Noms team, used as the storage
engine under Dolt) is both. It is a block-oriented ordered search tree whose every node is
named by the hash of its contents — a B-tree that is also a merkle DAG. It gives:

- ordered key access and range scans — the missing index;
- content addressing preserved at every level, so a divergence stays refusable all the way
  down rather than only at the blob boundary;
- structural sharing between versions — a shared subtree is stored once;
- history independence — insertion order does not change the tree, so equal content has
  equal identity, which is the property `_put_bytes` already enforces for blobs;
- **diff proportional to the size of the difference**, by comparing subtree hashes rather
  than walking records.

That last property is not an optimisation for a pedigree register. It is the register:
*what changed between these two states, and can you prove it*, answered by arithmetic
rather than by scanning.

Stated with its costs so this does not become an unexamined enthusiasm: chunk-boundary
selection is a tuning problem, writes are copy-on-write with real write amplification,
point-lookup latency is worse than a tuned B+tree, and the reference implementation
represents years of work. **This is a reading task before it is a build task.**

### 7.4 Surface — studbook adds none in v0

Studbook is a library over substrate. It gets no new language surface until there is
something running to describe.

If a surface is ever proposed, three constraints hold and are checkable today:

- **`~~>` is taken.** It is the WRL route arrow — `wrl_canonical.py:388` emits
  `route %s ~~%s~~> %s`. `~~` is the mailbox operator.
- **`#` opens a comment.** In the bootstrap surface `wrl_ir.py:201` does
  `raw.split("#", 1)[0]`; in WRL Core the comment character is `;` (`wrl_ir.py:423`,
  `:508`, `:522`). So any trailing-`#` form — `query#`, `snapshot#` — lexes as a bare
  token followed by a comment. It cannot parse.
- **`->` is unused.** It appears in no `wrl_*.py`. That makes it available, not chosen.

### 7.5 Names studbook must not reuse

- **Film.** Forge ships Film v0.7: a per-epoch record of world observables, compared
  byte-for-byte in every `binding_run*` battery. If studbook ever grows a replay or
  diagnostics artifact it needs its own name. Two artifacts sharing a load-bearing name
  inside one stack is a defect, not a convenience.
- Any `WRL_*` refusal code already in use. Studbook's refusals get their own namespace so
  a caller can tell which layer refused.

Records studbook owns should be versioned in the shape the tree already uses —
`forge.bundle.v1`, `forge.project.v2`, `forge.recovery.v1`, `forge.runtime_job.v1` — i.e.
`<owner>.<thing>.v<n>`, owned by `studbook`.

## 8. First slice — suggested, not planned

The narrowest useful slice appears to be **KILN's manifest and audit lineage**. It is
provenance-shaped, it has no user in it, it is already in core, and it is already being
written.

Concretely: an ordered, content-addressed store of manifests where each names its parents,
queryable by range, answering "what changed between these two runs" without a scan. That
exercises §7.3 against real data, does not require answering §6.2, and either demonstrates
the diff property or fails to — which is what a first slice is for.

This is a suggestion. §10.4 is the ruling.

> **A second candidate, added 2026-08-15: a publicly published track.** See
> `PUBLISH_PATH.md` at the repo root. The argument is §8's own: a **public** track has no
> user in it either — if every published track is world-readable, §6.2's hostility of
> content addressing to access control does not bite, because a public artifact has no
> confidentiality requirement to violate. It additionally closes a rung that
> `computedriven.com` currently prints as missing (*"a track cannot be published or
> addressed"*), which the KILN slice does not.
>
> Recorded as a candidate for the **same ruling (§10.4)**, not as a replacement for §8.
> Note that it does **not** dodge §10.5 — a track is a recording over an *OS* world, not a
> `sem-` world, so it still needs the prefix question answered. That distinction is the
> plan's risk R9 and it fails quietly; see `PUBLISH_PATH.md` §3.

## 9. Non-goals

- **Not a general-purpose database.** If a product needs joins and ad-hoc queries over
  user data, that is an argument for keeping Postgres for that product, and §6.1 says so
  honestly.
- **Not a SQLite competitor.** No point-lookup parity target, no SQL compatibility
  surface, no page cache, no GPU or NPU tier. A pedigree register does not need any of it,
  and adopting them would make every claim above unprovable for years.
- **Not a new identity rung** without §10.5.
- **Not a reason to migrate anything today.** Nothing moves off Supabase until studbook
  can show it holds the same data with the same guarantees.
- **Not a rewrite of substrate storage.** §5 is consumed, not reimplemented.

## 10. What has to be ruled before implementation starts

These are Travis's, not mine.

1. **What happens to the live data.** `fleet.*` serves KILN and FleetPrompt today, and
   `kag.*` (migrations 010–019) has been orphaned since the BendScript pivot on
   2026-04-27. Archiving the *lane* did not archive the *database*. Studbook does not get
   to pretend that data is not there.
2. **Where confidentiality comes from**, given §6.2. Until this is answered studbook
   cannot host anything with a user in it — which today means it cannot replace what
   WebHost.Systems and FleetPrompt use Supabase for.
3. **Whether studbook is one store or two.** Provenance records want content addressing.
   User accounts want mutability and secrecy. Forcing both into one design is how this
   gets worse than what it replaces. §7.3 resolves the index question only for the
   provenance half.
4. **Scope of the first slice** (§8).
5. **Whether the identity ladder admits a studbook prefix** (§7.2), and if not, what
   studbook is keyed by instead.

## 11. Prior art, and what each one settles

Named so the design is not re-derived from scratch, and so distinctiveness is not
overclaimed.

- **CozoDB** — embedded, transactional, relational-graph, recursive Datalog, with
  per-relation time travel. Settles that embedded + recursive + historical is buildable
  and shipped; anything studbook claims there is not novel.
- **Dolt / Noms** — SQL with a commit graph, branch, merge, cell-wise diff and lineage,
  built on prolly trees. This is the closest existing system to what §7 describes, and it
  is where §7.3 comes from.
- **Feldera / DBSP** — automatic incremental view maintenance for rich query languages
  (VLDB '23 best paper). Settles that "keep derived results correct as the world changes"
  is a solved research problem with an implementation, and is not a reason on its own to
  build a new engine.
- **Datomic** — immutable facts, transaction time, as-of queries. The model studbook's
  record shape is closest to conceptually.
- **SQLite** — the separation of pager, B-tree, WAL and VFS. Worth learning as a set of
  boundaries even though §9 declines to build them.

What none of them have is a record whose identity is derived by the same frozen spine
that seals the rest of this stack, so that a divergence is refusable across the boundary
rather than only inside the database. That is the only distinctiveness studbook should
claim, and it is the one that does not require out-building any of the systems above.
```
